Isaac loved Esau, because he had a taste for wild game, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the open country, exhausted.
Esau said to Jacob, "Let me gulp down some of that red stuff, that red stuff, for I am exhausted." That is why he was called Edom.
Jacob said, "First sell me your birthright."
Esau said, "Look, I am about to die. What good is a birthright to me?"
Jacob said, "Swear to me first." So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.
Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew. He ate and drank, then got up and left. So Esau despised his birthright.
Now there was a famine in the land, besides the earlier famine that had occurred in the days of Abraham, and Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, in Gerar.
The LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt. Live in the land that I tell you about.
Stay as a foreigner in this land, and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will fulfill the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.
I will multiply your offspring like the stars of the sky and give your offspring all these lands, and in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed,
because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes and my laws."

When the men of the place asked about his wife, he said, "She is my sister," for he was afraid to say, "my wife," thinking, "The men of the place might kill me because of Rebekah, for she is beautiful."
When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down through the window and saw Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.
So Abimelech summoned Isaac and said, "So she is your wife! How could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac said to him, "Because I thought I might die because of her."
Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt on us."
So Abimelech commanded all the people, "Whoever touches this man or his wife will surely be put to death."
Isaac sowed seed in that land, and that year he reaped a hundred times what he had sown, for the LORD blessed him.
The man became rich, and he kept growing richer until he was very rich.
He had flocks and herds and many servants, so that the Philistines envied him.
All the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham, the Philistines had stopped up and filled with dirt.
Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you have become much too powerful for us."
So Isaac went away from there, camped in the valley of Gerar and settled there.

Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham and that the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham's death, and he gave them the same names that his father had given them.
Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh water there.
But the herders of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herders, saying, "The water is ours." So he named the well Esek, because they had disputed with him.
Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that one too, so he named it Sitnah.
He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. So he named it Rehoboth, saying, "Now the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land."
From there he went up to Beersheba.

That night the LORD appeared to him and said, "I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your offspring for the sake of my servant Abraham."
So he built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD. He pitched his tent there, and Isaac's servants dug a well there.
Then Abimelech came to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, since you hate me and sent me away from you?"
They said, "We have clearly seen that the LORD has been with you. So we said, 'Let there be an oath between us, between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you,
that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you, and have done you nothing but good, and have sent you away in peace.' You are now blessed by the LORD."
So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank.
They got up early in the morning and swore an oath to one another. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.
That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug. They said to him, "We have found water!"
He named it Shibah. That is why the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
When Esau was 40 years old, he married Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
They made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac was old and his eyes were too weak to see, he called his older son Esau and said to him, "My son." He said to him, "Here I am."
He said, "Look, I am old, and I do not know the day of my death.
Now take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, go out to the open country and hunt game for me.
Then prepare me the tasty food that I love, and bring it to me to eat, so that I may bless you before I die."
Now Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his son Esau. When Esau went out to the open country to hunt game and bring it back,
Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "Look, I heard your father say to your brother Esau,
'Bring me game and prepare me tasty food to eat, so that I may bless you before the LORD before I die.'
Now, my son, listen to me and do what I tell you.
Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats from there, so that I can prepare them as tasty food for your father, the way he loves it.
Then take it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."
But Jacob said to his mother Rebekah, "Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.
Perhaps my father will touch me, and then I will seem to him to be mocking him, and I will bring a curse on myself and not a blessing."
His mother said to him, "Let your curse be on me, my son. Just obey me, and go get them for me."
So he went and got them and brought them to his mother, and his mother prepared tasty food, the way his father loved it.
Then Rebekah took the best clothes of her older son Esau, which she had with her in the house, and put them on her younger son Jacob.
She put the skins of the young goats on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.
Then she put the tasty food and the bread she had made into the hand of her son Jacob.
He went in to his father and said, "My father." He said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?"
Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may bless me."
Isaac said to his son, "How did you find it so quickly, my son?" He said, "Because the LORD your God made it happen for me."
Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near, so that I can touch you, my son, to know whether you are really my son Esau or not."
So Jacob came near to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
He did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau's hands. So he blessed him.
He said, "Are you really my son Esau?" He said, "I am."
Then he said, "Bring it near to me, so that I may eat some of my son's game and bless you." So he brought it to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.
Then his father Isaac said to him, "Please come near and kiss me, my son."
So he came near and kissed him. When Isaac smelled the smell of his clothes, he blessed him and said, "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.
May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth, and plenty of grain and new wine.
May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you."
As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had scarcely gone out from the presence of his father Isaac, his brother Esau came in from his hunting.
He too prepared tasty food and brought it to his father. He said to his father, "Let my father sit up and eat some of his son's game, so that you may bless me."
His father Isaac said to him, "Who are you?" He said, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."
Isaac trembled violently and said, "Who was it, then, who hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you came, and I blessed him. Yes, and he will be blessed!"
When Esau heard his father's words, he cried out with a loud and very bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me, me too, my father!"
But he said, "Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing."
Esau said, "Isn't he rightly named Jacob? He has cheated me these two times. He took my birthright, and look, now he has taken my blessing!" Then he said, "Haven't you kept back a blessing for me?"
Isaac answered Esau, "Look, I have made him lord over you, and I have given him all his brothers as servants, and I have sustained him with grain and new wine. What then can I do for you, my son?"
Esau said to his father, "Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me, me too, my father!" And Esau wept aloud.
Then his father Isaac answered him, "Look, away from the richness of the earth will your dwelling be, and away from the dew of heaven above.
By your sword you will live, and you will serve your brother. But when you grow restless, you will break his yoke from your neck."
Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are near; then I will kill my brother Jacob."
When Rebekah was told the words of her older son Esau, she sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, "Look, your brother Esau is consoling himself with the thought of killing you.
Now, my son, listen to me. Get up and flee to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay with him a while, until your brother's fury subsides,
until your brother's anger turns away from you and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there. Why should I lose you both in one day?"
Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am sick of my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women like these, one of the women of the land, what good will my life be to me?"
So Isaac called Jacob, blessed him and commanded him, "You must not marry one of the Canaanite women.
Get up, go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take a wife from there, from among the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother.
May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you become an assembly of peoples.
May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, so that you may take possession of the land where you are now living as a foreigner, which God gave to Abraham."
So Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.
Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he commanded him, "You must not marry one of the Canaanite women,"
and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram.
Esau saw that the Canaanite women displeased his father Isaac.
So Esau went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael and the sister of Nebaioth, in addition to the wives he had.
Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran.
He came to a certain place and spent the night there, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, put it under his head, and lay down to sleep in that place.
He dreamed, and there was a stairway set up on the earth, with its top reaching to heaven, and there were angels of God going up and down on it.
And there was the LORD, standing above it. He said, "I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. The land on which you are lying I will give to you and to your offspring.

Your offspring will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south. All the families of the earth will be blessed in you and in your offspring.
Look, I am with you and will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."
Then Jacob woke from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it."
He was afraid and said, "How awesome this place is! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."
Jacob got up early in the morning, took the stone that he had put under his head, set it up as a pillar and poured oil on top of it.
He named that place Bethel, though the name of the city was originally Luz.
Then Jacob made a vow, saying, "If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey that I am taking, and give me bread to eat and clothes to wear,
and I return safely to my father's house, then the LORD will be my God,
and this stone that I have set up as a pillar will be God's house, and of everything you give me I will surely give you a tenth."
Jacob set out and went to the land of the people of the east.
He looked, and there in the open country was a well, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it, because the flocks were watered from that well. The stone over the mouth of the well was large.
When all the flocks had gathered there, they would roll the stone off the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they would put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where are you from?" They said, "We are from Haran."
He said to them, "Do you know Laban son of Nahor?" They said, "We know him."
He said to them, "Is he well?" They said, "He is well. And look, here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep."
He said, "Look, it is still broad daylight. It is not time for the livestock to be gathered in. Water the sheep, and go and let them graze."
They said, "We can't, until all the flocks are gathered and the stone is rolled off the mouth of the well. Then we water the sheep."
While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherd.

When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his mother's brother Laban, and the sheep of his mother's brother Laban, he went up, rolled the stone off the mouth of the well, and watered the sheep of his mother's brother Laban.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel, and he wept aloud.
Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's relative and that he was Rebekah's son. She ran and told her father.
As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him. He hugged him and kissed him and brought him to his house, and Jacob told Laban all these things.
Laban said to him, "You really are my own flesh and blood." And Jacob stayed with him for a whole month.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "Should you work for me for nothing just because you are my relative? Tell me what your wages should be."
Now Laban had two daughters. The older one was named Leah, and the younger one was named Rachel.
Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel had a lovely figure and was beautiful to look at.
Jacob loved Rachel, so he said, "I will work for you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel."
Laban said, "It is better for me to give her to you than to give her to another man. Stay with me."
So Jacob worked seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him like only a few days, because he loved her.
Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my time is up, so that I may sleep with her."
So Laban gathered all the people of the place and held a feast.
But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her.
Laban gave his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her servant.
In the morning, there was Leah! Jacob said to Laban, "What have you done to me? Didn't I work for you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?"
Laban said, "It is not done in our place to give the younger daughter in marriage before the firstborn.
Finish this one's week, and we will give you the other one too, in return for working for me another seven years."
Jacob did so. He finished Leah's week, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant.
Jacob slept with Rachel too, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. And he worked for Laban another seven years.
When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, he opened her womb. But Rachel was unable to have children.
Leah became pregnant and gave birth to a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, "The LORD has seen my misery. Surely now my husband will love me."
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a son. She said, "The LORD heard that I was unloved, so he has given me this one too." So she named him Simeon.
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a son. She said, "Now this time my husband will become attached to me, for I have borne him three sons." That is why he was named Levi.
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a son. She said, "This time I will praise the LORD." That is why she named him Judah. Then she stopped having children.
When Rachel saw that she had not borne Jacob any children, she became jealous of her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die!"
Jacob became angry with Rachel and said, "Am I in the place of God, who has kept you from having children?"
She said, "Here is my servant Bilhah. Sleep with her, so that she can give birth on my knees, and I too can have children through her."
So she gave him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah became pregnant and bore Jacob a son.
Then Rachel said, "God has judged in my favor. He has also heard my voice and given me a son." That is why she named him Dan.
Rachel's servant Bilhah became pregnant again and bore Jacob a second son.
Then Rachel said, "I have wrestled mighty wrestlings with my sister, and I have won." So she named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped having children, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, "Good fortune has come!" So she named him Gad.
Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, "How happy I am! For women will call me happy." So she named him Asher.
During the wheat harvest Reuben went out and found some mandrakes in the field, and he brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."

But Leah said to her, "Isn't it enough that you have taken my husband? Will you take my son's mandrakes too?" Rachel said, "All right, he can sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes."
When Jacob came in from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You must sleep with me, for I have paid for you with my son's mandrakes." So he slept with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she became pregnant and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, "God has given me my wages, because I gave my servant to my husband." So she named him Issachar.
Leah became pregnant again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Leah said, "God has given me a good gift. This time my husband will honor me, for I have borne him six sons." So she named him Zebulun.
Afterward she gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.
Then God remembered Rachel. God listened to her and opened her womb.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son, and she said, "God has taken away my disgrace."
She named him Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add another son for me."
After Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Send me away, so that I can go to my own place and my own country.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have worked for you, and let me go. You know how I have worked for you."
But Laban said to him, "Please, if I have found favor with you … I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you."
He went on, "Name your wages, and I will pay them."
Jacob said to him, "You know how I have worked for you, and how your livestock have done in my care.
The little you had before I came has grown into a great amount, and the LORD has blessed you wherever I went. But now, when will I provide for my own household too?"
Laban said, "What shall I give you?" Jacob said, "Don't give me anything. If you will do this one thing for me, I will go back to pasturing and taking care of your flock.
Let me go through your whole flock today and remove from it every speckled or spotted animal, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. They will be my wages.

My honesty will answer for me in the future, when you come to check the wages I have received. Any goat in my possession that is not speckled or spotted, or any lamb that is not dark-colored, will count as stolen."
Laban said, "Good! Let it be as you have said."

But that same day Laban removed the male goats that were streaked or spotted, and all the female goats that were speckled or spotted, every one that had white on it, and every dark-colored lamb, and he put them in the care of his sons.
He put a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob was pasturing the rest of Laban's flock.
Then Jacob took fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees, and he peeled white stripes in them, exposing the white wood of the branches.
He set the branches he had peeled in the troughs, the watering places where the flocks came to drink, right in front of the flocks. And the animals mated when they came to drink.
The flocks mated in front of the branches, and they gave birth to young that were streaked, speckled and spotted.

Jacob separated out the lambs, and he made the flock face the streaked and all the dark-colored animals in Laban's flock. So he made separate flocks for himself and did not put them with Laban's flock.
Whenever the stronger animals were mating, Jacob would put the branches in the troughs in front of the animals, so that they would mate beside the branches.
But when the animals were weak, he would not put them there. So the weak ones went to Laban, and the strong ones to Jacob.
So the man became extremely rich. He had large flocks, female and male servants, camels and donkeys.
Jacob heard what Laban's sons were saying: "Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father. He has made all this wealth from what belonged to our father."
And Jacob saw from Laban's face that he was not as friendly toward him as before.
Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Go back to the land of your fathers and to your relatives, and I will be with you."
So Jacob sent for Rachel and Leah and called them out to the field where his flock was.
He said to them, "I can see from your father's face that he is not as friendly toward me as before. But the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have worked for your father with all my strength.
Yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times. But God did not let him harm me.

If he said, 'The speckled ones will be your wages,' then the whole flock gave birth to speckled young. And if he said, 'The streaked ones will be your wages,' then the whole flock gave birth to streaked young.
So God has taken away your father's livestock and given them to me.
Once, in the season when the flock was mating, I looked up and saw in a dream that the male goats mating with the flock were streaked, speckled and mottled.
The angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob!' And I said, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Look up and see: all the male goats mating with the flock are streaked, speckled and mottled. For I have seen everything that Laban has been doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a standing stone and made a vow to me. Now get up, leave this land, and go back to the land of your birth.'"
Rachel and Leah answered him, "Do we still have any share or inheritance in our father's house?
Doesn't he regard us as foreigners? For he has sold us, and he has completely used up the money paid for us.
All the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and to our children. So now do whatever God has told you."
Then Jacob got up and put his children and his wives on the camels.
He drove all his livestock ahead of him, with all the property he had acquired, the livestock he owned, which he had acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
Now Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole the household gods that belonged to her father.
And Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away.
So he ran away with everything he had. He set out, crossed the River, and headed for the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day Laban was told that Jacob had run away.
He took his relatives with him and pursued Jacob for seven days, and he caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream at night and said to him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad."
Laban caught up with Jacob. Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban and his relatives camped in the hill country of Gilead.
Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done? You have deceived me and carried off my daughters like prisoners of war!
Why did you run away secretly and deceive me, and not tell me? I would have sent you off with celebration and songs, with tambourines and harps.
You did not even let me kiss my grandchildren and my daughters goodbye. You have acted foolishly.
I have the power to do you harm. But last night the God of your father said to me, 'Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.'
Now you have gone away because you longed so much for your father's house. But why did you steal my gods?"
Jacob answered Laban, "I was afraid, because I thought you would take your daughters away from me by force.
But anyone you find with your gods will not live. In front of our relatives, point out anything of yours that is with me, and take it." Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.
So Laban went into Jacob's tent, into Leah's tent, and into the tent of the two servants, but he did not find them. He came out of Leah's tent and went into Rachel's tent.
Now Rachel had taken the household gods, put them in the camel's saddle, and sat on them. Laban felt through the whole tent but did not find them.
She said to her father, "Don't be angry, my lord, that I cannot get up in front of you, for I am having my period." He searched, but he did not find the household gods.
Then Jacob became angry and quarreled with Laban. Jacob said to Laban, "What is my crime? What is my sin, that you have chased after me so hotly?
You have felt through all my things. What have you found of all your household things? Put it here in front of my relatives and your relatives, and let them decide between the two of us.
I have been with you these twenty years. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flock.
I did not bring you any animal torn by wild beasts; I bore the loss myself. You demanded payment from me for anything stolen, whether by day or by night.
This is how I was: by day the heat consumed me, and by night the cold, and sleep fled from my eyes.
These twenty years I have been in your household. I worked for you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been on my side, you would surely have sent me away empty-handed by now. But God has seen my misery and the hard work of my hands, and last night he gave his verdict."

Laban answered Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and everything you see is mine. But what can I do today about these daughters of mine, or about the children they have borne?
So come, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between me and you."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a standing stone.
Jacob said to his relatives, "Gather stones." So they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there beside the heap.
Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.
Laban said, "This heap is a witness between me and you today." That is why it was named Galeed.
It was also called Mizpah, because he said, "May the LORD keep watch between me and you when we are out of each other's sight.
If you mistreat my daughters, or if you take other wives besides my daughters, even though no one is with us, see: God is a witness between me and you."
Laban also said to Jacob, "Here is this heap, and here is the standing stone that I have set up between me and you.
This heap is a witness, and the standing stone is a witness, that I will not go past this heap to you, and you will not go past this heap and this standing stone to me, to do harm.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat a meal. They ate the meal and spent the night on the mountain.
Early in the morning Laban got up, kissed his grandchildren and his daughters, and blessed them. Then Laban left and went back home.
Jacob also went on his way, and angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, "This is God's camp!" So he named that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom.
He instructed them, "This is what you are to say to my lord Esau: 'Your servant Jacob says this: I have been living with Laban as a foreigner, and I have stayed there until now.
I have oxen and donkeys, flocks, and male and female servants. I am sending this message to my lord in the hope of finding favor with you.'"
The messengers came back to Jacob and said, "We went to your brother Esau. He is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him."
Jacob was very afraid and distressed. He divided the people who were with him, and the flocks, the cattle and the camels, into two camps.
He thought, "If Esau comes to one camp and attacks it, the camp that is left can escape."
Then Jacob said, "God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, LORD, you who said to me, 'Go back to your country and your relatives, and I will do you good,'
I am not worthy of all the faithful love and all the faithfulness you have shown your servant. For I crossed this Jordan with only my staff, and now I have become two camps.
Please rescue me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, for I am afraid of him. He may come and attack me, and the mothers with the children.
But you said, 'I will certainly do you good and make your descendants like the sand of the sea, which is too much to be counted.'"
He spent that night there. Then from what he had with him he chose a gift for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
He put each herd by itself in the care of his servants, and he said to his servants, "Go on ahead of me, and keep some space between one herd and the next."
He instructed the first one, "When my brother Esau meets you and asks you, 'Whose servant are you? Where are you going? And whose animals are these in front of you?'
then say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift sent to my lord Esau. And look, he himself is right behind us.'"
He gave the same instructions to the second, to the third, and to all who were following the herds: "Say this same thing to Esau when you find him.

And say, 'Look, your servant Jacob himself is right behind us.'" For he thought, "I will win him over with the gift that is going ahead of me. Afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will accept me."
So the gift went on ahead of him, while he himself spent that night in the camp.
That night he got up and took his two wives, his two servants and his eleven children, and he crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them across the stream, and he sent across everything he had.
So Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he touched the socket of his hip, and Jacob's hip was wrenched as he wrestled with him.
Then the man said, "Let me go, for dawn is breaking." But Jacob said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
He said to him, "What is your name?" He said, "Jacob."
He said, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, for you have struggled with God and with human beings, and you have won."
Jacob asked him, "Please tell me your name." But he said, "Why do you ask my name?" And he blessed him there.
So Jacob named the place Peniel, "because I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been spared."
The sun rose on him as he passed Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip.
That is why to this day the Israelites do not eat the sinew of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because he touched the socket of Jacob's hip at the sinew of the thigh.
Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming, and four hundred men with him. So he divided the children among Leah, Rachel and the two servants.
He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children behind them, and Rachel and Joseph at the back.
He himself went on ahead of them, and he bowed down to the ground seven times until he came near his brother.
But Esau ran to meet him and hugged him. He threw his arms around his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
When Esau looked up and saw the women and the children, he said, "Who are these with you?" Jacob said, "The children God has graciously given your servant."
Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed down.
Leah also came near with her children, and they bowed down. Last of all Joseph and Rachel came near, and they bowed down.
Esau said, "What do you mean by all this company that I met?" Jacob said, "To find favor with my lord."
But Esau said, "I have plenty, my brother. Keep what you have for yourself."
Jacob said, "No, please! If I have found favor with you, accept my gift from my hand. For seeing your face is like seeing the face of God, now that you have received me kindly.
Please accept my blessing that has been brought to you, because God has been gracious to me, and I have everything I need." And he kept urging him, and Esau accepted it.
Then Esau said, "Let us set out and be on our way. I will go alongside you."

But Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are frail, and that the flocks and cattle that are nursing their young are in my care. If they are driven hard for even one day, all the flocks will die.
Please let my lord go on ahead of his servant. I will move along slowly, at the pace of the livestock in front of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir."
Esau said, "Then let me leave with you some of the people who are with me." But Jacob said, "Why do that? Just let me find favor with my lord."
So that day Esau went back on his way to Seir.
But Jacob traveled on to Succoth. He built a house for himself there and made shelters for his livestock. That is why the place is called Succoth.
After Jacob came from Paddan-aram, he arrived safely at the town of Shechem in the land of Canaan, and he camped in front of the town.
He bought the piece of land where he had pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, for a hundred qesitah.
There he set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.
Now Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the women of the land.
Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the ruler of the region, saw her. He took her, lay with her, and violated her.
But he became deeply attached to Dinah, Jacob's daughter. He loved the young woman and spoke tenderly to her.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, "Get me this girl as my wife."
Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah. But his sons were out in the field with his livestock, so Jacob kept quiet until they came home.
Then Shechem's father Hamor went out to Jacob to speak with him.

Jacob's sons came in from the field when they heard. The men were deeply hurt and very angry, because Shechem had done a disgraceful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter. Such a thing should not be done.
But Hamor spoke with them and said, "My son Shechem has set his heart on your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife.
Intermarry with us. Give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves.
You can live with us, and the land will be open to you. Live in it, trade in it, and acquire property in it."
Then Shechem said to Dinah's father and brothers, "Let me find favor with you, and I will give you whatever you ask of me.
Ask me for as great a bride-price and gift as you like, and I will give whatever you tell me. Only give me the young woman as my wife."
Jacob's sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor with deceit when they spoke, because he had defiled their sister Dinah.
They said to them, "We cannot do this. We cannot give our sister to a man who is uncircumcised, for that would be a disgrace to us.
We will agree to your request on only one condition: that you become like us by having every male among you circumcised.
Then we will give our daughters to you, and we will take your daughters for ourselves. We will live with you and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, we will take our daughter and go."
Their proposal pleased Hamor and Hamor's son Shechem.
The young man lost no time in doing it, because he was delighted with Jacob's daughter. He was the most honored member of his father's whole household.
So Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their town and spoke to the men of their town.

"These men are friendly toward us," they said. "Let them live in the land and trade in it. Look, the land has plenty of room for them. We can take their daughters as our wives, and we can give them our daughters.
But the men will agree to live with us and become one people on only one condition: that every male among us be circumcised, as they are circumcised.
Won't their livestock, their property and all their animals become ours? Only let us agree to their terms, and they will live with us."
All the men who went out of the gate of his town listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his town.
On the third day, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, each took his sword. They came against the town, which felt secure, and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, took Dinah from Shechem's house, and left.
Jacob's sons came upon the dead and plundered the town, because the people had defiled their sister.
They took their flocks, their cattle and their donkeys, and whatever was in the town and in the fields.
They carried off all their wealth, and they took captive all their little children and their wives. They plundered everything in the houses.

Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me by making me hateful to the people who live in the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I have only a few men. If they gather together against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed."
But they said, "Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?"
God said to Jacob, "Get up, go up to Bethel, and live there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were running away from your brother Esau."
So Jacob said to his household and to everyone who was with him, "Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you. Purify yourselves, and change your clothes.
Then let us get up and go up to Bethel. I will make an altar there to the God who answered me when I was in distress and who has been with me wherever I have gone."
So they gave Jacob all the foreign gods they had, and the rings that were in their ears, and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.
As they set out, a terror from God fell on the towns all around them, so that no one pursued Jacob's sons.
Jacob and all the people who were with him came to Luz (that is, Bethel) in the land of Canaan.
There he built an altar, and he called the place El-bethel, because it was there that God had revealed himself to him when he was running away from his brother.
Rebekah's nurse Deborah died, and she was buried under the oak below Bethel. So it was named Allon-bacuth.
God appeared to Jacob again after he came from Paddan-aram, and he blessed him.
God said to him, "Your name is Jacob. You will no longer be called Jacob; your name will be Israel." So he named him Israel.
God also said to him, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation, and a whole company of nations, will come from you, and kings will be among your descendants.
The land I gave to Abraham and to Isaac I will give to you, and I will give the land to your descendants after you."
Then God went up from him at the place where he had spoken with him.
Jacob set up a standing stone at the place where God had spoken with him, a marker of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it.
Jacob named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
Then they set out from Bethel. While they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor, and her labor was hard.
While she was in the hardest part of her labor, the midwife said to her, "Don't be afraid, for you have another son."
As her life was slipping away, for she was dying, she named him Ben-oni. But his father called him Benjamin.
So Rachel died, and she was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).
Jacob set up a standing stone over her grave. It is the marker of Rachel's grave to this day.
Israel set out again and pitched his tent beyond Migdal-eder.
While Israel was living in that region, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard about it. Jacob had twelve sons.
The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Rachel's servant Bilhah: Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Leah's servant Zilpah: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had lived as foreigners.
Then Isaac breathed his last and died, and he was gathered to his people, old and full of years. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom).
Esau took his wives from the women of Canaan: Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon the Hivite,
and Basemath daughter of Ishmael, the sister of Nebaioth.
Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau, and Basemath bore Reuel.
Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These were the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters, all the people of his household, his livestock, all his animals, and all the property he had acquired in the land of Canaan, and he went to another land, away from his brother Jacob.
For their possessions were too great for them to live together. The land where they were living as foreigners could not support them because of their livestock.
So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
These are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz, the son of Esau's wife Adah, and Reuel, the son of Esau's wife Basemath.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz.
Timna was a concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. These were the descendants of Esau's wife Adah.
These were the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the descendants of Esau's wife Basemath.
These were the sons of Esau's wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon: she bore Esau Jeush, Jalam and Korah.
These are the chiefs among Esau's descendants. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn: chief Teman, chief Omar, chief Zepho, chief Kenaz,
chief Korah, chief Gatam and chief Amalek. These are the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom. They were the descendants of Adah.

These are the sons of Esau's son Reuel: chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah and chief Mizzah. These are the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom. They were the descendants of Esau's wife Basemath.
These are the sons of Esau's wife Oholibamah: chief Jeush, chief Jalam and chief Korah. These are the chiefs descended from Esau's wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
These were the sons of Esau, and these were their chiefs. That is Edom.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who were living in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam, and Lotan's sister was Timna.
These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam.
These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness while he was pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
These are the children of Anah: Dishon, and Oholibamah daughter of Anah.
These are the sons of Dishan: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran.
These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan and Akan.
These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
These are the chiefs of the Horites: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, chief Anah,
chief Dishon, chief Ezer and chief Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, chief by chief, in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites:
Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah became king in his place.
When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites became king in his place.
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, became king in his place. The name of his city was Avith.
When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became king in his place.
When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the River became king in his place.
When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor became king in his place.
When Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, Hadar became king in his place. The name of his city was Pau, and his wife's name was Mehetabel daughter of Matred, daughter of Me-zahab.
These are the names of the chiefs descended from Esau, by their clans and their places, name by name: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth,
chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon,
chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar,
chief Magdiel and chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, according to their settlements in the land they possessed. This is Esau, the father of Edom.
Jacob settled in the land where his father had lived as a foreigner, the land of Canaan.

These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, a young man of seventeen, was tending the flock with his brothers. He was a helper to the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought their father a bad report about them.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his other sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a special robe.
When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him.
Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him even more.
He said to them, "Please listen to this dream I had.
We were binding sheaves of grain out in the field. Then my sheaf got up and stood upright, and your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf."
His brothers said to him, "Are you really going to be king over us? Are you really going to rule over us?" And they hated him even more because of his dreams and what he said.
Then he had another dream and told it to his brothers. He said, "Listen, I have had another dream. The sun, the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me."

When he told it to his father and his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, "What is this dream you have had? Are your mother and I and your brothers really going to come and bow down to the ground before you?"
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
His brothers went to pasture their father's flock near Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, "Your brothers are pasturing the flock at Shechem, aren't they? Come, I am going to send you to them." He said to him, "Here I am."
So he said to him, "Go and see how your brothers are doing and how the flock is doing, and bring word back to me." So he sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and Joseph came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering in the countryside, and the man asked him, "What are you looking for?"
He said, "I am looking for my brothers. Please tell me where they are pasturing the flock."
The man said, "They have moved on from here, for I heard them say, 'Let's go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
They saw him in the distance, and before he reached them, they plotted to kill him.
They said to one another, "Look, here comes that dreamer!
Come on now, let's kill him and throw him into one of the pits. We will say that a wild animal ate him. Then we will see what becomes of his dreams."
But when Reuben heard this, he rescued him from their hands. He said, "Let's not take his life."

Reuben said to them, "Don't shed blood. Throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but don't lay a hand on him." He said this so that he could rescue him from their hands and bring him back to his father.
So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the special robe he was wearing.
They took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.

Then they sat down to eat a meal. When they looked up, they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm and myrrh, and they were on their way down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, "What will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood?
Come, let's sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay our hands on him. After all, he is our brother, our own flesh." His brothers agreed.
Some Midianite traders passed by, and they pulled Joseph up out of the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. And they took Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben returned to the pit, Joseph was not in the pit! He tore his clothes.
He went back to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone! And I, where can I go?"
Then they took Joseph's robe, slaughtered a male goat, and dipped the robe in the blood.
They sent the special robe and had it brought to their father, and they said, "We found this. Please look at it closely. Is it your son's robe or not?"
He recognized it and said, "It is my son's robe! A wild animal has eaten him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!"
Then Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned for his son for many days.
All his sons and all his daughters came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, "No, I will go down to my son in Sheol, mourning." And his father wept for him.
Meanwhile the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh's officials, the captain of the guard.
About that time Judah left his brothers and went down to stay with a man of Adullam named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He married her and slept with her.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son, and he named him Er.
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a son, and she named him Onan.
She gave birth to yet another son and named him Shelah. He was at Chezib when she gave birth to him.
Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, "Sleep with your brother's wife and do your duty to her as her husband's brother. Raise up children for your brother."
But Onan knew that the children would not be his. So whenever he slept with his brother's wife, he spilled his semen on the ground, so that he would not give children to his brother.
What he did was evil in the sight of the LORD, so he put him to death too.

Then Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, "Live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up." For he thought, "He too may die like his brothers." So Tamar went and lived in her father's house.
A long time passed, and Shua's daughter, Judah's wife, died. When Judah had been comforted, he went up to Timnah to the men who were shearing his sheep, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep."

So she took off her widow's clothes, covered herself with a veil, and wrapped herself up. Then she sat down at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as his wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
He turned aside to her by the road and said, "Come, let me sleep with you," for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, "What will you give me for sleeping with me?"
He said, "I will send you a young goat from the flock." She said, "Only if you give me a pledge until you send it."
He said, "What pledge shall I give you?" She said, "Your seal and its cord, and the staff in your hand." So he gave them to her and slept with her, and she became pregnant by him.
Then she got up and left. She took off her veil and put on her widow's clothes again.
Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to get the pledge back from the woman, but he did not find her.
He asked the men of that place, "Where is the shrine prostitute who was by the road at Enaim?" They said, "There has been no shrine prostitute here."
So he went back to Judah and said, "I did not find her. Also, the men of the place said, 'There has been no shrine prostitute here.'"
Judah said, "Let her keep the things, or we will become a laughingstock. After all, I did send this young goat, but you could not find her."

About three months later Judah was told, "Your daughter-in-law Tamar has acted as a prostitute, and now she is pregnant as a result of her prostitution." Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned!"

As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law: "I am pregnant by the man who owns these things." And she said, "Please look closely. Whose are these, the seal, the cord and the staff?"
Judah recognized them and said, "She is more in the right than I am, because I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not sleep with her again.
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twins in her womb.
While she was giving birth, one of them put out a hand. The midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it on his hand, saying, "This one came out first."
But as he drew back his hand, his brother came out. She said, "What a breach you have made for yourself!" So he was named Perez.
Afterward his brother came out, with the scarlet thread on his hand, and he was named Zerah.
Now Joseph had been taken down to Egypt. Potiphar, an Egyptian, one of Pharaoh's officials and the captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had taken him down there.
The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man. He lived in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD made everything he did succeed.
Joseph found favor with him and became his personal attendant. Potiphar put him in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned.

From the time he put him in charge of his household and of everything he owned, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's household because of Joseph. The LORD's blessing was on everything he owned, in the house and in the fields.
So he left everything he owned in Joseph's care, and with Joseph there he did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate. Now Joseph was well built and handsome.
Some time later his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, "Sleep with me."
But he refused. He said to his master's wife, "Look, with me here, my master does not concern himself with anything in the house, and he has entrusted me with everything he owns.
No one in this house is greater than I am. He has kept nothing back from me except you, because you are his wife. How then could I do this great evil and sin against God?"
Though she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her and lie beside her or be with her.
One day he went into the house to do his work, and none of the men of the household were there in the house.
She grabbed him by his garment and said, "Sleep with me!" But he left his garment in her hand and ran out of the house.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and run outside,
she called the men of her household and said to them, "Look, he has brought us a Hebrew man to make fools of us. He came to me to sleep with me, and I screamed.
When he heard me raise my voice and scream, he left his garment beside me and ran outside."
She kept his garment beside her until his master came home.
Then she told him the same story: "The Hebrew slave you brought us came to me to make a fool of me.
But when I raised my voice and screamed, he left his garment beside me and ran outside."
When his master heard what his wife told him, "This is what your slave did to me," he was furious.
Joseph's master took him and put him in the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were held. And he remained there in the prison.
But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him faithful love. He gave him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.
The warden put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners in the prison, and he was responsible for everything that was done there.
The warden paid no attention to anything in Joseph's care, because the LORD was with him, and the LORD made whatever he did succeed.
Some time later, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt offended their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was angry with his two officials, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker,
and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was being held.
The captain of the guard assigned Joseph to them, and he attended them. They were in custody for some time.
One night both of them, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were being held in the prison, had a dream. Each had his own dream, and each dream had its own meaning.
When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were upset.
So he asked Pharaoh's officials who were in custody with him in his master's house, "Why do you look so troubled today?"
They said to him, "We have each had a dream, and there is no one to interpret it." Joseph said to them, "Don't interpretations belong to God? Please tell me your dreams."
So the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream. He said to him, "In my dream there was a vine in front of me.
On the vine were three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms came out, and its clusters ripened into grapes.
Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. I took the grapes, squeezed them into Pharaoh's cup, and put the cup in Pharaoh's hand."
Joseph said to him, "This is what it means: the three branches are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your position. You will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand, just as you used to do when you were his cupbearer.
But remember me when things go well for you. Please show me faithful love: mention me to Pharaoh, and get me out of this place.
For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing to deserve being put in this dungeon."
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, "I too had a dream. There were three baskets of white bread on my head.
In the top basket there were all kinds of baked food for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating it out of the basket on my head."
Joseph answered, "This is what it means: the three baskets are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head from you and hang you on a tree, and the birds will eat the flesh off you."
The third day was Pharaoh's birthday, and he gave a feast for all his servants. In the presence of his servants he lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker.
He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he put the cup in Pharaoh's hand again.
But he hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had interpreted to them.
Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph; he forgot him.
Two full years later, Pharaoh had a dream. He was standing by the Nile.
Seven cows came up out of the Nile, sleek and fat, and they grazed among the reeds.
After them seven other cows came up out of the Nile, ugly and thin, and they stood beside the other cows on the bank of the Nile.
The ugly, thin cows ate up the seven sleek, fat cows. Then Pharaoh woke up.
He fell asleep again and had a second dream. Seven heads of grain, plump and good, were growing on a single stalk.
After them seven other heads of grain sprouted, thin and scorched by the east wind.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven plump, full heads. Then Pharaoh woke up, and it had been a dream.
In the morning his spirit was troubled, so he sent for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dream, but there was no one who could interpret them for Pharaoh.
Then the chief cupbearer spoke to Pharaoh. "Today I must mention my offenses," he said.
"Pharaoh was angry with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker in custody in the house of the captain of the guard.
One night we both had dreams, he and I, and each dream had its own meaning.
A young Hebrew man was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he interpreted them for us, giving each of us the meaning of his own dream.
And it turned out exactly as he interpreted it to us: I was restored to my position, and the baker was hanged."
So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they quickly brought him out of the dungeon. He shaved, changed his clothes, and came in to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have had a dream, and no one can interpret it. But I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream, you can interpret it."
Joseph answered Pharaoh, "It is not in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer for his good."
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile.
Seven cows came up out of the Nile, fat and sleek, and they grazed among the reeds.
After them seven other cows came up, scrawny, very ugly and thin. I have never seen such ugly cows in all the land of Egypt.
The thin, ugly cows ate up the first seven fat cows.
But when they had eaten them, no one could tell that they had eaten them; they looked just as ugly as before. Then I woke up.
In my dream I also saw seven heads of grain, full and good, growing on a single stalk.
After them seven other heads of grain sprouted, withered, thin and scorched by the east wind.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven good heads. I told this to the magicians, but no one could explain it to me."
Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Pharaoh's dreams are one and the same. God has told Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. It is one dream.
The seven thin, ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and so are the seven empty heads of grain scorched by the east wind. They will be seven years of famine.
It is just as I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
Seven years of great plenty are coming throughout the land of Egypt.
But after them will come seven years of famine. All the plenty in the land of Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will exhaust the land.
The plenty in the land will not be remembered because of the famine that follows, for it will be very severe.
The dream was given to Pharaoh twice because the matter has been firmly decided by God, and God will soon make it happen.
So now let Pharaoh look for a man who is discerning and wise and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh act and appoint overseers over the land, and let him take a fifth of the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven years of plenty.
Let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming, and store up grain under Pharaoh's authority, to be kept as food in the cities.
This food will be a reserve for the land for the seven years of famine that will come on the land of Egypt, so that the land will not be destroyed by the famine."
The proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants.
So Pharaoh said to his servants, "Can we find anyone like this, a man in whom is the spirit of God?"
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has made all this known to you, there is no one as discerning and wise as you.
You will be in charge of my household, and all my people will submit to your orders. Only in the matter of the throne will I be greater than you."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Look, I have put you in charge of the whole land of Egypt."
Then Pharaoh took his signet ring off his hand and put it on Joseph's hand. He dressed him in robes of fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck.
He had him ride in the chariot of his second-in-command, and they shouted before him, "Abrek!" So he put him in charge of the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, but without your consent no one will lift a hand or foot in all the land of Egypt."
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and he gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, as his wife. And Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. Joseph went out from Pharaoh's presence and traveled throughout the land of Egypt.
During the seven years of plenty the land produced abundant crops.
Joseph gathered all the food of the seven years that came in the land of Egypt, and he stored the food in the cities. In each city he stored the food from the fields around it.
Joseph stored up grain in great quantities, like the sand of the sea. There was so much that he stopped measuring it, because it was beyond measure.
Before the years of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph, whom Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore to him.
Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh, "because God has made me forget all my trouble and all my father's household."
He named the second Ephraim, "because God has made me fruitful in the land of my suffering."
The seven years of plenty in the land of Egypt came to an end,
and the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all the other lands, but in the whole land of Egypt there was food.
When the whole land of Egypt began to go hungry, the people cried out to Pharaoh for food. Pharaoh told all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph, and do whatever he tells you."
The famine spread over the whole face of the earth. Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, for the famine was severe in the land of Egypt.
People from all over the world came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was severe all over the world.
When Jacob learned that there was grain in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why do you keep looking at one another?"
He said, "I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die."
So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Joseph's brother Benjamin with his brothers, for he thought, "Something terrible might happen to him."
So Israel's sons came to buy grain among the others who were coming, for the famine was in the land of Canaan.
Now Joseph was the governor of the land; he was the one who sold grain to all the people of the land. Joseph's brothers came and bowed down to him with their faces to the ground.

When Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he acted like a stranger to them and spoke harshly to them. "Where have you come from?" he asked. They said, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food."
Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them, and he said to them, "You are spies! You have come to see where the land is unprotected."
They said to him, "No, my lord. Your servants have come to buy food.
We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants are not spies."
But he said to them, "No, you have come to see where the land is unprotected."
They said, "We, your servants, were twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is now with our father, and one is no more."
Joseph said to them, "It is just as I told you: you are spies!
This is how you will be tested: as surely as Pharaoh lives, you will not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here.

Send one of you to get your brother, while the rest of you are kept in prison. Then your words will be tested to see whether you are telling the truth. If not, then as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!"
And he put them all in custody for three days.
On the third day Joseph said to them, "Do this and you will live, for I fear God.
If you are honest men, let one of your brothers stay in prison where you are being held, while the rest of you go and take grain back for your starving households.
Then bring your youngest brother to me, so that your words will be proved true and you will not die." And they agreed to do so.
They said to one another, "We are truly guilty because of our brother. We saw how distressed he was when he begged us for mercy, but we would not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us."
Reuben answered them, "Didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen. Now we must answer for his blood."
They did not know that Joseph understood them, for he spoke to them through an interpreter.
He turned away from them and wept. Then he came back and spoke to them. He took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.
Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, to put each man's money back in his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. And this was done for them.
They loaded their grain on their donkeys and left.
At the place where they stopped for the night, one of them opened his sack to give his donkey some feed, and he saw his money there in the mouth of his sack.
He said to his brothers, "My money has been returned! Here it is in my sack!" Their hearts sank. Trembling, they turned to one another and said, "What is this that God has done to us?"
When they came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, they told him everything that had happened to them. They said,
"The man who is lord of the land spoke harshly to us and treated us as if we were spying on the land.
But we said to him, 'We are honest men. We are not spies.
We were twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no more, and the youngest is now with our father in the land of Canaan.'
Then the man who is lord of the land said to us, 'This is how I will know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, take grain for your starving households, and go.
Bring your youngest brother to me. Then I will know that you are not spies but honest men. I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.'"
As they were emptying their sacks, there in each man's sack was his bag of money! When they and their father saw their bags of money, they were afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, "You have robbed me of my children. Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin. Everything is against me!"
Then Reuben said to his father, "You may put my two sons to death if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my care, and I will bring him back to you."

But Jacob said, "My son will not go down with you. His brother is dead, and he alone is left. If anything terrible happens to him on the journey you are taking, you will bring my gray head down to Sheol in sorrow."
The famine was still severe in the land.
When they had eaten up the grain they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Go back and buy us a little food."
But Judah said to him, "The man solemnly warned us, 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'
If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy food for you.
But if you will not send him, we will not go down, because the man said to us, 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'"
Israel said, "Why did you bring this trouble on me by telling the man you had another brother?"

They said, "The man asked us all about ourselves and our family: 'Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?' We just answered his questions. How could we know that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?"
Then Judah said to his father Israel, "Send the boy with me, and we will get up and go, so that we may live and not die, we and you and our little children.
I myself will guarantee his safety; you can hold me responsible for him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, I will bear the blame before you all my life.
If we had not delayed, we could have gone there and back twice by now."

Then their father Israel said to them, "If it must be so, then do this: take some of the best products of the land in your bags and take them down to the man as a gift: a little balm and a little honey, spices and myrrh, pistachio nuts and almonds.
Take double the money with you, and take back with you the money that was returned in the mouths of your sacks. Perhaps it was a mistake.
Take your brother too, and get up and go back to the man.
May God Almighty make the man show you mercy, so that he will let your other brother and Benjamin come back with you. As for me, if I am to lose my children, I lose them."
So the men took the gift, and they took double the money with them, and Benjamin. They got up and went down to Egypt, and they stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the man in charge of his house, "Take these men into the house. Slaughter an animal and prepare a meal, for the men will eat with me at noon."
The man did as Joseph said, and he took the men into Joseph's house.

The men were afraid because they were taken to Joseph's house. They thought, "We have been brought here because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time. He wants to attack us and overpower us, and take us as slaves, along with our donkeys."
So they went up to the man in charge of Joseph's house and spoke to him at the entrance of the house.
They said, "Please, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food.

But when we came to the place where we stopped for the night and opened our sacks, there was each man's money in the mouth of his sack, our money in its full weight. So we have brought it back with us.
We have also brought down other money with us to buy food. We don't know who put our money in our sacks."
He said, "Peace to you! Don't be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, has put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your money." Then he brought Simeon out to them.
The man took the men into Joseph's house and gave them water, and they washed their feet. He also gave feed to their donkeys.
They got the gift ready for Joseph's arrival at noon, for they had heard that they were to eat a meal there.
When Joseph came home, they brought the gift they had with them into the house to him, and they bowed down to the ground before him.
He asked how they were, and said, "How is your elderly father you told me about? Is he still alive?"
They said, "Your servant our father is well; he is still alive." And they bowed low and paid him honor.
When he looked up and saw his brother Benjamin, his own mother's son, he said, "Is this your youngest brother, whom you told me about?" And he said, "May God be gracious to you, my son."
Joseph hurried out, because he was deeply moved at the sight of his brother, and he was about to weep. He went into a private room and wept there.
Then he washed his face and came out. Controlling himself, he said, "Serve the meal."

They served him by himself, the brothers by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because the Egyptians could not eat a meal with the Hebrews, for that is detestable to the Egyptians.
The brothers were seated before him from the firstborn, as his birthright gave him, to the youngest, as his youth gave him, and the men looked at one another in amazement.
Portions were brought to them from Joseph's table, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. So they drank with him and drank freely.
Then Joseph instructed the man in charge of his house, "Fill the men's sacks with as much food as they can carry, and put each man's money in the mouth of his sack.
Put my cup, the silver cup, in the mouth of the youngest one's sack, along with his money for the grain." And he did as Joseph told him.
At first light the men were sent off with their donkeys.

They had gone only a short distance from the city when Joseph said to the man in charge of his house, "Get up, go after the men. When you catch up with them, say to them, 'Why have you repaid good with evil?
Isn't this the cup my master drinks from? He uses it to read omens. What you have done is wicked.'"
When he caught up with them, he said these words to them.
They said to him, "Why does my lord say such things? Your servants would never do such a thing!
Look, we brought back to you from the land of Canaan the money we found in the mouths of our sacks. So why would we steal silver or gold from your master's house?
If any of your servants is found to have it, he will die, and the rest of us will become my lord's slaves."
He said, "Very well, let it be as you say. The one who is found to have it will become my slave, and the rest of you will go free."
Each of them quickly lowered his sack to the ground and opened it.
He searched, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest, and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
Then they tore their clothes. Each of them loaded his donkey, and they went back to the city.
When Judah and his brothers came into Joseph's house, he was still there, and they threw themselves on the ground before him.
Joseph said to them, "What is this you have done? Don't you know that a man like me can read omens?"
