Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance of the city gate, and Abimelech and the troops with him rose from their hiding place.
When Gaal saw the troops, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" Zebul said to him, "You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as if they were men."
Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming by way of the Diviners' Oak."
Zebul said to him, "Where is your big talk now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Aren't these the people you despised? Go out now and fight them!"
So Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought against Abimelech.
Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. Many fell wounded, all the way to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech stayed at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers, so that they could not stay in Shechem.
The next day the people went out into the fields, and Abimelech was told about it.
He took his troops, divided them into three companies, and lay in wait in the fields. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he rose against them and struck them down.
Abimelech and the company with him rushed forward and took their stand at the entrance of the city gate, while the two other companies rushed on all who were in the fields and struck them down.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people in it. Then he tore down the city and sowed it with salt.
When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they went into the stronghold of the temple of El-berith.
Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem had gathered together.

So Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon, he and all the troops with him. Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut a branch from the trees. He lifted it up and put it on his shoulder, and he said to the troops with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do the same."

So all the troops each cut down a branch and followed Abimelech. They piled them against the stronghold and set the stronghold on fire over the people inside. So all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about a thousand men and women.
Then Abimelech went to Thebez. He camped against Thebez and captured it.
But there was a strong tower inside the city, and all the men and women, all the leaders of the city, fled there. They shut themselves in and went up on the roof of the tower.
Abimelech came to the tower and attacked it. He came up to the entrance of the tower to set it on fire.
But a woman threw an upper millstone down on Abimelech's head and cracked his skull.

He quickly called the young man who carried his weapons and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, so that people will not say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" So his young man ran him through, and he died.
When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home.
So God paid back Abimelech for the evil he had done to his father by killing his seventy brothers.
God also brought all the evil of the men of Shechem back on their own heads, and the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them.
After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, rose to save Israel. He lived in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.
After him rose Jair the Gileadite, and he judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty towns. To this day they are called Havvoth-jair, and they are in the land of Gilead.
Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

Once again the Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They served the Baals and the Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites and the gods of the Philistines. They abandoned the LORD and did not serve him.
So the LORD's anger burned against Israel, and he sold them into the power of the Philistines and of the Ammonites.
That year they shattered and crushed the Israelites. For eighteen years they oppressed all the Israelites who were on the other side of the Jordan, in the land of the Amorites, in Gilead.
The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, Benjamin and the house of Ephraim, and Israel was in great distress.
Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, "We have sinned against you, for we have abandoned our God and served the Baals."
The LORD said to the Israelites, "Didn't I save you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites and the Philistines?
When the Sidonians, Amalek and Maon oppressed you, and you cried out to me, I saved you from their power.
But you have abandoned me and served other gods. So I will not save you again.
Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of trouble."
The Israelites said to the LORD, "We have sinned. Do to us whatever you think best. Only please rescue us today."
So they got rid of the foreign gods among them and served the LORD, and he could no longer bear Israel's misery.
The Ammonites were called to arms and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites gathered and camped at Mizpah.
The people, the leaders of Gilead, said to one another, "Whoever will begin the fight against the Ammonites will be head over all the people living in Gilead."
Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior. He was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was Jephthah's father.
Gilead's wife also bore him sons. When his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You will have no inheritance in our father's family, for you are the son of another woman."
So Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Worthless men gathered around Jephthah and went out with him.
Some time later the Ammonites made war on Israel.
When the Ammonites made war on Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob.
They said to Jephthah, "Come and be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites."
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Didn't you hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now, when you are in trouble?"
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have come back to you now. Come with us and fight against the Ammonites, and you will be our head, over all the people living in Gilead."
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me back to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD hands them over to me, I will be your head."
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD is our witness: we will do just as you say."
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and commander over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?"
The king of the Ammonites said to Jephthah's messengers, "Because Israel took my land when they came up from Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Now give it back peacefully."
Jephthah sent messengers again to the king of the Ammonites,
with this message: "This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.
When they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.

Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let me pass through your land.' But the king of Edom would not listen. They also sent to the king of Moab, but he refused. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

Then they traveled through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab. They came to the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. They did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the border of Moab.
Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, the king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our place.'
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. Sihon gathered all his people and camped at Jahaz, and he fought against Israel.
The LORD, the God of Israel, handed Sihon and all his people over to Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who lived in that land.
They took possession of all the territory of the Amorites, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
So now that the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites before his people Israel, are you to take possession of it?
Don't you take possession of whatever Chemosh your god gives you to possess? So we will take possession of everything that the LORD our God has driven out before us.
Now, are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever quarrel with Israel, or ever fight against them?
While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, in Aroer and its villages, and in all the towns along the Arnon for three hundred years, why didn't you take them back during that time?
I have not sinned against you, but you are doing me wrong by making war on me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites."
But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the message that Jephthah sent him.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came on Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh. He passed through Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he went on against the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will hand the Ammonites over to me,
then whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return safely from the Ammonites, will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering."
So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD handed them over to him.
He defeated them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty towns, and as far as Abel-keramim. It was a very great defeat, and the Ammonites were brought low before the Israelites.
When Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah, there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing! She was his only child; apart from her he had neither son nor daughter.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Oh no, my daughter! You have brought me to my knees, and you have become the cause of my ruin! For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take it back."
She said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD. Do to me as you have promised, now that the LORD has taken vengeance for you on your enemies, the Ammonites."
She said to her father, "Let this one thing be done for me. Leave me alone for two months, so that I may go and wander on the mountains and weep over my virginity, I and my friends."
He said, "Go." He sent her away for two months, and she went with her friends and wept over her virginity on the mountains.
At the end of two months she came back to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. She had never slept with a man. It became a custom in Israel
that each year the young women of Israel would go out for four days to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.

The men of Ephraim were called to arms. They crossed over to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down over you!"
Jephthah said to them, "I and my people were in a bitter struggle with the Ammonites. I called you, but you did not save me from their power.
When I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hands and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD handed them over to me. So why have you come up against me today to fight me?"

Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck down Ephraim, because the Ephraimites had said, "You Gileadites are only fugitives from Ephraim, in the middle of Ephraim and Manasseh."

The Gileadites seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Ephraim. Whenever a fugitive from Ephraim said, "Let me cross over," the men of Gilead would ask him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" If he said, "No,"

they would say to him, "Then say 'Shibboleth.'" He would say "Sibboleth," because he could not pronounce it correctly. Then they would seize him and kill him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time forty-two thousand Ephraimites fell.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in one of the towns of Gilead.
After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons. He gave thirty daughters in marriage outside his clan, and he brought in thirty young women from outside for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years.
Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.
After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel. He judged Israel for ten years.
Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
After him Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.
Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
Once again the Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD handed them over to the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man from Zorah, of the clan of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. His wife was unable to have children, and she had borne none.
The angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "You are unable to have children and have borne none, but you will become pregnant and give birth to a son.
So now be careful not to drink wine or beer, and do not eat anything unclean.

For you will become pregnant and give birth to a son. No razor is to touch his head, for the boy will be a Nazirite dedicated to God from the womb. He will begin to save Israel from the power of the Philistines."
The woman went and told her husband, "A man of God came to me. He looked like the angel of God, very awe-inspiring. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name.

But he said to me, 'You will become pregnant and give birth to a son. So now do not drink wine or beer, and do not eat anything unclean, for the boy will be a Nazirite dedicated to God from the womb until the day he dies.'"
Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "Please, Lord, let the man of God whom you sent come to us again and teach us what we are to do for the boy who is to be born."
God listened to Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman while she was sitting in the field. Her husband Manoah was not with her.
The woman ran quickly and told her husband. She said to him, "The man who came to me the other day has appeared to me!"
Manoah got up and followed his wife. He came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to the woman?" He said, "I am."
Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the boy's way of life, and what is he to do?"
The angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "The woman must take care to do everything I told her.
She must not eat anything that comes from the grapevine. She must not drink wine or beer, or eat anything unclean. She must observe everything I commanded her."
Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please stay with us, and let us prepare a young goat for you."

The angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Even if you keep me here, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.)
Then Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that when your word comes true we may honor you?"
The angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name? It is wonderful."
So Manoah took the young goat and the grain offering and offered them on the rock to the LORD. Then he did a wonderful thing, while Manoah and his wife watched.
As the flame went up from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Manoah and his wife watched, and they fell face down to the ground.
The angel of the LORD did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.
Manoah said to his wife, "We will surely die, for we have seen God!"

But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering from our hands. He would not have shown us all these things, or told us anything like this now."
The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him.
The Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah, and in Timnah he saw a woman, one of the Philistine women.
He came back up and told his father and mother, "I have seen a woman in Timnah, one of the Philistine women. Now get her for me as my wife."

His father and mother said to him, "Isn't there a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all my people, that you must go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is the one I like."
His father and mother did not know that this was from the LORD, for he was seeking an occasion against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. When they came to the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion suddenly came roaring toward him.
The Spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and he tore the lion apart as one tears apart a young goat, with nothing in his hand. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was the one Samson liked.
Some time later, when he went back to marry her, he turned aside to look at the lion's carcass. There was a swarm of bees in the lion's body, and honey.

He scraped the honey out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. When he came to his father and mother, he gave some to them, and they ate it. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey out of the lion's body.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson held a feast there, for that was what young men used to do.
When the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.

Samson said to them, "Let me tell you a riddle. If you can give me the answer within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of fine clothes.
But if you cannot give me the answer, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of fine clothes." They said to him, "Tell us your riddle. Let us hear it."
He said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came something sweet." For three days they could not give the answer to the riddle.
On the seventh day they said to Samson's wife, "Coax your husband into telling us the riddle, or we will burn you and your father's family to death. Did you invite us here to rob us?"

So Samson's wife wept in front of him and said, "You only hate me! You don't love me. You have told my people a riddle, but you haven't told me the answer." He said to her, "Look, I haven't told my father or my mother. Should I tell you?"
She wept in front of him for the rest of the seven days of their feast. On the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him so hard. Then she told the riddle to her people.

On the seventh day, before the sun went down, the men of the town said to him, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" He said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."

Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him. He went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty of their men. He took what they wore and gave the sets of clothes to those who had answered the riddle. Then, burning with anger, he went up to his father's house.
And Samson's wife was given to his companion, the one who had been his friend at the wedding.
Some time later, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. He said, "I am going in to my wife in her room." But her father would not let him go in.
Her father said, "I was sure that you hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Isn't her younger sister more beautiful than she is? Please take her instead."
Samson said to them, "This time I will be in the right with the Philistines when I do them harm."
So Samson went and caught three hundred foxes. He took torches, turned the foxes tail to tail, and put a torch between each pair of tails.
He set the torches on fire and let the foxes loose in the Philistines' standing grain. He burned up the stacked grain and the standing grain, and the vineyards and the olive groves too.

The Philistines asked, "Who did this?" They were told, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took Samson's wife and gave her to his companion." So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death.
Samson said to them, "Since you act like this, I will take revenge on you, and only then will I stop."
He struck them down without mercy, a great slaughter. Then he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.
The Philistines went up and camped in Judah, and they spread out at Lehi.
The men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to tie up Samson, to do to him as he did to us."

Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Don't you know that the Philistines rule over us? What is this you have done to us?" He said to them, "As they did to me, so I have done to them."
They said to him, "We have come down to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines." Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves."
They said to him, "No, we will only tie you up and hand you over to them. We certainly won't kill you." So they tied him up with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and the ropes on his arms became like flax that has caught fire, and the bonds melted off his hands.
He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey. He reached out his hand, took it, and struck down a thousand men with it.
Then Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps! With the jawbone of a donkey I have struck down a thousand men."
When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand, and that place was called Ramath-lehi.
He was very thirsty, and he called out to the LORD, "You have given this great victory by the hand of your servant. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"
So God split open the hollow at Lehi, and water came out of it. When he drank, his strength returned, and he revived. That is why it was named En-hakkore. It is in Lehi to this day.
Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
Samson went to Gaza. There he saw a prostitute, and he slept with her.
The people of Gaza were told, "Samson has come here!" So they surrounded the place and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. All night they kept quiet, saying, "At dawn we will kill him."

But Samson lay there until midnight. At midnight he got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and the two gateposts, and pulled them up, bar and all. He put them on his shoulders and carried them up to the top of the hill that faces Hebron.
After this he fell in love with a woman in the Sorek Valley, whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines went up to her and said to her, "Coax him, and find out what makes his strength so great, and how we can overpower him, so that we can tie him up and subdue him. Each of us will give you 1,100 pieces of silver."
So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me what makes your strength so great, and how you could be tied up and subdued."
Samson said to her, "If they tie me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become weak and be like any other man."
So the rulers of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him with them.

She had men lying in wait in an inner room. She said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings as a strand of yarn snaps when it touches fire. So the secret of his strength was not discovered.
Then Delilah said to Samson, "You have made a fool of me and told me lies. Now please tell me how you could be tied up."
He said to her, "If they tie me tightly with new ropes that have never been used, I will become weak and be like any other man."

So Delilah took new ropes and tied him with them, and she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" The men lying in wait were in the inner room. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like thread.

Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have made a fool of me and told me lies. Tell me how you could be tied up." He said to her, "If you weave the seven braids of my hair into the fabric on the loom …"
She fastened it with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" He woke up from his sleep and pulled out the pin of the loom, and the fabric.
Then she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? Three times now you have made a fool of me, and you have not told me what makes your strength so great."
Day after day she pressed him with her words and nagged him, until he was worn out to death.

So he told her everything and said to her, "No razor has ever touched my head, for I have been a Nazirite dedicated to God from my mother's womb. If I were shaved, my strength would leave me, and I would become weak and be like any other man."

When Delilah saw that he had told her everything, she sent word to the rulers of the Philistines: "Come up this once, for he has told me everything." So the rulers of the Philistines came up to her, and they brought the silver with them.
She lulled him to sleep on her knees and called a man, and she had the seven braids of his hair shaved off. Then she began to subdue him, and his strength left him.
She said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" He woke up from his sleep and thought, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.
The Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes. They took him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze chains, and he was made to grind grain in the prison.
But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
Now the rulers of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to celebrate. They said, "Our god has handed over to us Samson our enemy."
When the people saw him, they praised their god, for they said, "Our god has handed over to us our enemy, who laid waste our land and killed so many of us."
When they were in high spirits, they said, "Call Samson to entertain us." So they called Samson from the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.
Samson said to the young man who was leading him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars that hold up the temple, so that I can lean against them."
Now the temple was full of men and women. All the rulers of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about three thousand men and women watching Samson entertain them.
Then Samson called out to the LORD, "Lord GOD, please remember me. Please give me strength just this once, O God, so that with one act of revenge I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes."
Samson took hold of the two central pillars that held up the temple, and he braced himself against them, one with his right hand and the other with his left.

Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines!" He pushed with all his strength, and the temple fell on the rulers and on all the people in it. So those he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his life.
His brothers and all his father's family came down and took him. They brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
There was a man from the hill country of Ephraim named Micah.

He said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you pronounced a curse, and said it in my hearing too: look, the silver is with me. I took it." His mother said, "May my son be blessed by the LORD!"

He gave the 1,100 pieces of silver back to his mother, and his mother said, "I solemnly dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a cast idol. So now I will give it back to you."

So he gave the silver back to his mother, and his mother took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a carved image and a cast idol. And it was in Micah's house.
This man Micah had a shrine. He made an ephod and household gods, and he installed one of his sons, who became his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah, of the clan of Judah. He was a Levite, and he had been living there as a foreigner.
The man left the town, Bethlehem in Judah, to live wherever he could find a place. On his journey he came to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah's house.
Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" He said to him, "I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to live wherever I can find a place."
Micah said to him, "Stay with me and be a father and a priest to me. I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, a set of clothes, and your food." So the Levite went in.
The Levite agreed to live with the man, and the young man became like one of his sons.
Micah installed the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in Micah's house.
Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will make me prosper, because I have a Levite as my priest."

In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the Danites was looking for territory of its own to live in, because until then no inheritance had fallen to it among the tribes of Israel.

So the Danites sent five men from their whole clan, capable men from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and explore it. They said to them, "Go and explore the land." The men came to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah's house, and spent the night there.

When they were near Micah's house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. So they turned aside there and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?"
He said to them, "Micah has done this and that for me. He has hired me, and I have become his priest."
They said to him, "Please ask God, so that we may know whether the journey we are on will succeed."
The priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey you are on is under the eye of the LORD."

So the five men went on and came to Laish. They saw that the people there were living in security, in the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting. There was no one in the land to do them any harm or to rule over them by force. They were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.
When they came back to their kinsmen at Zorah and Eshtaol, their kinsmen said to them, "What news?"
They said, "Come on, let us go up against them! We have seen the land, and it is very good. Are you going to sit still? Don't hesitate to go and enter the land and take possession of it.
When you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people and a spacious land. God has handed it over to you, a place where nothing on earth is lacking."
So six hundred men of the clan of the Danites set out from there, from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed with weapons of war.
They went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day. It is west of Kiriath-jearim.
From there they passed on into the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah's house.

Then the five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish said to their kinsmen, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image and a cast idol? Now think about what you should do."
So they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at Micah's house, and greeted him.
The six hundred Danite men, armed with their weapons of war, stood at the entrance of the gate.

The five men who had gone to spy out the land went up and went in there. They took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods and the cast idol, while the priest stood at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred men armed with weapons of war.
When these men went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods and the cast idol, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"

They said to him, "Be quiet! Put your hand over your mouth and come with us, and be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be priest to one man's household, or to be priest to a tribe and a clan in Israel?"
The priest was glad. He took the ephod, the household gods and the carved image, and went along in the middle of the people.
They turned and went on their way, putting the little children, the livestock and their goods in front of them.
When they were some distance from Micah's house, the men who lived in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they caught up with the Danites.
They shouted at the Danites, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you have called out your men?"
He said, "You have taken my gods that I made, and the priest, and gone away. What do I have left? How can you say to me, 'What is the matter with you?'"
The Danites said to him, "Don't let your voice be heard among us, or some hot-tempered men will attack you, and you will lose your life and the lives of your household."
Then the Danites went on their way. When Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back home.
They took what Micah had made, and the priest who had belonged to him, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting. They put them to the sword and burned the city.
There was no one to rescue them, because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. The Danites rebuilt the city and settled in it.
They named the city Dan, after their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel. But the city was formerly called Laish.
The Danites set up the carved image for themselves. Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, and his sons were priests for the tribe of the Danites until the time the land went into exile.
They kept for themselves the carved image that Micah had made, all the time that the house of God was at Shiloh.
In those days, when there was no king in Israel, there was a Levite living in the far parts of the hill country of Ephraim. He took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
But his concubine was unfaithful to him, and she left him and went to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah. She was there for four months.

Then her husband got up and went after her to speak tenderly to her and bring her back. He had his servant with him and a pair of donkeys. She brought him into her father's house, and when the young woman's father saw him, he was glad to meet him.
His father-in-law, the young woman's father, made him stay, and he stayed with him three days. They ate and drank and spent the nights there.
On the fourth day they got up early in the morning, and he got ready to leave. But the young woman's father said to his son-in-law, "Have a bite to eat to refresh yourself, and then you can go."
So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. Then the young woman's father said to the man, "Please agree to stay the night, and enjoy yourself."
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law urged him, so he stayed there again that night.
On the fifth day he got up early in the morning to leave, and the young woman's father said, "Please refresh yourself, and wait until the afternoon." So the two of them ate.

When the man got up to leave, with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law, the young woman's father, said to him, "Look, the day is drawing toward evening. Please spend the night. The day is coming to an end. Stay here and enjoy yourself. Tomorrow you can get up early for your journey and go home."
But the man was not willing to spend the night. He got up and left, and he came opposite Jebus, that is, Jerusalem. He had with him a pair of saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him.
When they were near Jebus, the day was almost gone, and the servant said to his master, "Come, let's turn aside into this city of the Jebusites and spend the night in it."
His master said to him, "We will not turn aside into a city of foreigners, who are not Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah."
He said to his servant, "Come, let's try to reach one of these places and spend the night in Gibeah or in Ramah."
So they passed on and went their way, and the sun set on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turned aside there to go in and spend the night in Gibeah. He went in and sat down in the city square, but no one took them into his house for the night.
Then in the evening an old man came in from his work in the fields. He was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he was living as a foreigner in Gibeah. The men of the place were Benjaminites.
When he looked up and saw the traveler in the city square, the old man said, "Where are you going? Where do you come from?"

He said to him, "We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the far parts of the hill country of Ephraim. That is where I am from. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to the house of the LORD. But no one will take me into his house.
We have both straw and fodder for our donkeys, and there is also bread and wine for me, for your servant woman, and for the young man with your servants. We don't need anything."
The old man said, "Peace be with you. Let me take care of all your needs. Only don't spend the night in the square."
So he brought him into his house and gave the donkeys fodder. They washed their feet and ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, the men of the city, worthless men, surrounded the house and pounded on the door. They said to the old man, the owner of the house, "Bring out the man who came to your house, so that we can have sex with him."
The man, the owner of the house, went out to them and said to them, "No, my brothers, please don't do such an evil thing. Since this man has come into my house, don't do this outrageous thing.
Here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out now. Violate them and do to them whatever you like. But don't do such an outrageous thing to this man."

But the men would not listen to him. So the man took hold of his concubine and pushed her outside to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and they let her go as dawn was breaking.
At daybreak the woman came and fell down at the entrance of the man's house where her master was, and she lay there until it was light.

In the morning her master got up, opened the doors of the house, and went out to go on his way. And there was the woman, his concubine, lying at the entrance of the house with her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, "Get up. Let's go." But there was no answer. Then he put her on the donkey, and the man set out and went home.
When he reached his house, he took the knife, took hold of his concubine, and cut her up limb by limb into twelve pieces. And he sent her throughout the territory of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has ever happened or been seen from the day the Israelites came up out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think about it! Take counsel, and speak!"
Then all the Israelites came out, from Dan to Beersheba and from the land of Gilead, and the community assembled as one man before the LORD at Mizpah.
The leaders of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, took their places in the assembly of the people of God: four hundred thousand foot soldiers armed with swords.
The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites said, "Tell us how this evil thing happened."
The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered, "I came with my concubine to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
The men of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house at night because of me. They meant to kill me, and they violated my concubine, and she died.
So I took hold of my concubine, cut her in pieces, and sent her throughout the whole territory of Israel's inheritance, because they have committed a lewd and outrageous act in Israel.
Now, all of you Israelites, give your word and your advice here."
All the people rose as one man and said, "None of us will go home to his tent. None of us will return to his house.
Now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot.

We will take ten men out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand, to get provisions for the troops. Then, when they come to Geba in Benjamin, they can pay it back for all the outrage it has committed in Israel."
So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one man.
The tribes of Israel sent men throughout the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What is this evil thing that has happened among you?
Now hand over the men, those worthless men in Gibeah, so that we may put them to death and purge the evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to their brothers, the Israelites.
Instead the Benjaminites came together from their towns to Gibeah, to go out to battle against the Israelites.
On that day the Benjaminites mustered from their towns twenty-six thousand men armed with swords, besides the people of Gibeah, who mustered seven hundred chosen men.
Among all these troops there were seven hundred chosen men who were left-handed. Every one of them could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
The men of Israel, not counting Benjamin, mustered four hundred thousand men armed with swords, all of them warriors.
The Israelites set out and went up to Bethel and asked God, "Which of us is to go up first to battle against the Benjaminites?" The LORD said, "Judah first."
The Israelites got up in the morning and camped against Gibeah.
The men of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up their battle lines against them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and cut down twenty-two thousand Israelites on the battlefield that day.
But the troops, the men of Israel, took courage, and they again drew up their battle lines in the same place where they had drawn them up on the first day.
The Israelites went up and wept before the LORD until evening. They asked the LORD, "Shall we go out again to battle against our brothers the Benjaminites?" The LORD said, "Go up against them."
So the Israelites advanced against the Benjaminites on the second day.
On the second day Benjamin came out of Gibeah to meet them, and they cut down eighteen thousand more Israelites on the battlefield, all of them armed with swords.

Then all the Israelites, the whole army, went up to Bethel. They wept and sat there before the LORD, and they fasted that day until evening. They offered burnt offerings and fellowship offerings before the LORD.
The Israelites asked the LORD (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,

and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, served before it in those days), "Shall we go out yet again to battle against our brothers the Benjaminites, or shall we stop?" The LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will hand them over to you."
So Israel set men in ambush all around Gibeah.
On the third day the Israelites went up against the Benjaminites and drew up their battle lines against Gibeah as before.

The Benjaminites came out to meet the troops and were drawn away from the city. As before, they began to strike down and kill some of the troops on the roads, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, in the open country. About thirty men of Israel were killed.
The Benjaminites said, "They are being defeated before us, as before." But the Israelites said, "Let us retreat and draw them away from the city to the roads."
All the men of Israel rose from their places and drew up their battle lines at Baal-tamar, while the Israelites in ambush burst out of their position at Maareh-geba.
Ten thousand chosen men from all Israel came against Gibeah, and the fighting was heavy. But the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them.
The LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and that day the Israelites cut down 25,100 men of Benjamin, all of them armed with swords.
Then the Benjaminites saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel had given ground to Benjamin, because they were relying on the ambush they had set against Gibeah.
The men in ambush moved quickly and rushed against Gibeah. They spread out and put the whole city to the sword.
The men of Israel had agreed on a signal with the men in ambush: they were to send up a great cloud of smoke from the city.
Then the men of Israel turned around in the battle. Benjamin had begun to strike down and kill about thirty men of Israel, for they said, "They are surely defeated before us, as in the first battle."
But the signal began to rise from the city, a column of smoke, and when the Benjaminites looked behind them, the whole city was going up in smoke to the sky.
Then the men of Israel turned around, and the men of Benjamin were terrified, for they saw that disaster had struck them.
So they turned their backs before the men of Israel and fled toward the wilderness, but the battle caught up with them, and those who came out of the towns cut them down among them.
They surrounded the Benjaminites and chased them. They trampled them down with ease as far as a point opposite Gibeah on the east.
Of Benjamin, 18,000 men fell, all of them valiant warriors.
They turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. The Israelites picked off 5,000 men on the roads, and they pursued them closely as far as Gidom and struck down 2,000 more of them.
So all the Benjaminites who fell that day were 25,000 men armed with swords, all of them valiant warriors.
But 600 men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and they stayed at the rock of Rimmon for four months.
The men of Israel turned back against the Benjaminites and put them to the sword, the people of the towns and the animals, everything they found. They also set on fire all the towns they came to.
The men of Israel had sworn an oath at Mizpah: "None of us will give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife."
The people came to Bethel and sat there before God until evening. They wept aloud, with bitter weeping.
They said, "LORD, God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today one tribe should be missing from Israel?"
The next day the people got up early and built an altar there, and they offered burnt offerings and fellowship offerings.

Then the Israelites said, "Who from all the tribes of Israel did not come up to the assembly before the LORD?" For they had taken a solemn oath concerning anyone who did not come up to the LORD at Mizpah: "He must be put to death."
The Israelites felt sorry for their brother Benjamin, and they said, "Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel.
What shall we do about wives for those who are left? We have sworn by the LORD not to give them any of our daughters as wives."
They said, "Which one of the tribes of Israel did not come up to the LORD at Mizpah?" And it turned out that no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp, to the assembly.
For when the people were counted, not one of the people living in Jabesh-gilead was there.
So the community sent twelve thousand of their bravest men there, and commanded them, "Go and put the people living in Jabesh-gilead to the sword, including the women and the little children.
This is what you are to do: devote to destruction every male and every woman who has slept with a man."
Among the people living in Jabesh-gilead they found four hundred young women who were virgins, who had never slept with a man, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.
Then the whole community sent word to the Benjaminites who were at the rock of Rimmon, and they offered them peace.
So Benjamin came back at that time, and they gave them the women of Jabesh-gilead whom they had kept alive. But there were not enough for them.
The people felt sorry for Benjamin, because the LORD had made a gap in the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the community said, "What shall we do about wives for those who are left, since the women of Benjamin have been wiped out?"
They said, "The survivors of Benjamin must have heirs, so that a tribe will not be blotted out from Israel.
But we cannot give them wives from our daughters, for the Israelites have sworn, 'Cursed is anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin.'"
Then they said, "Look, there is the yearly festival of the LORD at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."
So they instructed the Benjaminites, "Go and lie in wait in the vineyards.

Watch, and when the young women of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, come out of the vineyards and each of you seize a wife for himself from the young women of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

When their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, 'Be kind to us and let them have them, because we did not get a wife for each of them in the battle. And you are not guilty, because you did not give your daughters to them.'"
The Benjaminites did so. They took wives, as many as they were, from the dancers they had seized. Then they went back to their inheritance, rebuilt the towns, and lived in them.
At that time the Israelites left there, each to his tribe and his clan. Each of them went out from there to his own inheritance.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land. A man from Bethlehem in Judah went to live for a while in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons.

The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came to the country of Moab and stayed there.
Then Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.
They married Moabite women. One was named Orpah and the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years.
Then both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and the woman was left without her two boys and without her husband.
So she got up with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard in the country of Moab that the LORD had come to the help of his people and given them food.
She set out from the place where she had been living, and her two daughters-in-law went with her. They went along the road to return to the land of Judah.
Then Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you, to your mother's house. May the LORD show you faithful love, as you have shown it to the dead and to me.
May the LORD grant that each of you find rest in the home of a husband." Then she kissed them, and they wept aloud.
They said to her, "No, we will go back with you to your people."
But Naomi said, "Go back, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Do I still have sons in my womb who could become your husbands?
Go back, my daughters, go, for I am too old to have a husband. Even if I said, 'There is hope for me,' even if I had a husband tonight and then gave birth to sons,

would you wait for them until they grew up? Would you keep yourselves from marrying for them? No, my daughters. It is far more bitter for me than for you, for the hand of the LORD has gone out against me."
Then they wept aloud again. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.
Naomi said, "Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods. Go back with your sister-in-law."
But Ruth said, "Don't urge me to leave you or to turn back from following you. For where you go, I will go, and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD do this to me, and more besides, if anything but death separates me from you."
When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she said no more to her.
So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. When they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women said, "Can this be Naomi?"
She said to them, "Don't call me Naomi. Call me Mara, for the Almighty has made my life very bitter.
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has brought disaster on me?"
So Naomi came back, and with her Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, who came back from the country of Moab. They came to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Naomi had a relative on her husband's side, a man of standing from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the fields and glean among the ears of grain behind anyone who will be kind to me." Naomi said to her, "Go, my daughter."
So she went and came and gleaned in the field behind the reapers. As it happened, she came to the part of the field that belonged to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.
Just then Boaz came from Bethlehem. He said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you!" They said to him, "The LORD bless you!"
Boaz said to his servant who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?"
The servant in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the young Moabite woman who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.
She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the reapers.' So she came, and she has been on her feet from early morning until now, except for a short rest in the shelter."
Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen to me, my daughter. Don't go to glean in another field, and don't leave this one. Stay close to my young women here.

Keep your eyes on the field they are reaping, and follow after them. I have ordered the young men not to touch you. And when you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink from what the young men have drawn."
Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor with you, that you take notice of me, when I am a foreigner?"

Boaz answered her, "I have been told everything you have done for your mother-in-law since your husband died: how you left your father and your mother and the land of your birth, and came to a people you did not know before.
May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you receive a full reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge."
She said, "May I go on finding favor with you, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not even like one of your servants."

At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come over here and eat some of the bread, and dip your piece in the vinegar." So she sat down beside the reapers, and he handed her roasted grain. She ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over.
When she got up to glean, Boaz ordered his young men, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and don't humiliate her.
And pull out some stalks for her from the bundles and leave them for her to glean. Don't rebuke her."
So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it came to about an ephah of barley.
She picked it up and went into the town, and her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. Then Ruth brought out and gave her what she had left over after she had eaten her fill.

Her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today? Where did you work? May the man who took notice of you be blessed!" So she told her mother-in-law about the man she had worked with. She said, "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz."

Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not stopped showing his faithful love to the living and the dead!" Naomi also said to her, "The man is a close relative of ours. He is one of our guardian-redeemers."
Ruth the Moabite said, "He even said to me, 'Stay close to my young men until they have finished all my harvest.'"
Naomi said to Ruth her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, so that no one will harm you in another field."
So she stayed close to the young women of Boaz to glean until the end of the barley harvest and the wheat harvest. And she lived with her mother-in-law.
Then Naomi her mother-in-law said to her, "My daughter, shouldn't I look for a home for you, where you will be well provided for?
Now, isn't Boaz, whose young women you have been with, a relative of ours? Tonight he will be winnowing barley at the threshing floor.
So wash, put on perfume, and get dressed, and go down to the threshing floor. But don't let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking.
When he lies down, note the place where he lies. Then go in, uncover his feet, and lie down. He will tell you what to do."
She said to her, "I will do everything you tell me."
So she went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had instructed her.
When Boaz had eaten and drunk and was in good spirits, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came quietly, uncovered his feet, and lay down.
In the middle of the night the man was startled and turned over, and there was a woman lying at his feet!
He said, "Who are you?" She said, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread the corner of your garment over your servant, for you are a guardian-redeemer."
He said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. This last act of faithful love is greater than the first, for you have not gone after the young men, whether poor or rich.
Now, my daughter, don't be afraid. I will do for you everything you ask, for everyone in the town knows that you are a woman of worth.
It is true that I am a guardian-redeemer, but there is another guardian-redeemer more closely related than I am.

Stay here tonight. In the morning, if he will act as your guardian-redeemer, good; let him do it. But if he is not willing to act as your guardian-redeemer, then, as surely as the LORD lives, I will do it myself. Lie down until morning."
So she lay at his feet until morning, but she got up before anyone could recognize anyone else. He said, "It must not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor."
He said, "Bring the shawl you are wearing and hold it out." She held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then he went into the town.
When she came to her mother-in-law, Naomi said, "How did it go, my daughter?" Then she told her everything the man had done for her.
She said, "He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said to me, 'Don't go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.'"
Naomi said, "Wait here, my daughter, until you find out how the matter turns out. For the man will not rest until he has settled the matter today."

Meanwhile Boaz went up to the town gate and sat down there. Just then the guardian-redeemer Boaz had spoken about came by. Boaz said, "Come over here, my friend, and sit down." So he came over and sat down.
Boaz took ten men from the elders of the town and said, "Sit down here." And they sat down.
Then he said to the guardian-redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the piece of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech.

I thought I should let you know and say, 'Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people.' If you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not redeem it, tell me, so that I may know. For there is no one but you to redeem it, and I come after you." He said, "I will redeem it."
Then Boaz said, "On the day you buy the field from Naomi, you are also acquiring Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's widow, in order to keep the dead man's name alive on his inheritance."
The guardian-redeemer said, "Then I cannot redeem it for myself, or I would ruin my own inheritance. Take over my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it."

In earlier times in Israel, this was the custom for redeeming and exchanging property, to make any transaction final: one man took off his sandal and gave it to the other. This was the way of confirming a transaction in Israel.
So the guardian-redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it yourself," and he took off his sandal.
Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses today that I have bought from Naomi everything that belonged to Elimelech and everything that belonged to Chilion and Mahlon.

I have also acquired Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's widow, to be my wife, in order to keep the dead man's name alive on his inheritance, so that the dead man's name will not be cut off from among his relatives or from the gate of his town. You are witnesses today."

All the people at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman who is coming into your house like Rachel and Leah, the two who built up the house of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and be famous in Bethlehem.
And through the children that the LORD will give you by this young woman, may your family be like the family of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah."
So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. He slept with her, and the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son.
Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you without a guardian-redeemer today! May his name be famous in Israel!
He will restore your life and take care of you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given birth to him."
Then Naomi took the child, held him in her lap, and cared for him.
The neighbor women gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi!" They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.
These are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron,
Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab,
Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon,
Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed,
Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.
There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim. His name was Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the other was Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
Year after year this man went up from his town to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of Armies at Shiloh. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD there.
On the day Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But to Hannah he would give a double portion, because he loved Hannah, though the LORD had closed her womb.
Her rival would provoke her bitterly, to upset her, because the LORD had closed her womb.
So it went on year after year. Whenever she went up to the house of the LORD, her rival would provoke her, and she would weep and not eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Hannah, why are you weeping? Why aren't you eating? Why are you so sad? Am I not better to you than ten sons?"
After they had eaten and drunk at Shiloh, Hannah got up. Now Eli the priest was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.
She was deeply distressed, and she prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.

She made a vow and said, "LORD of Armies, if you will only look on the misery of your servant and remember me, and not forget your servant, but give your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD for all the days of his life, and no razor will ever touch his head."
As she went on praying before the LORD, Eli was watching her mouth.
Hannah was speaking in her heart. Only her lips were moving, and her voice could not be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, "How long are you going to be drunk? Put away your wine!"
Hannah answered, "No, my lord. I am a deeply troubled woman. I have not drunk wine or beer. I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.
Do not take your servant for a worthless woman. I have been speaking all this time out of my great anguish and grief."
Eli answered, "Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant you what you have asked of him."
She said, "May your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.
They got up early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD. Then they went back home to Ramah. Elkanah slept with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In due time Hannah became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, "because I asked the LORD for him."
The man Elkanah went up with all his household to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and to fulfill his vow.
But Hannah did not go up. She said to her husband, "Not until the boy is weaned. Then I will bring him, so that he may appear before the LORD and stay there forever."
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Do what seems best to you. Stay here until you have weaned him. Only, may the LORD confirm his word." So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him.
When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, an ephah of flour and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. The boy was young.
They slaughtered the bull, and they brought the boy to Eli.
She said, "Pardon me, my lord! As surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you, praying to the LORD.
I prayed for this boy, and the LORD has given me what I asked of him.
So I in turn have given him to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is given over to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there.
Hannah prayed and said, "My heart rejoices in the LORD; my horn is lifted high in the LORD. My mouth laughs at my enemies, for I rejoice in your salvation.
There is no one holy like the LORD; there is no one besides you. There is no rock like our God.
Do not keep talking so proudly, or let arrogant words come out of your mouth. For the LORD is a God who knows, and by him actions are weighed.
The bows of the mighty are broken, but those who stumbled are clothed with strength.
Those who were full hire themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry hunger no more. The woman who could not have children has given birth to seven, but the mother of many sons wastes away.
The LORD puts to death and brings to life. He brings down to Sheol and raises up.
The LORD makes poor and makes rich. He brings low; he also lifts up.

He raises the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to seat them with nobles and give them a seat of honor. For the pillars of the earth belong to the LORD, and he has set the world on them.
He guards the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked are silenced in darkness, for no one wins by strength.

Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered; he will thunder against them from heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to his king and lift high the horn of his anointed."
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy served the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest.
Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD.
This was how the priests dealt with the people: whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant would come while the meat was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand.

He would plunge it into the pan, or the kettle, or the cauldron, or the pot, and the priest would take for himself whatever the fork brought up. This is what they did to all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh.
Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give the priest some meat to roast. He will not take boiled meat from you, only raw."
If the man said to him, "Let them burn the fat first, and then take whatever you want," he would say, "No, you must give it now. If not, I will take it by force."
So the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the LORD's offering with contempt.
But Samuel was serving before the LORD, a boy wearing a linen ephod.
His mother would make him a little robe and bring it up to him every year, when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife and say, "May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she asked for and gave to the LORD." Then they would go home.
The LORD came to help Hannah. She became pregnant and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD.
Eli was very old. He heard about everything his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they slept with the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
He said to them, "Why do you do such things? I hear about your evil deeds from all the people.
No, my sons! The report I hear spreading among the LORD's people is not good.

If one person sins against another, God may mediate for him. But if someone sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?" But they would not listen to their father, for the LORD wanted to put them to death.
And the boy Samuel kept growing, both in stature and in favor with the LORD and with people.
A man of God came to Eli and said to him, "This is what the LORD says: 'Did I not reveal myself to your father's family when they were in Egypt, subject to Pharaoh's household?

I chose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod in my presence. And I gave your father's family all the offerings by fire from the Israelites.

Why do you kick at my sacrifice and my offering, which I commanded for my dwelling? Why do you honor your sons more than me, by making yourselves fat on the best part of every offering of my people Israel?

Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: I did say that your family and your father's family would walk before me forever. But now the LORD declares: Far be it from me! For those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be treated with contempt.
The days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's family, so that there will be no old man in your family.
You will see distress in my dwelling, in spite of all the good done for Israel, and there will never be an old man in your family.
Any man of yours whom I do not cut off from my altar will be left only to wear out your eyes and grieve your heart. And all the descendants of your family will die in the prime of life.
And what happens to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will be the sign for you: both of them will die on the same day.
I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do what is in my heart and my mind. I will build him a lasting house, and he will walk before my anointed forever.

Everyone who is left in your family will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread. He will say, "Please appoint me to one of the priestly offices, so that I may have a scrap of bread to eat."'"
The boy Samuel was serving the LORD under Eli. In those days the word of the LORD was rare; visions were not common.
One day Eli was lying down in his usual place. His eyes had begun to grow dim, and he could not see.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.
Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, "Here I am."
He ran to Eli and said, "Here I am. You called me." But Eli said, "I did not call you. Go back and lie down." So he went and lay down.
The LORD called again, "Samuel!" Samuel got up, went to Eli and said, "Here I am. You called me." But Eli said, "I did not call you, my son. Go back and lie down."
Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.
The LORD called Samuel a third time. He got up, went to Eli and said, "Here I am. You called me." Then Eli understood that the LORD was calling the boy.
So Eli said to Samuel, "Go and lie down. If he calls you, say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The LORD came and stood there, and called as he had before, "Samuel! Samuel!" Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant is listening."
The LORD said to Samuel, "I am about to do something in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears about it tingle.
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken against his family, from beginning to end.
I have told him that I am going to judge his family forever because of the guilt he knew about: his sons were bringing a curse on themselves, and he did not restrain them.
Therefore I have sworn to the family of Eli that the guilt of Eli's family will never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering."
Samuel lay down until morning. Then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
But Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." He said, "Here I am."
Eli said, "What was it that he said to you? Please do not hide it from me. May God deal with you, and more severely, if you hide from me a single word of all he said to you."
So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And Eli said, "He is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him."
Samuel grew up, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.
All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD.
The LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh through the word of the LORD.
And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Israel went out to fight against the Philistines. They camped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines drew up their lines to face Israel. The battle spread, and Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who struck down about four thousand men on the battlefield.

When the troops came back to the camp, the elders of Israel said, "Why has the LORD let us be defeated today by the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the LORD's covenant here from Shiloh, so that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies."

So the people sent men to Shiloh, and they brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies, who is enthroned on the cherubim. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of the LORD's covenant came into the camp, all Israel gave a great shout, so that the ground shook.
When the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said, "What is this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?" When they learned that the ark of the LORD had come into the camp,
the Philistines were afraid, for they said, "God has come into the camp." They said, "We are in trouble! Nothing like this has ever happened before.
We are in trouble! Who will rescue us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Be strong, Philistines, and act like men, or you will be slaves to the Hebrews as they have been slaves to you. Act like men and fight!"
So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and every man fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great: thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.
The ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh that same day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head.
When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat beside the road, watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. When the man came into the town and told the news, the whole town cried out.
When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he asked, "What is this uproar?" The man hurried over and told Eli.
Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes were set, so that he could not see.
The man said to Eli, "I am the one who has come from the battle line. I fled from the battle line today." Eli said, "What happened, my son?"

The messenger answered, "Israel fled from the Philistines, and there has also been a great slaughter among the troops. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead too, and the ark of God has been captured."
When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward off his seat beside the gate. His neck was broken, and he died, for he was an old man and heavy. He had judged Israel for forty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and about to give birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she crouched down and gave birth, for her labor pains came on her suddenly.
As she was dying, the women standing beside her said, "Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son." But she did not answer or pay any attention.
She named the boy Ichabod, saying, "Glory has gone into exile from Israel," because the ark of God had been captured, and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
She said, "Glory has gone into exile from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
After the Philistines had captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
The Philistines took the ark of God, brought it into the temple of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon.
When the people of Ashdod got up early the next day, there was Dagon, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD. They took Dagon and put him back in his place.

But when they got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD. Dagon's head and both his hands lay broken off on the threshold. Only Dagon's body was left.
That is why to this day neither the priests of Dagon nor anyone who enters the temple of Dagon steps on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod.
The hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod. He devastated them and struck them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory.
When the men of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not stay with us, for his hand is hard on us and on Dagon our god."

So they sent for all the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together, and asked, "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be moved to Gath." So they moved the ark of the God of Israel there.
