But if you go back to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king. I was your father's servant in the past, but now I will be your servant,' then you can defeat the advice of Ahithophel for me.
Won't Zadok and Abiathar the priests be there with you? Whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.
Their two sons are there with them, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send me by them everything you hear."
So Hushai, David's friend, came to the city, just as Absalom was coming into Jerusalem.

When David had gone a little beyond the summit, there was Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, coming to meet him with a pair of saddled donkeys. On them were two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits and a skin of wine.

The king said to Ziba, "What do you mean by these?" Ziba said, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who become exhausted in the wilderness to drink."
The king said, "And where is your master's grandson?" Ziba said to the king, "He is staying in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back my grandfather's kingdom.'"
The king said to Ziba, "All that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." Ziba said, "I bow down. May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king."
When King David came to Bahurim, a man from the clan of Saul's house came out from there. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and he came out cursing as he went.
He threw stones at David and at all King David's servants, though all the troops and all the warriors were on his right and on his left.
This is what Shimei said as he cursed: "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you scoundrel!

The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has handed the kingdom over to your son Absalom. Look at you now, in your own disaster, because you are a man of blood!"
Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head."
But the king said, "What do I have to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, for the LORD has told him, 'Curse David.' Who then can say, 'Why have you done this?'"

David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Look, my own son, who came from my own body, is seeking my life. How much more now this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.
Perhaps the LORD will look on my tears, and the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today."
So David and his men went on their way, while Shimei went along the hillside opposite him, cursing as he went, throwing stones at him and flinging dust.
The king and all the people who were with him arrived exhausted, and he refreshed himself there.
Meanwhile Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"
Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why didn't you go with your friend?"
Hushai said to Absalom, "No. The one whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will stay.
Besides, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I served your father, so I will serve you."
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your advice. What should we do?"

Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Sleep with your father's concubines, whom he left to look after the house. Then all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and all who are with you will be encouraged."
So they pitched the tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom slept with his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days the advice Ahithophel gave was like that of someone who inquires of the word of God. That is how all the advice of Ahithophel was regarded, both by David and by Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will set out and pursue David tonight.
I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged. I will throw him into panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king,
and I will bring all the people back to you. The return of everyone depends on the man you are seeking. Then all the people will be at peace."
The advice seemed right to Absalom and to all the elders of Israel.
Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite too, and let us hear what he has to say as well."
When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "This is what Ahithophel has said. Should we do what he says? If not, you speak."
Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the advice Ahithophel has given is not good."

Hushai went on, "You know your father and his men, that they are warriors, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the wild. Your father is an experienced soldier, and he will not spend the night with the troops.

Even now he is hidden in one of the caves or in some other place. If some of the troops fall at the start, whoever hears of it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom.'
Then even the bravest man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly lose heart. For all Israel knows that your father is a warrior, and that those who are with him are brave men.
So this is my advice: Let all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the sand by the sea, and you yourself go into battle.
Then we will come upon him in whatever place he may be found, and we will fall on him as the dew falls on the ground. Not one will be left, neither he nor any of the men who are with him.
If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down into the valley until not even a pebble is found there."

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than the advice of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained that the good advice of Ahithophel should be defeated, so that the LORD might bring disaster on Absalom.
Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "This and this is what Ahithophel advised Absalom and the elders of Israel, and this and this is what I advised.
Now send quickly and tell David, 'Do not spend the night at the plains of the wilderness, but be sure to cross over, or the king and all the people who are with him will be swallowed up.'"
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A servant girl would go and tell them, and they would go and tell King David, for they could not risk being seen coming into the city.
But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So the two of them left quickly and came to the house of a man in Bahurim who had a well in his courtyard, and they went down into it.
The man's wife took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well and scattered grain on it, so that nothing was known.

When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" The woman said to them, "They crossed over the stream of water." They searched but did not find them, so they went back to Jerusalem.
After they had gone, the men came up out of the well and went and told King David. They said to David, "Get up and cross the water quickly, for this is what Ahithophel has advised against you."
So David and all the people who were with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, he saddled his donkey and set out, and he went home to his own town. He gave instructions to his household and hanged himself. So he died and was buried in his father's tomb.
David came to Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan, he and all the men of Israel with him.
Absalom had put Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite, who had slept with Abigail daughter of Nahash, the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Israel and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, basins and pottery, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils and roasted grain,
honey, curds, sheep, and cheese from the herd, for David and the people who were with him to eat. For they said, "The people are hungry and exhausted and thirsty in the wilderness."
David mustered the troops who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.

David sent out the troops, a third under the command of Joab, a third under the command of Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and a third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. The king said to the troops, "I myself will certainly go out with you too."

But the troops said, "You must not go out. For if we have to flee, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care about us. For now there are ten thousand like us. Now it is better for you to be ready to help us from the city."
The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood beside the gate, while all the troops went out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king commanded Joab, Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the troops heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom.
So the troops went out into the field against Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.
There the people of Israel were defeated by David's servants. The slaughter there was great that day: twenty thousand men.
The battle spread out over the whole countryside, and the forest devoured more of the people that day than the sword devoured.

Absalom happened to meet David's servants. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak. His head caught fast in the oak, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on.
A man saw it and told Joab, "Look, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak."
Joab said to the man who told him, "You saw him! Why didn't you strike him to the ground there? Then I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a belt."

The man said to Joab, "Even if I felt the weight of a thousand pieces of silver in my hands, I would not lift my hand against the king's son. For in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'Whoever you are, protect the young man Absalom.'
Or if I had acted treacherously against my own life (and nothing is hidden from the king), you yourself would have stood aloof."
Joab said, "I will not wait like this for you." He took three spears in his hand and thrust them into Absalom's heart while he was still alive in the heart of the oak.
Ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom, struck him and killed him.
Then Joab blew the ram's horn, and the troops turned back from pursuing Israel, for Joab held the troops back.
They took Absalom, threw him into a great pit in the forest, and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled, each to his home.

During his lifetime Absalom had taken and set up for himself a pillar, which is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar by his own name, and it is called Absalom's Monument to this day.
Then Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Let me run and bring the king the good news that the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies."
Joab said to him, "You are not the man to take news today. You may take news another day, but today you must not take news, because the king's son is dead."
Then Joab said to a Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed down to Joab and ran.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said once more to Joab, "Whatever happens, please let me run too, after the Cushite." Joab said, "Why should you run, my son, when you have no news that will bring you a reward?"
"Whatever happens, I will run." So he said to him, "Run!" Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain and outran the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and he looked up and saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." He kept coming closer and closer.
Then the watchman saw another man running. The watchman called to the gatekeeper and said, "Look, another man running alone!" The king said, "He too is bringing news."
The watchman said, "I think the first one runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok." The king said, "He is a good man, and he comes with good news."

Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, "All is well!" He bowed down to the king with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hand against my lord the king."
The king said, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz said, "I saw a great commotion when Joab sent the king's servant and me, your servant, but I don't know what it was."
The king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still.
Then the Cushite arrived, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king! The LORD has delivered you today from the hand of all who rose up against you."
The king said to the Cushite, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" The Cushite said, "May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you to do you harm, be like that young man."
The king was shaken. He went up to the room over the gate and wept. As he went, he said, "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you! Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab was told, "The king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."
So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the troops, because the troops heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son."
The troops stole into the city that day, as troops steal in when they are ashamed because they have fled in battle.
The king covered his face, and the king cried out with a loud voice, "My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"

Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "Today you have shamed all your servants, who have saved your life today, and the lives of your sons and your daughters, the lives of your wives and the lives of your concubines,

by loving those who hate you and hating those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants mean nothing to you. For I know today that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then it would be right in your eyes.

Now get up, go out and speak kindly to your servants. For I swear by the LORD that if you do not go out, not one man will stay with you tonight. That will be worse for you than all the trouble that has come upon you from your youth until now."

So the king got up and sat in the gate. When all the troops were told, "Look, the king is sitting in the gate," all the troops came before the king. Meanwhile the Israelites had fled, each to his home.

All the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king rescued us from the hand of our enemies, and he saved us from the hand of the Philistines. But now he has fled from the land because of Absalom.
And Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. So now, why are you saying nothing about bringing the king back?"

King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Speak to the elders of Judah and say, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house? What all Israel is saying has reached the king at his house.
You are my brothers; you are my own flesh and blood. Why should you be the last to bring the king back?'
And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my own flesh and blood? May God deal with me, and more severely, if you are not commander of my army from now on, in place of Joab.'"
So he won over the hearts of all the men of Judah as one man, and they sent word to the king: "Come back, you and all your servants."
So the king came back as far as the Jordan. Judah had come to Gilgal to go and meet the king and to bring the king across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
With him were a thousand men from Benjamin, and Ziba, the steward of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants. They rushed down to the Jordan ahead of the king.
They crossed the ford to bring the king's household over and to do whatever he wished. Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king as he was crossing the Jordan.
He said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty. Do not remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Let not the king take it to heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. But look, today I have come, the first of all the house of Joseph, to come down to meet my lord the king."
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, "Shouldn't Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?"

But David said, "What do I have to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should become an adversary to me today? Should anyone be put to death in Israel today? Don't I know that today I am king over Israel?"
The king said to Shimei, "You will not die." And the king swore an oath to him.

Mephibosheth, the grandson of Saul, also came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he came back in peace.
When he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why didn't you go with me, Mephibosheth?"
He said, "My lord the king, my servant deceived me. Your servant said, 'Let me saddle the donkey for myself, so that I may ride on it and go with the king,' for your servant is lame.
He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God. So do whatever seems good to you.

For all my father's house were nothing but men doomed to death before my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What right do I have, then, to cry out to the king any more?"
The king said to him, "Why do you go on talking? I have decided: you and Ziba are to divide the land."
Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him take it all, now that my lord the king has come home in peace."
Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he crossed the Jordan with the king, to send him on his way across the Jordan.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years old. He had provided for the king while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.
The king said to Barzillai, "Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem."
But Barzillai said to the king, "How many more years do I have to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

I am now eighty years old. Can I tell the difference between good and bad? Can your servant taste what I eat or what I drink? Can I still listen to the voices of men and women singing? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will go only a little way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?

Please let your servant go back, so that I may die in my own town, near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."
The king said, "Chimham will cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you. And anything you ask of me I will do for you."
Then all the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed over. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he went back to his own place.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the troops of Judah brought the king over, and also half the troops of Israel.

Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, and all David's men with him?"

All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why are you angry about this? Have we eaten anything at the king's expense? Or has any gift been given to us?"

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and we have more claim on David than you do. Why then did you treat us with contempt? Weren't we the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were harsher than the words of the men of Israel.

Now a worthless man happened to be there, named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. He blew the ram's horn and said, "We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse! Every man to his tents, Israel!"
So all the men of Israel deserted David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed close to their king, from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

When David came to his house in Jerusalem, the king took the ten women, the concubines he had left to look after the house, and put them in a house under guard. He provided for them, but he did not sleep with them. They were shut away until the day of their death, living as widows.
The king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together for me within three days, and be here yourself."
So Amasa went to call Judah together, but he took longer than the time David had set him.
David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom did. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, or he will find himself fortified cities and escape from our sight."
So Joab's men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites and all the warriors went out after him. They left Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.

When they were at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was wearing his military tunic, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened at his waist. As he stepped forward, it fell out.
Joab said to Amasa, "Are you well, my brother?" And Joab's right hand took Amasa by the beard to kiss him.

Amasa was not on guard against the sword in Joab's hand. Joab struck him in the stomach with it, and his insides spilled out on the ground. He did not strike him a second time, and he died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young men stood over Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, follow Joab!"

Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that all the troops were stopping, he moved Amasa from the road into the field and threw a garment over him, because he saw that everyone who came by him stopped.
Once he had been removed from the road, everyone went on after Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.
Sheba went through all the tribes of Israel to Abel and Beth-maacah, and all the Berites. They assembled and followed him in.

They came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They piled up a siege ramp against the city, and it stood against the outer wall. All the troops who were with Joab were battering the wall to bring it down.
Then a wise woman called out from the city, "Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab, 'Come here, so that I may speak with you.'"
He came near to her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He said, "I am." She said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." He said, "I am listening."
She said, "In the old days they used to say, 'Let them ask at Abel,' and that settled the matter.
I am one of the peaceful and faithful in Israel. You are trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?"
Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy!

That is not the case. A man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has lifted his hand against the king, against David. Hand over just this one man, and I will withdraw from the city." The woman said to Joab, "His head will be thrown to you over the wall."

Then the woman went to all the people with her wisdom, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. He blew the ram's horn, and they dispersed from the city, each to his home. And Joab went back to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab was over the whole army of Israel. Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites.
Adoram was over the forced labor. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder.
Sheva was secretary. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
And Ira the Jairite was David's priest.

In the days of David there was a famine for three years, year after year. David sought the face of the LORD, and the LORD said, "It is because of Saul and his house, stained with blood, because he put the Gibeonites to death."

So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (The Gibeonites were not Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites. The Israelites had sworn an oath to them, but Saul had tried to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah.)
David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? How shall I make atonement, so that you will bless the inheritance of the LORD?"

The Gibeonites said to him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house, and it is not for us to put anyone to death in Israel." He said, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."
They said to the king, "The man who consumed us and planned against us, so that we have been wiped out and have no place anywhere in the territory of Israel,
let seven men of his sons be handed over to us, and we will execute them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen one of the LORD." The king said, "I will hand them over."
But the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath before the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan son of Saul.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Michal daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

He handed them over to the Gibeonites, and they executed them on the mountain before the LORD. The seven of them fell together. They were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Then Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on the rock, from the beginning of the harvest until rain poured down on them from the sky. She did not let the birds of the sky settle on them by day, or the wild animals by night.
When David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine, had done,

David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the citizens of Jabesh-gilead. They had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them on the day the Philistines struck down Saul at Gilboa.
He brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan, and they gathered the bones of those who had been executed.

They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin, at Zela, in the tomb of his father Kish. They did everything the king commanded. After that, God answered prayers for the land.
Once again there was war between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his servants, and they fought against the Philistines, and David grew exhausted.
Then Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the Raphah, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, and who was armed with a new weapon, said he would kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his help, struck the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men swore to him, "You must never again go out with us to battle, so that you do not put out the lamp of Israel."
After this there was another battle with the Philistines, at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who was one of the descendants of the Raphah.
There was another battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.
There was yet another battle, at Gath, where there was a man of great size who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number. He too was descended from the Raphah.
When he taunted Israel, Jonathan son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down.
These four were descended from the Raphah in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
David spoke the words of this song to the LORD on the day when the LORD rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
He said: "The LORD is my rock, my fortress and my deliverer.
My God, my rock, in whom I take refuge; my shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge; my savior, you save me from violence.
I call on the LORD, who is worthy of praise, and I am saved from my enemies.
For the breakers of death surrounded me; the torrents of destruction terrified me.
The cords of Sheol coiled around me; the snares of death confronted me.
In my distress I called on the LORD; to my God I called. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry for help reached his ears.
Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of the heavens quaked; they shook because he was angry.
Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; coals blazed out from him.
He bent the heavens and came down, with thick darkness under his feet.
He rode on a cherub and flew; he was seen on the wings of the wind.
He made darkness a shelter around him, a mass of waters, thick clouds of the skies.
Out of the brightness before him coals of fire blazed.
The LORD thundered from heaven; the Most High uttered his voice.
He sent out arrows and scattered them, lightning, and threw them into confusion.
The channels of the sea were seen; the foundations of the world were laid bare at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
He reached down from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters.
He rescued me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too strong for me.
They confronted me on the day of my disaster, but the LORD was my support.
He brought me out into a wide place; he rescued me because he delighted in me.
The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he repaid me.
For I have kept the ways of the LORD, and I have not done evil by turning from my God.
For all his rulings are before me, and from his decrees I have not turned aside.
I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from my guilt.
So the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in his sight.
With the faithful you show yourself faithful; with the blameless warrior you show yourself blameless.
With the pure you show yourself pure, but with the crooked you show yourself shrewd.
You save a humble people, but your eyes are on the haughty, to bring them low.
For you are my lamp, LORD; the LORD lights up my darkness.
For with you I can charge against a troop; with my God I can leap over a wall.
This God, his way is perfect; the word of the LORD is refined. He is a shield to all who take refuge in him.
For who is God besides the LORD? And who is a rock besides our God?
This God is my strong refuge, and he sets my way free and blameless.
He makes my feet like the feet of a deer, and sets me on my heights.
He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.
You have given me the shield of your salvation; your help has made me great.
You make a wide place for my steps beneath me, and my ankles have not slipped.
I pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn back until they were finished off.
I finished them off and crushed them, so that they could not rise; they fell beneath my feet.
You armed me with strength for battle; you made those who rose against me bow down beneath me.
You made my enemies turn their backs to me; those who hated me, I destroyed them.
They looked for help, but there was no one to save them; they looked to the LORD, but he did not answer them.
I beat them as fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed them and trampled them like the mud of the streets.
You rescued me from the strife of my people; you kept me as the head of nations. A people I did not know now serve me.
Foreigners come cringing to me; as soon as they hear of me, they obey me.
Foreigners lose heart, and they come limping out of their strongholds.
The LORD lives! Blessed be my rock! Exalted be God, the rock of my salvation,
the God who grants me vengeance and brings peoples down under me,
who brings me out from my enemies. You lift me high above those who rise against me; you rescue me from violent men.
So I will praise you, LORD, among the nations, and sing praises to your name.
He is a tower of salvation for his king; he shows faithful love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever."

These are the last words of David: "The declaration of David son of Jesse, the declaration of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet singer of the songs of Israel:
The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; his word was on my tongue.
The God of Israel spoke; the Rock of Israel said to me: 'One who rules over people in righteousness, who rules in the fear of God,
is like the light of morning when the sun rises, a morning without clouds, when the grass springs from the earth through sunshine after rain.'
Is not my house like this with God? For he has made an everlasting covenant with me, ordered in every part and secured. Will he not make all my salvation and all my desire grow?
But the worthless are all like thorns that are tossed away, for they cannot be picked up by hand.
Whoever touches them must arm himself with iron or the shaft of a spear, and they are utterly burned up with fire where they lie."
These are the names of David's mighty warriors: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite, the chief of the officers. He was Adino the Eznite, who killed eight hundred men at one time.
Next to him was Eleazar son of Dodo, son of Ahohi, one of the three mighty warriors with David when they taunted the Philistines who were gathered there for battle. The men of Israel withdrew,

but he stood his ground and struck down the Philistines until his hand grew tired and stuck to the sword. The LORD brought about a great victory that day, and the troops came back after him only to strip the dead.
Next to him was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines had gathered together at Lehi, where there was a plot of ground full of lentils, and the troops fled from the Philistines.
But he took his stand in the middle of the plot, defended it and struck down the Philistines. And the LORD brought about a great victory.
Three of the Thirty, the chiefs, went down at harvest time and came to David at the cave of Adullam, while a band of Philistines was camped in the Valley of Rephaim.
At that time David was in the stronghold, and a Philistine garrison was then at Bethlehem.
David felt a craving and said, "If only someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!"

So the three mighty warriors broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate, and carried it back to David. But he would not drink it. He poured it out to the LORD

and said, "Far be it from me, LORD, that I should do this! Is it not the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" So he would not drink it. These were the deeds of the three mighty warriors.
Abishai, the brother of Joab son of Zeruiah, was chief of the Three. He wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them, and he won a name among the Three.
Was he not the most honored of the Three? He became their commander, but he did not attain to the Three.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was the son of a valiant man from Kabzeel, a man of great deeds. He struck down two champions of Moab. He also went down and killed a lion inside a pit on a snowy day.

He also struck down an Egyptian, a man of impressive appearance. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to him with a club, snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear.
These were the deeds of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he won a name among the three mighty warriors.
He was more honored than the Thirty, but he did not attain to the Three. And David put him in charge of his bodyguard.
Among the Thirty were Asahel the brother of Joab; Elhanan son of Dodo, of Bethlehem;
Shammah the Harodite; Elika the Harodite;
Helez the Paltite; Ira son of Ikkesh, the Tekoite;
Abiezer the Anathothite; Mebunnai the Hushathite;
Zalmon the Ahohite; Maharai the Netophathite;
Heleb son of Baanah, the Netophathite; Ittai son of Ribai, from Gibeah of the Benjaminites;
Benaiah the Pirathonite; Hiddai of the ravines of Gaash;
Abi-albon the Arbathite; Azmaveth the Barhumite;
Eliahba the Shaalbonite; the sons of Jashen; Jonathan;
Shammah the Hararite; Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite;
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite; Eliam son of Ahithophel, the Gilonite;
Hezrai the Carmelite; Paarai the Arbite;
Igal son of Nathan, from Zobah; Bani the Gadite;
Zelek the Ammonite; Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah;
Ira the Ithrite; Gareb the Ithrite;
and Uriah the Hittite. Thirty-seven in all.
Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, count Israel and Judah."

So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and register the people, so that I may know the number of the people."
Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God multiply the people a hundred times over, while the eyes of my lord the king can still see it! But why does my lord the king want to do this?"
But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army went out from the king's presence to register the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and camped at Aroer, south of the town that is in the middle of the valley, toward Gad and on to Jazer.
Then they came to Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and they came to Dan-jaan and around toward Sidon.
They came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the towns of the Hivites and the Canaanites, and they went out to the Negev of Judah at Beersheba.
So they went through the whole land, and at the end of nine months and twenty days they came back to Jerusalem.
Joab gave the king the total from the registration of the people: in Israel there were eight hundred thousand valiant men who could draw the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand.

But David's conscience troubled him after he had counted the people. David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, LORD, please take away the guilt of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."
When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to the prophet Gad, David's seer:
"Go and tell David, 'This is what the LORD says: I am setting three things before you. Choose one of them, and I will do it to you.'"

So Gad came to David and told him. He said to him, "Shall seven years of famine come upon you in your land? Or shall you flee for three months before your enemies while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days of plague in your land? Now consider and decide what answer I should take back to the one who sent me."
David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great, but do not let me fall into human hands."
So the LORD sent a plague on Israel from the morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand of the people died, from Dan to Beersheba.

When the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented concerning the disaster and said to the angel who was destroying the people, "Enough! Now hold back your hand." The angel of the LORD was then by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel who was striking down the people, he said to the LORD, "I am the one who has sinned; I am the one who has done wrong. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house."
That day Gad came to David and said to him, "Go up and set up an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
So David went up at Gad's word, as the LORD had commanded.
When Araunah looked down and saw the king and his servants coming over toward him, Araunah went out and bowed down to the king with his face to the ground.
Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David said, "To buy the threshing floor from you, to build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague may be held back from the people."

Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take it and offer up whatever seems good to him. Look, here are the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the oxen's yokes for the wood.
All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king." And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept you."

But the king said to Araunah, "No, I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
David built an altar to the LORD there and offered burnt offerings and fellowship offerings. Then the LORD answered prayers for the land, and the plague was held back from Israel.
King David was old, well on in years. They covered him with blankets, but he could not get warm.

So his servants said to him, "Let a young woman, a virgin, be found for my lord the king. Let her wait on the king and take care of him. She can lie in your arms, and then my lord the king will get warm."
So they searched throughout the territory of Israel for a beautiful young woman. They found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king.
The young woman was very beautiful. She took care of the king and served him, but the king did not have sexual relations with her.
Now Adonijah son of Haggith was putting himself forward, saying, "I will be king." He got himself chariots and horsemen, with fifty men to run ahead of him.
His father had never once crossed him by asking, "Why have you done this?" He was also very handsome, and he was born next after Absalom.
He conferred with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they followed Adonijah and supported him.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei and David's warriors did not side with Adonijah.

Adonijah sacrificed sheep, cattle and fattened calves by the Stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En-rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the men of Judah who were the king's servants.
But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the warriors, or his brother Solomon.
Then Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, "Haven't you heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king, and our lord David does not know it?
So now come, let me give you some advice, so that you can save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.
Go in to King David and say to him, 'My lord the king, did you not swear to your servant, "Your son Solomon will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne"? Why then has Adonijah become king?'
Then, while you are still there speaking with the king, I will come in after you and confirm what you say."
So Bathsheba went in to the king in his room. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was serving the king.
Bathsheba bowed low and knelt before the king. The king said, "What do you want?"
She said to him, "My lord, you yourself swore to your servant by the LORD your God, 'Your son Solomon will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne.'
But now, look, Adonijah has become king, and now, my lord the king, you do not know it.

He has sacrificed oxen, fattened calves and sheep in great numbers, and he has invited all the king's sons, Abiathar the priest and Joab the commander of the army. But he has not invited your servant Solomon.
As for you, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, for you to tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.
Otherwise, when my lord the king sleeps with his ancestors, my son Solomon and I will be treated as criminals."
While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet arrived.
The king was told, "Nathan the prophet is here." He came before the king and bowed down to the king with his face to the ground.
Nathan said, "My lord the king, have you said, 'Adonijah will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne'?

For today he has gone down and sacrificed oxen, fattened calves and sheep in great numbers. He has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army and Abiathar the priest. They are there now, eating and drinking in his presence, and they are saying, 'Long live King Adonijah!'
But he has not invited me, your servant, or Zadok the priest, or Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.
Has my lord the king done this without letting your servant know who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?"
Then King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." She came into the king's presence and stood before the king.
The king swore an oath and said, "As the LORD lives, who has rescued my life from every trouble,
just as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Your son Solomon will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place,' so I will do this very day."
Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and knelt before the king. She said, "May my lord King David live forever!"
King David said, "Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet and Benaiah son of Jehoiada to me." They came before the king,
and the king said to them, "Take your lord's servants with you. Have my son Solomon ride on my own mule, and take him down to Gihon.
There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint him king over Israel. Blow the ram's horn and say, 'Long live King Solomon!'
Then come up after him, and he is to come and sit on my throne. He will be king in my place. I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah."
Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so too.
As the LORD has been with my lord the king, so may he be with Solomon, and may he make his throne even greater than the throne of my lord King David."
So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down. They had Solomon ride on King David's mule, and they took him to Gihon.
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. They blew the ram's horn, and all the people said, "Long live King Solomon!"
All the people went up after him, playing flutes and rejoicing greatly, so that the earth split with the noise.
Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they finished eating. When Joab heard the sound of the ram's horn, he said, "Why is the city in such an uproar?"
While he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said, "Come in, for you are a worthy man, and you must be bringing good news."
Jonathan answered Adonijah, "Not at all! Our lord King David has made Solomon king.
The king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and they have had him ride on the king's mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon. They have gone up from there rejoicing, and the city is in an uproar. That is the noise you have heard.
Solomon has even taken his seat on the royal throne.

And the king's servants have come to congratulate our lord King David, saying, 'May God make the name of Solomon more famous than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne!' And the king bowed down on his bed.
The king also said this: 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has today provided someone to sit on my throne, while my own eyes see it.'"
Then all Adonijah's guests trembled. They got up and went their own ways.
Adonijah was afraid of Solomon. He got up, went and took hold of the horns of the altar.

Solomon was told, "Adonijah is afraid of King Solomon. He has taken hold of the horns of the altar and is saying, 'Let King Solomon swear to me today that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.'"
Solomon said, "If he proves to be a worthy man, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground. But if wrongdoing is found in him, he will die."
Then King Solomon sent men, and they brought him down from the altar. He came and bowed down to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, "Go home."
When the time drew near for David to die, he gave his son Solomon these instructions:
"I am about to go the way of all the earth. So be strong, and show yourself a man.

Keep the charge of the LORD your God: walk in his ways, and keep his decrees, his commands, his rulings and his statutes, as it is written in the Law of Moses, so that you may succeed in everything you do and wherever you turn,

and so that the LORD may keep the promise he made about me: 'If your sons take care how they live, walking before me faithfully with all their heart and with all their soul, you will never lack a man on the throne of Israel.'

"You also know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them, shedding the blood of war in peacetime, and he put the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet.
Act according to your wisdom, and do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace.
But show faithful love to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for they stood by me when I fled from your brother Absalom.

"Look, you have with you Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim. He cursed me with a bitter curse on the day I went to Mahanaim. When he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, 'I will not put you to death with the sword.'
But now, do not let him go unpunished. You are a wise man, and you will know what to do to him. Bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood."
Then David slept with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David.
David reigned over Israel for forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
So Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established.
Then Adonijah son of Haggith came to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. She said, "Do you come in peace?" He said, "In peace."
Then he said, "I have something to say to you." She said, "Speak."
He said, "You know that the kingship was mine, and all Israel looked to me to be their king. But the kingship has turned around and gone to my brother, for it came to him from the LORD.
Now I have one request to ask of you. Do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak."
He said, "Please speak to King Solomon, for he will not refuse you, and ask him to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife."
Bathsheba said, "Very well. I will speak to the king for you."

So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him for Adonijah. The king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat down on his throne and had a throne set for the king's mother, and she sat at his right hand.
She said, "I have one small request to ask of you. Do not refuse me." The king said to her, "Ask, my mother, for I will not refuse you."
She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife."

King Solomon answered his mother, "Why are you asking for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for the kingdom for him too, since he is my older brother, for him and for Abiathar the priest and for Joab son of Zeruiah!"
Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, "May God deal with me, and more besides, if Adonijah has not made this request at the cost of his life!
Now, as the LORD lives, who has established me and set me on the throne of my father David, and who has made me a house as he promised, Adonijah will be put to death today."
So King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he struck Adonijah down, and he died.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your fields. You deserve to die, but I will not put you to death today, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David, and because you shared in all the hardships my father suffered."
So Solomon banished Abiathar from being a priest of the LORD, fulfilling the word that the LORD had spoken at Shiloh about the house of Eli.
When the news reached Joab, for Joab had sided with Adonijah, though he had not sided with Absalom, Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and took hold of the horns of the altar.
King Solomon was told, "Joab has fled to the tent of the LORD, and he is there beside the altar." So Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down."

Benaiah went to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "This is what the king says: 'Come out!'" But he said, "No, I will die here." Benaiah brought word back to the king: "This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me."
The king said to him, "Do as he has said. Strike him down and bury him, and so take away from me and from my father's house the blood that Joab shed without cause.

The LORD will bring his blood back on his own head, because he struck down two men more righteous and better than he was, and killed them with the sword without my father David knowing it: Abner son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah.
Their blood will come back on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants forever. But for David and his descendants, his house and his throne, there will be peace from the LORD forever."
So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck Joab down and killed him. He was buried at his own home in the wilderness.
The king put Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army in his place, and the king put Zadok the priest in place of Abiathar.
Then the king sent for Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there. Do not go out from there anywhere at all.
On the day you go out and cross the Kidron Valley, know for certain that you will die. Your blood will be on your own head."
Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good. Your servant will do just as my lord the king has said." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.
But at the end of three years, two of Shimei's slaves ran away to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei was told, "Your slaves are in Gath."
So Shimei got up, saddled his donkey and went to Achish at Gath to look for his slaves. Shimei went and brought his slaves back from Gath.
Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had come back.

The king sent for Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD, and warn you, 'On the day you go out and go anywhere at all, know for certain that you will die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is good. I have heard it.'
Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the command I gave you?"
The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your heart all the wrong you did to my father David. The LORD will bring your wrongdoing back on your own head.
But King Solomon will be blessed, and the throne of David will be established before the LORD forever."
Then the king gave orders to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck Shimei down, and he died. So the kingdom was firmly established in Solomon's hands.

Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He married Pharaoh's daughter and brought her to the City of David, until he had finished building his own house, the house of the LORD, and the wall around Jerusalem.
The people, however, were still sacrificing at the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD in those days.
Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the decrees of his father David, except that he offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, because that was the great high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream at night, and God said, "Ask for whatever you want me to give you."

Solomon said, "You have shown great faithful love to your servant, my father David, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness and with an upright heart toward you. And you have kept this great faithful love for him and have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is today.
Now, LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of my father David. But I am only a young boy. I do not know how to go out or come in.
And your servant is here among your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted.
So give your servant a listening heart to govern your people and to discern between good and evil. For who is able to govern this great people of yours?"
It was good in the eyes of the Lord that Solomon had asked for this.

So God said to him, "Because you have asked for this, and have not asked for a long life for yourself, or asked for riches for yourself, or asked for the lives of your enemies, but have asked for understanding to discern what is just,
I am now doing as you asked. I am giving you a wise and discerning heart, so that there has been no one like you before you, and no one like you will arise after you.
I am also giving you what you have not asked for, both riches and honor, so that no one among the kings will be like you as long as you live.
And if you walk in my ways, keeping my decrees and my commands, as your father David walked, I will give you a long life."

Then Solomon woke up, and he realized it had been a dream. He went to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. He offered burnt offerings and fellowship offerings, and he held a feast for all his servants.
Then two women who were prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.
One of the women said, "Please, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house.
On the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. We were alone. There was no one else with us in the house, only the two of us in the house.
During the night this woman's son died, because she lay on him.
She got up in the middle of the night and took my son from beside me while your servant was asleep. She laid him in her arms, and she laid her dead son in my arms.
When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, there he was, dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, I saw that he was not the son I had borne."

The other woman said, "No! The living one is my son, and the dead one is your son." But the first woman said, "No! The dead one is your son, and the living one is my son." So they argued before the king.
Then the king said, "This one says, 'This is my son, the living one, and your son is the dead one.' And that one says, 'No! Your son is the dead one, and my son is the living one.'"
So the king said, "Bring me a sword." And they brought a sword before the king.
Then the king said, "Cut the living child in two, and give half to one and half to the other."

But the woman whose son was the living one spoke to the king, because her heart went out to her son. She said, "Please, my lord, give her the living baby! Do not kill him!" But the other said, "He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!"
Then the king answered, "Give the living baby to the first woman, and do not kill him. She is his mother."
When all Israel heard the judgment the king had given, they stood in awe of the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
King Solomon was king over all Israel.
These were his officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest.
Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, were secretaries. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the army. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Azariah son of Nathan was over the governors. Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and the king's friend.
Ahishar was in charge of the palace. Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon had twelve governors over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each one had to provide food for one month in the year.
These are their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim;
Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan;
Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (Socoh and all the land of Hepher were his);
Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath daughter of Solomon as his wife);
Baana son of Ahilud, in Taanach and Megiddo, and all Beth-shean, which is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam;
Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (the villages of Jair son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, were his, and the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, was his: sixty large cities with walls and bronze bars);
Ahinadab son of Iddo, in Mahanaim;
Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he too had married Basemath daughter of Solomon);
Baana son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah, in Issachar;
Shimei son of Ela, in Benjamin;
Geber son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the land of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was in the land.
The people of Judah and Israel were as many as the sand on the seashore. They ate and drank and were happy.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.
Solomon's provisions for one day were thirty kors of fine flour and sixty kors of meal,
ten fattened oxen, twenty oxen from the pasture and a hundred sheep and goats, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks and fattened fowl.
For he had dominion over the whole region west of the River, from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the River, and he had peace on every side around him.
Judah and Israel lived in safety, each man under his own vine and under his own fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen.
Those governors provided food for King Solomon and for everyone who came to King Solomon's table, each in his month. They let nothing be lacking.
They also brought barley and straw for the horses and the chariot horses to the place where it was needed, each according to his assignment.
God gave Solomon wisdom and very great understanding, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom was greater than the wisdom of all the people of the east, and greater than all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than anyone else, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol. His fame spread through all the surrounding nations.
He spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs numbered 1,005.
He spoke about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He also spoke about animals, birds, creatures that creep on the ground, and fish.
People came from all nations to hear Solomon's wisdom, sent by all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.
Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon when he heard that he had been anointed king in place of his father, for Hiram had always been a friend of David.
Solomon sent this message to Hiram:
"You know that my father David could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the wars that surrounded him, until the LORD put his enemies under the soles of my feet.
But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is no adversary and no misfortune.
So I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD told my father David: 'Your son, whom I will put on your throne in your place, will build the house for my name.'

So now give orders for cedars to be cut for me from Lebanon. My servants will work with your servants, and I will pay you whatever wages you set for your servants. For you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."
When Hiram heard Solomon's message, he was very glad and said, "Blessed be the LORD today, who has given David a wise son over this great people."
Hiram sent word to Solomon: "I have heard the message you sent me. I will do all you want in the matter of cedar timber and cypress timber.

My servants will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea, and I will make them into rafts on the sea to go to the place you tell me. There I will break them up, and you can take them away. And you will do what I want by providing food for my household."
So Hiram gave Solomon all the cedar timber and cypress timber he wanted.
Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat as food for his household, and twenty kors of pressed olive oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year after year.
The LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
King Solomon conscripted forced labor from all Israel, and the forced labor numbered 30,000 men.
He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of 10,000 a month. They spent a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon had 70,000 men who carried loads and 80,000 who cut stone in the hills,
besides Solomon's 3,300 chief officers who were in charge of the work and directed the people doing the work.
At the king's command they quarried large stones, costly stones, to lay the foundation of the house with dressed stone.
Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the men of Gebal cut them, and they prepared the timber and the stones to build the house.

In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house for the LORD.
The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty wide and thirty cubits high.
The porch in front of the main hall of the house was twenty cubits long, across the width of the house, and it extended ten cubits in front of the house.
He made windows for the house with recessed frames.
Against the wall of the house he built a side structure all around, against the walls of the house all around the main hall and the inner sanctuary, and he made side rooms all around.

The lowest story was five cubits wide, the middle one six cubits wide and the third seven cubits wide. For he made offsets all around the outside of the house, so that the beams would not be set into the walls of the house.
When the house was built, it was built with stone finished at the quarry. No hammer or axe or any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.
The entrance to the middle story of side rooms was on the south side of the house. Stairs went up to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third.
So he built the house and finished it. He roofed the house with beams and planks of cedar.
He built the side structure against the whole house, each story five cubits high, and it was joined to the house with cedar beams.
Then the word of the LORD came to Solomon:
"As for this house you are building, if you walk in my decrees, carry out my rulings and keep all my commands by walking in them, I will fulfill through you the promise I made to your father David.
I will live among the Israelites, and I will not abandon my people Israel."
So Solomon built the house and finished it.

He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house up to the ceiling he covered them with wood on the inside, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress.
He built off twenty cubits at the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor up to the ceiling. He built this inside as an inner sanctuary, as the most holy place.
The house, that is, the main hall in front of it, was forty cubits long.
The cedar inside the house was carved with gourds and open flowers. All was cedar. No stone was seen.
He prepared the inner sanctuary inside the house, to put the ark of the covenant of the LORD there.
The inside of the inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid the altar with cedar.
Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold. He stretched chains of gold across the front of the inner sanctuary, and he overlaid it with gold.
He overlaid the whole house with gold, until the whole house was finished. He also overlaid with gold the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary.
In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high.
One wing of the cherub was five cubits long, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits long: ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.
The second cherub also measured ten cubits. Both cherubim had the same measurements and the same shape.
The height of the one cherub was ten cubits, and so was that of the other cherub.

He put the cherubim in the middle of the inner room of the house. The wings of the cherubim were spread out, so that the wing of one touched the one wall and the wing of the other cherub touched the other wall, while their wings touched each other in the middle of the room, wing to wing.
He overlaid the cherubim with gold.
On all the walls of the house all around he carved engravings of cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, in both the inner and the outer rooms.
He overlaid the floor of the house with gold, in both the inner and the outer rooms.
For the entrance of the inner sanctuary he made doors of olive wood. The lintel and the doorposts formed a fifth.
On the two doors of olive wood he carved cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold. He spread the gold over the cherubim and the palm trees.
In the same way, for the entrance of the main hall he made doorposts of olive wood, a fourth.
There were two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door turned on pivots, and the two leaves of the other door turned on pivots.
He carved cherubim, palm trees and open flowers on them, and he overlaid them with gold fitted evenly over the carving.
He built the inner courtyard with three courses of dressed stone and one course of cedar beams.
In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv.
In the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its details and according to all its specifications. He spent seven years building it.
Solomon spent thirteen years building his own house, and he finished his whole house.
He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide and thirty cubits high, on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.
It was roofed with cedar above the beams that were on the pillars, forty-five of them, fifteen in each row.
There were three rows of window frames, with window facing window three times.
All the doorways and doorposts had square frames, with window facing window three times.
He made the Hall of Pillars fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. There was a porch in front of the pillars, with pillars and a canopy in front of them.
He made the Hall of the Throne where he was to judge, the Hall of Judgment. It was lined with cedar from floor to floor.
His own house where he was to live, in the other courtyard set back from the hall, was of the same workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married.

All these were made of costly stones, dressed stone cut to measure and trimmed with saws on the inside and the outside, from the foundation to the coping, and on the outside as far as the great courtyard.
The foundation was laid with costly stones, large stones, stones of ten cubits and stones of eight cubits.
Above them were costly stones, dressed stone cut to measure, and cedar.
The great courtyard had three courses of dressed stone all around and one course of cedar beams, as did the inner courtyard of the house of the LORD and the porch of the house.
King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.

He was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a craftsman in bronze. He was filled with wisdom, understanding and skill for doing every kind of work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work.
He cast the two pillars of bronze. The one pillar was eighteen cubits high, and a cord of twelve cubits went around the other pillar.
He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The one capital was five cubits high, and the other capital was five cubits high.
There were lattices of network and wreaths of chainwork for the capitals on top of the pillars, seven for the one capital and seven for the other capital.
He made the pillars, and there were two rows all around on the one network, to cover the capitals that were on top of the pomegranates. He did the same for the other capital.
The capitals that were on top of the pillars in the porch were of lily work, four cubits.
The capitals on the two pillars also had pomegranates above, next to the rounded part beside the network. There were two hundred pomegranates in rows all around, on the other capital as well.
He set up the pillars at the porch of the main hall. He set up the pillar on the right and named it Jakin, and he set up the pillar on the left and named it Boaz.
On top of the pillars was lily work. So the work on the pillars was finished.
He made the Sea of cast metal, ten cubits from rim to rim, round all around and five cubits high. A line of thirty cubits measured around it.
Under its rim, gourds encircled it all around, ten to a cubit, going all around the Sea. The gourds were in two rows, cast in one piece with it.
It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south and three facing east. The Sea rested on top of them, and all their hindquarters were toward the center.
It was a handbreadth thick, and its rim was made like the rim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It held two thousand baths.
He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide and three cubits high.
This is how the stands were made: they had panels, and the panels were set between the frames.
On the panels between the frames were lions, oxen and cherubim. On the frames there was a pedestal above, and below the lions and the oxen were wreaths of hanging work.
Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles, and its four feet had supports. The supports were cast underneath the basin, with wreaths at the side of each.
Its opening inside the crown and upward was a cubit. Its opening was round, made like a pedestal, a cubit and a half. On its opening there were also engravings. Their panels were square, not round.
The four wheels were underneath the panels, and the axles of the wheels were in the stand. Each wheel was a cubit and a half high.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels. Their axles, rims, spokes and hubs were all of cast metal.
There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were of one piece with the stand.
At the top of the stand there was a round band half a cubit high. On top of the stand, its stays and its panels were of one piece with it.
On the surfaces of its stays and on its panels he engraved cherubim, lions and palm trees, wherever there was space, with wreaths all around.
This is how he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, with the same measurements and the same shape.
He made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, and each basin measured four cubits. There was one basin on each of the ten stands.
He put five of the stands on the south side of the house and five on the north side. He put the Sea on the south side of the house, toward the southeast.
Hiram also made the basins, the shovels and the bowls. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD:
the two pillars; the two bowls of the capitals that were on top of the pillars; the two networks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on top of the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars;
the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands;
the one Sea, and the twelve oxen under the Sea;
and the pots, the shovels and the bowls. All these utensils that Hiram made for King Solomon for the house of the LORD were of polished bronze.
The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon left all the utensils unweighed, because there were so very many. The weight of the bronze was never determined.
Solomon also made all the utensils that were in the house of the LORD: the gold altar; the gold table on which the bread of the Presence was placed;
the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, in front of the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps and the tongs, of gold;

the cups, the wick trimmers, the bowls, the dishes and the firepans, of pure gold; and the sockets for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, the main hall, of gold.

So all the work that King Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. Then Solomon brought in the things his father David had dedicated: the silver, the gold and the utensils. He put them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.

Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the ancestral families of the Israelites, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the City of David, which is Zion.
All the men of Israel assembled before King Solomon at the festival in the month of Ethanim, which is the seventh month.
When all the elders of Israel had come, the priests took up the ark.
They brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting and all the holy utensils that were in the tent. The priests and the Levites brought them up.
King Solomon and the whole community of Israel who had gathered to him were with him before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and cattle that they could not be counted or numbered.
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place, in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the most holy place, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
