I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined at home. He said, "Let us meet at the house of God, inside the temple, and let us shut the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you tonight."
But I said, "Should a man like me run away? And can a man like me go into the temple and live? I will not go in."
Then I realized that God had not sent him. He had spoken this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
He had been hired for this purpose: to frighten me, so that I would do as he said and sin, and they would have a reason to give me a bad name, so that they could taunt me.
Remember, my God, Tobiah and Sanballat for these deeds of theirs, and also Noadiah the prophetess and the rest of the prophets who were trying to frighten me.
So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days.
When all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and lost their confidence, for they knew that this work had been done by our God.
In those days too, the nobles of Judah were sending many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters were coming to them.
For many in Judah were bound to him by oath, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.
They also kept telling me about his good deeds and reporting my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to frighten me.
When the wall had been rebuilt and I had set up the doors, the gatekeepers, the singers and the Levites were appointed.
I put my brother Hanani in charge of Jerusalem, along with Hananiah the commander of the fortress, for he was a faithful man and feared God more than most.

I said to them, "The gates of Jerusalem are not to be opened until the sun is hot. While the gatekeepers are still on duty, let them shut the doors and bar them. And appoint guards from the inhabitants of Jerusalem, each at his post and each opposite his own house."
The city was wide and large, but there were few people in it, and the houses had not been rebuilt.

Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles, the officials and the people, to be registered by their genealogy. I found the book of the genealogy of those who had come up at the first, and I found this written in it:

These are the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of the exiles, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile. They returned to Jerusalem and to Judah, each to his own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
the descendants of Pahath-moab, through the descendants of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818;
the descendants of Ater, through Hezekiah, 98;
the men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188;
the men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah and Beeroth, 743;
the men of Ramah and Geba, 621;
the men of Bethel and Ai, 123;
the men of the other Nebo, 52;
the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254;
the people of Lod, Hadid and Ono, 721;
The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973;
The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua, through Kadmiel, through the descendants of Hodevah, 74.
The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 148.
The gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, the descendants of Ater, the descendants of Talmon, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hatita and the descendants of Shobai, 138.
The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth,
the descendants of Keros, the descendants of Sia, the descendants of Padon,
the descendants of Lebana, the descendants of Hagaba, the descendants of Shalmai,
the descendants of Hanan, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Gahar,
the descendants of Reaiah, the descendants of Rezin, the descendants of Nekoda,
the descendants of Gazzam, the descendants of Uzza, the descendants of Paseah,
the descendants of Besai, the descendants of the Meunim, the descendants of the Nephishesim,
the descendants of Bakbuk, the descendants of Hakupha, the descendants of Harhur,
the descendants of Bazlith, the descendants of Mehida, the descendants of Harsha,
the descendants of Barkos, the descendants of Sisera, the descendants of Temah,
the descendants of Neziah and the descendants of Hatipha.
The descendants of Solomon's servants: the descendants of Sotai, the descendants of Sophereth, the descendants of Perida,
the descendants of Jaala, the descendants of Darkon, the descendants of Giddel,
the descendants of Shephatiah, the descendants of Hattil, the descendants of Pochereth-hazzebaim and the descendants of Amon.
All the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants: 392.
These are the ones who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon and Immer, but they could not show that their ancestral families and their descent were from Israel:
the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah and the descendants of Nekoda, 642.

And of the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz and the descendants of Barzillai, who had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name.
These searched for their entry among those recorded in the genealogies, but it was not found, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean.
The governor told them not to eat any of the most holy food until the priest arose who could consult the Urim and Thummim.
besides their male and female servants, who numbered 7,337. They also had 245 male and female singers.
The camels numbered 435, and the donkeys 6,720.
Some of the heads of the ancestral families gave to the work. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 basins and 530 priests' garments.
And some of the heads of the ancestral families gave to the treasury for the work 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver.
What the rest of the people gave was 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver and 67 priests' garments.

So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants and all Israel settled in their towns. The seventh month came, and the Israelites were in their towns.
All the people gathered as one man in the square in front of the Water Gate. They asked Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the Law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded Israel.
So on the first day of the seventh month Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, men and women and all who could understand what they heard.

He read from it in the square in front of the Water Gate from daybreak until midday, in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand. And all the people listened closely to the book of the Law.

Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that had been made for the purpose. Beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah on his right, and Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah and Meshullam on his left.
Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it, all the people stood up.
Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, "Amen! Amen!" lifting up their hands. Then they bowed down and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.

Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah and the Levites helped the people understand the Law, while the people stayed in their places.
They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood what was read.

Then Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were teaching the people said to all the people, "This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep." For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law.

He said to them, "Go, eat rich food and drink sweet drinks, and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, for this day is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength."
The Levites calmed all the people, saying, "Be still, for the day is holy. Do not grieve."
Then all the people went away to eat and drink, to send portions and to celebrate with great joy, because they had understood the words that had been made known to them.
On the second day the heads of the ancestral families of all the people, the priests and the Levites gathered to Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law.
They found written in the Law, which the LORD had commanded through Moses, that the Israelites were to live in shelters during the festival in the seventh month,

and that they were to announce it and send a proclamation through all their towns and in Jerusalem: "Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, of wild olive, of myrtle, of palm and of leafy trees, to make shelters, as it is written."

So the people went out and brought them, and they made shelters for themselves, each on his roof, and in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, in the square at the Water Gate and in the square at the Gate of Ephraim.

The whole assembly of those who had returned from the captivity made shelters and lived in the shelters. From the days of Joshua son of Nun to that day the Israelites had not done so. And there was very great joy.
Day after day, from the first day to the last day, Ezra read from the book of the Law of God. They kept the festival for seven days, and on the eighth day there was a closing assembly, as prescribed.
On the twenty-fourth day of this month the Israelites assembled, fasting and wearing sackcloth, with earth on their heads.
Those of Israelite descent separated themselves from all foreigners, and they stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their ancestors.
They stood up in their places and read from the book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day, and for another quarter they confessed and worshiped the LORD their God.
On the platform of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani and Chenani, and they cried out with a loud voice to the LORD their God.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah and Pethahiah, said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting! May they bless your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.

You alone are the LORD. You made the heavens, the highest heavens and all their host, the earth and everything on it, the seas and everything in them. You give life to them all, and the host of heaven worships you.
You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham.

You found his heart faithful before you, and you made the covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites and the Girgashites, to give it to his descendants. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.
You saw the affliction of our ancestors in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea.

You performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against all his servants and against all the people of his land, for you knew how arrogantly they had treated them. You made a name for yourself, as it is today.
You split the sea before them, and they passed through the middle of the sea on dry ground. But you threw their pursuers into the depths, like a stone into mighty waters.
By a pillar of cloud you led them by day, and by a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way they were to go.
You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven. You gave them right rulings and true instructions, good decrees and commands.
You made known to them your holy Sabbath, and through your servant Moses you gave them commands, decrees and a law.
You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger, and you brought water out of the rock for their thirst. You told them to go in and take possession of the land that you had sworn to give them.
But they, our ancestors, acted arrogantly. They stiffened their necks and did not listen to your commands.

They refused to listen and did not remember the wonders you had done among them. They stiffened their necks and in their rebellion appointed a leader to go back to their slavery. But you are a God of forgiveness, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in faithful love, and you did not forsake them.
Even when they made for themselves a calf of cast metal and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,' and committed great blasphemies,

you in your great compassion did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud did not leave them by day, to lead them on the way, nor the pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way they were to go.
You gave your good spirit to instruct them. You did not withhold your manna from their mouths, and you gave them water for their thirst.
For forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell.
You gave them kingdoms and peoples, and you allotted them to every corner. They took possession of the land of Sihon, the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan.
You made their children as many as the stars of the sky, and you brought them into the land that you had told their ancestors to enter and possess.

So the children went in and took possession of the land. You subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hands, with their kings and the peoples of the land, to do with them as they pleased.

They captured fortified cities and fertile land. They took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already dug, vineyards, olive groves and fruit trees in abundance. They ate and were filled and grew fat, and they delighted in your great goodness.

But they were disobedient and rebelled against you. They threw your law behind their backs. They killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies.

So you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who oppressed them. But in the time of their distress they cried out to you, and you heard from heaven, and in your great compassion you gave them deliverers, who delivered them from the hand of their enemies.

But as soon as they had rest, they again did evil before you. So you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, who ruled over them. Then they cried out to you again, and you heard from heaven, and in your compassion you rescued them many times.

You warned them, to turn them back to your law, but they acted arrogantly and did not listen to your commands. They sinned against your rulings, which give life to the one who does them. They turned a stubborn shoulder, stiffened their necks and would not listen.
For many years you were patient with them. You warned them by your spirit through your prophets, but they would not listen. So you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands.
But in your great compassion you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and compassionate God.

So now, our God, the great, mighty and awesome God, who keeps covenant and faithful love, do not treat as small all the hardship that has come upon us, upon our kings, our leaders, our priests, our prophets, our ancestors and all your people, from the days of the kings of Assyria until this day.
You have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have acted faithfully, but we have done wrong.
Our kings, our leaders, our priests and our ancestors did not keep your law. They did not pay attention to your commands and your statutes, which you solemnly declared to them.
Even in their own kingdom, amid the great goodness that you gave them, and in the broad and fertile land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their evil deeds.
Here we are, slaves today, slaves in the very land that you gave our ancestors to enjoy its fruit and its good things.
Its rich produce goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress."
Because of all this, we are making a firm agreement and putting it in writing. On the sealed document are the names of our leaders, our Levites and our priests.
On the sealed documents were: Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah;
Maaziah, Bilgai and Shemaiah. These were the priests.
The Levites: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the descendants of Henadad, Kadmiel,
and their kinsmen: Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
The leaders of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani,

The rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants and all who had separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to keep the Law of God, with their wives, their sons and their daughters, all who had knowledge and understanding,

joined with their kinsmen, their nobles, and bound themselves with a curse and an oath to walk in the Law of God, which was given through Moses the servant of God, and to keep and do all the commands of the LORD our Lord, and his rulings and his decrees.
We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land, and we will not take their daughters for our sons.

When the peoples of the land bring goods or any grain to sell on the Sabbath day, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day. And in the seventh year we will leave the land unworked and cancel every debt.
We also take on ourselves the obligation to give a third of a shekel each year for the service of the house of our God:

for the bread of the Presence, for the regular grain offering and the regular burnt offering, for the Sabbaths, the new moons and the appointed festivals, for the holy offerings, and for the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.

We, the priests, the Levites and the people, have cast lots for the wood offering, to bring it to the house of our God by our ancestral families at appointed times year by year, to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.
We will bring the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all the fruit of every tree year by year to the house of the LORD.

We will also bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God, the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock, as it is written in the Law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks.

We will bring the first of our dough, our contributions, the fruit of every tree, the new wine and the olive oil to the priests, to the storerooms of the house of our God, and the tithe of our ground to the Levites, for it is the Levites who collect the tithes in all the towns where we work.

A priest descended from Aaron is to be with the Levites when the Levites collect the tithes, and the Levites are to bring a tenth of the tithes up to the house of our God, to the storerooms of the treasury.

For the Israelites and the descendants of Levi are to bring the contribution of grain, new wine and olive oil to the storerooms, where the articles of the sanctuary are kept, and where the priests who minister, the gatekeepers and the singers are. We will not neglect the house of our God.
The leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of every ten to live in Jerusalem, the holy city, while the other nine stayed in the towns.
The people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.

These are the heads of the province who lived in Jerusalem. In the towns of Judah, each lived on his own property in their towns: Israelites, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants.

In Jerusalem lived some of the descendants of Judah and some of the descendants of Benjamin. Of the descendants of Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, of the descendants of Perez;
and Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite.
All the descendants of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were 468 capable men.
These are the descendants of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah;
and after him Gabbai and Sallai, 928.
Joel son of Zichri was the officer over them, and Judah son of Hassenuah was second in command over the city.
Of the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jachin,
Seraiah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the officer in charge of the house of God,
and their kinsmen who did the work of the house, 822; and Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah,
and his kinsmen, heads of ancestral families, 242; and Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer,
and their kinsmen, capable warriors, 128. The officer over them was Zabdiel son of Haggedolim.
Of the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni;
and Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the heads of the Levites, who were in charge of the outside work of the house of God;

and Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, the leader who began the thanksgiving at prayer, and Bakbukiah, the second among his kinsmen; and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.
All the Levites in the holy city were 284.
The gatekeepers: Akkub, Talmon and their kinsmen, who kept watch at the gates, 172.
The rest of Israel, the priests and the Levites, were in all the towns of Judah, each on his own inheritance.
The temple servants lived on the Ophel, and Ziha and Gishpa were in charge of the temple servants.
The officer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, of the descendants of Asaph, the singers, over the work of the house of God.
For there was a command from the king concerning them, and a fixed arrangement for the singers, as each day required.
Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, of the descendants of Zerah son of Judah, was the king's agent in every matter concerning the people.
As for the villages with their fields: some of the descendants of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba and its settlements, in Dibon and its settlements, in Jekabzeel and its villages,
in Jeshua, in Moladah and in Beth-pelet,
in Hazar-shual, in Beersheba and its settlements,
in Ziklag, in Meconah and its settlements,
in En-rimmon, in Zorah and in Jarmuth,
Zanoah, Adullam and their villages, Lachish and its fields, Azekah and its settlements. So they camped from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom.
The descendants of Benjamin lived from Geba onward: at Michmash, Aija, Bethel and its settlements,
Lod and Ono, and the Valley of the Craftsmen.
Some divisions of the Levites of Judah were joined to Benjamin.
These are the priests and the Levites who came up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra,
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah and Jedaiah. These were the heads of the priests and of their kinsmen in the days of Jeshua.
The Levites: Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who with his kinsmen was in charge of the songs of thanksgiving.
Bakbukiah and Unni, their kinsmen, stood opposite them in the services.
Jeshua was the father of Joiakim, Joiakim the father of Eliashib, Eliashib the father of Joiada,
Joiada the father of Jonathan, and Jonathan the father of Jaddua.
In the days of Joiakim the priests who were heads of ancestral families were these: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah;
of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan;
of Melicu, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph;
of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai;
of Iddo, Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam;
of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin, …; of Moadiah, Piltai;
of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jehonathan;
of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi;
of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber;
of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; of Jedaiah, Nethanel.
In the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, the Levites were recorded as heads of ancestral families, and so were the priests, until the reign of Darius the Persian.
The descendants of Levi, the heads of ancestral families, were recorded in the book of the chronicles, up to the days of Johanan son of Eliashib.

The heads of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah and Jeshua son of Kadmiel, with their kinsmen opposite them, to praise and give thanks as David the man of God had commanded, one division answering another.
Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon and Akkub were gatekeepers standing guard at the storehouses of the gates.
These served in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua, son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and of Ezra the priest and scribe.

At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought out the Levites from all the places where they lived, to bring them to Jerusalem to celebrate the dedication with joy, with thanksgiving and with singing, with cymbals, harps and lyres.
The singers gathered together from the region around Jerusalem, from the villages of the Netophathites,
from Beth-gilgal, and from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, for the singers had built themselves villages around Jerusalem.
The priests and the Levites purified themselves, and they purified the people, the gates and the wall.
Then I brought the leaders of Judah up onto the wall, and I appointed two large thanksgiving choirs to go in procession. One went to the right on the wall, toward the Dung Gate.
Behind them went Hoshaiah and half the leaders of Judah,
and some of the priests with trumpets; and Zechariah son of Jonathan, son of Shemaiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micaiah, son of Zaccur, son of Asaph,
and his kinsmen, Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God. Ezra the scribe went in front of them.
At the Fountain Gate they went straight up the steps of the City of David, where the wall goes up, above the house of David, as far as the Water Gate on the east.
The second thanksgiving choir went the opposite way, and I followed it with half the people, on the wall, above the Tower of the Ovens, to the Broad Wall,
and above the Gate of Ephraim, by the Old Gate, by the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Sheep Gate. They stopped at the Gate of the Guard.
So the two thanksgiving choirs took their places in the house of God, and so did I and half of the officials with me,
and the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah and Hananiah, with trumpets,
and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam and Ezer. The singers sang out, with Jezrahiah as their leader.
That day they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy. The women and the children also rejoiced. And the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away.

On that day men were appointed over the storerooms for the contributions, the firstfruits and the tithes, to gather into them from the fields of the towns the portions required by the Law for the priests and for the Levites. For Judah rejoiced over the priests and the Levites who ministered.
They performed the service of their God and the service of purification, as did the singers and the gatekeepers, according to the command of David and of his son Solomon.
For long ago, in the days of David and Asaph, there were leaders of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving to God.

So in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah all Israel gave the portions for the singers and the gatekeepers, as each day required. They set apart what was due to the Levites, and the Levites set apart what was due to the descendants of Aaron.
On that day the book of Moses was read aloud in the hearing of the people, and it was found written in it that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God,
because they had not met the Israelites with bread and water, but had hired Balaam against them to curse them. But our God turned the curse into a blessing.
When the people heard the Law, they separated from Israel everyone of mixed descent.
Before this, Eliashib the priest, who had been put in charge of the storerooms of the house of our God, and who was related to Tobiah,

had prepared for Tobiah a large storeroom where they had previously kept the grain offerings, the frankincense, the articles, and the tithes of grain, new wine and olive oil commanded for the Levites, the singers and the gatekeepers, and the contributions for the priests.
While all this was happening I was not in Jerusalem, for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon I had gone to the king. After some time I asked the king for leave
and came to Jerusalem. Then I learned of the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, preparing a storeroom for him in the courts of the house of God.
I was very displeased, and I threw all of Tobiah's household goods out of the storeroom.
Then I gave orders, and they purified the storerooms, and I brought back into them the articles of the house of God, with the grain offerings and the frankincense.
I also learned that the portions of the Levites had not been given to them, so that the Levites and the singers who did the work had gone back, each to his own field.
So I confronted the officials and said, "Why is the house of God neglected?" Then I gathered the Levites together and set them at their posts.
And all Judah brought the tithe of the grain, new wine and olive oil into the storehouses.

I put in charge of the storehouses Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe and Pedaiah of the Levites, and as their assistant Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, for they were considered trustworthy. Their duty was to distribute the shares to their kinsmen.
Remember me for this, my God, and do not wipe out the loyal deeds I have done for the house of my God and for its services.

In those days I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in heaps of grain and loading them on donkeys, and also wine, grapes, figs and every kind of load, and bringing them into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. I warned them on the day they sold the food.
People from Tyre who lived in the city were bringing in fish and all kinds of goods and selling them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah, and in Jerusalem.
So I confronted the nobles of Judah and said to them, "What is this evil thing you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day?
Did not your ancestors do the same, so that our God brought all this disaster on us and on this city? Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath."

When the gates of Jerusalem began to grow dark before the Sabbath, I gave orders for the doors to be shut, and I ordered that they were not to be opened until after the Sabbath. I stationed some of my servants at the gates, so that no load would come in on the Sabbath day.
Once or twice the merchants and the sellers of all kinds of goods spent the night outside Jerusalem.
But I warned them and said to them, "Why are you spending the night in front of the wall? If you do it again, I will lay hands on you." From that time on they did not come on the Sabbath.

Then I told the Levites to purify themselves and to come and guard the gates, to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember this also in my favor, my God, and spare me according to the greatness of your faithful love.
In those days I also saw Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab.
Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod, and they could not speak the language of Judah, but only the language of one people or another.

I confronted them and cursed them. I beat some of the men and pulled out their hair. I made them swear by God, "You shall not give your daughters to their sons, and you shall not take any of their daughters for your sons or for yourselves.

Was it not because of women like these that Solomon king of Israel sinned? Among the many nations there was no king like him. He was loved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Yet foreign women made even him sin.
Shall we then listen to you and do all this great evil, acting unfaithfully toward our God by marrying foreign women?"
One of the sons of Joiada son of Eliashib the high priest was a son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite, so I drove him away from me.
Remember them, my God, for they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.
So I purified them from everything foreign, and I set up the duties of the priests and the Levites, each in his own work,
and I provided for the wood offering at the appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me for good, my God.
This happened in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned over 127 provinces, from India to Cush.
In those days, when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in the citadel of Susa,
in the third year of his reign he gave a banquet for all his officials and his servants. The army of Persia and Media, the nobles and the officials of the provinces were in his presence,
while he displayed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days.

When these days were over, the king gave a banquet lasting seven days for all the people who were present in the citadel of Susa, from the greatest to the least, in the court of the garden of the king's palace.

There were hangings of white cotton and violet, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and marble pillars. There were couches of gold and silver on a pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl and precious stones.
Drinks were served in gold vessels, each vessel different from the others, and there was royal wine in abundance, as befitted the king's generosity.
The drinking was according to the law: no one was compelled. For the king had instructed all the officials of his household to do as each man wished.
Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the royal palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus.
On the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he told Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus,
to bring Queen Vashti before the king wearing the royal crown, to show the peoples and the officials her beauty, for she was beautiful to look at.
But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command, which the eunuchs brought. The king became very angry, and his rage burned within him.
Then the king spoke to the wise men who understood the times, for this was the king's practice with all who knew law and justice.
Those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan, the seven officials of Persia and Media who had access to the king and held the first place in the kingdom.
He asked, "According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti, because she has not obeyed the command of King Ahasuerus, which the eunuchs brought?"

Memucan said in the presence of the king and the officials, "Queen Vashti has done wrong not only to the king, but also to all the officials and all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.

For what the queen has done will become known to all the women, and they will look on their husbands with contempt. They will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she did not come.'
This very day the noble ladies of Persia and Media who have heard what the queen has done will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be no end of contempt and anger.

If it pleases the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of Persia and Media, so that it cannot be revoked, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another woman who is better than she.
When the king's edict that he makes is heard throughout his whole kingdom, vast as it is, all the women will give honor to their husbands, from the greatest to the least."
The advice pleased the king and the officials, and the king did as Memucan proposed.

He sent letters to all the king's provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, that every man should be master in his own house and should speak the language of his own people.
After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had died down, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her.
Then the king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king.

Let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather every beautiful young virgin to the citadel of Susa, to the house of the women, into the care of Hegai, the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women, and let their beauty treatments be given to them.
And let the young woman who pleases the king become queen instead of Vashti." This pleased the king, and he did so.
Now there was a Jewish man in the citadel of Susa whose name was Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite.
He had been taken into exile from Jerusalem with the exiles who were carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile.

He was bringing up Hadassah, that is, Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was lovely in form and beautiful to look at, and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.

When the king's command and his law had been proclaimed, and many young women had been gathered to the citadel of Susa into the care of Hegai, Esther also was taken to the king's palace, into the care of Hegai, who was in charge of the women.

The young woman pleased him and won his favor. He quickly provided her with her beauty treatments and her portions of food, and with seven young women chosen from the king's palace, and he moved her and her young women to the best place in the house of the women.
Esther had not made known her people or her family background, because Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known.
Every day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the court of the house of the women, to learn how Esther was and what was being done with her.

Each young woman's turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus after she had been treated for twelve months according to the regulations for the women. For this was how the days of their beauty treatment were completed: six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with spices and the cosmetics for women.
Then the young woman would go in to the king like this: whatever she asked for was given to her to take with her from the house of the women to the king's palace.

In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second house of the women, into the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again unless the king desired her and she was summoned by name.

When the turn came for Esther daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the women, advised. And Esther won the favor of all who saw her.
Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, to his royal palace, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.
The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won his grace and favor more than all the virgins. So he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.
Then the king gave a great banquet for all his officials and his servants, Esther's banquet. He granted a holiday to the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.
When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate.
Esther had still not made known her family background or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther obeyed Mordecai's word, just as she had when she was being brought up by him.
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the threshold, became angry and plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The plot became known to Mordecai, and he told Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in Mordecai's name.
When the matter was investigated and found to be true, both men were hanged on a pole. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the king's presence.
After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite. He raised him up and set his seat above all the officials who were with him.
All the king's servants who were in the king's gate would kneel and bow down to Haman, for the king had commanded this concerning him. But Mordecai would not kneel or bow down.
Then the king's servants who were in the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you disobey the king's command?"
When they had spoken to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's words would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai would not kneel or bow down to him, Haman was filled with rage.

But he scorned laying hands on Mordecai alone, for they had told him who Mordecai's people were. So Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.

In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast pur, that is, the lot, before Haman, from day to day and from month to month, until the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.

Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws. It is not in the king's interest to let them be.

If it pleases the king, let an order be written to destroy them, and I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who carry out the work, to bring into the king's treasuries."
So the king took his signet ring off his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king said to Haman, "The silver is given to you, and the people as well, to do with them as you see fit."

Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an order was written, just as Haman commanded, to the king's satraps, to the governors over each province and to the officials of each people, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.

Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces, to destroy, to kill and to annihilate all the Jews, young and old, children and women, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.
A copy of the document was to be issued as law in every province and made known to all the peoples, so that they would be ready for that day.
The couriers went out in haste at the king's command, and the law was issued in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes. He went out into the middle of the city and cried out with a loud and bitter cry.
He went only as far as the front of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate wearing sackcloth.
In every province, wherever the king's command and his law reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping and lamenting, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.

When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent clothes for Mordecai to put on, so that he would take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.
Then Esther called Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, whom he had appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was happening.
So Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king's gate.
Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact amount of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.

He also gave him a copy of the written law that had been issued in Susa for their destruction, to show Esther and explain to her, and to order her to go to the king to plead with him and make a request before him for her people.
Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach and ordered him to say to Mordecai,

"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that for any man or woman who goes to the king in the inner court without being summoned, there is one law: to be put to death, unless the king holds out the gold scepter to him, so that he may live. And I have not been summoned to come to the king for these thirty days."
When Esther's words were reported to Mordecai,
Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you alone of all the Jews will escape.

For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether it was not for a time like this that you have come to the kingdom?"
Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai,

"Go, gather all the Jews who are found in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. My young women and I will also fast in the same way. Then I will go in to the king, though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish."
So Mordecai went away and did everything that Esther had commanded him.

On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, opposite the king's hall. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal hall, facing the entrance of the hall.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won his favor, and the king held out to Esther the gold scepter that was in his hand. So Esther came near and touched the tip of the scepter.
The king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be given to you."
Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to the banquet that I have prepared for him."
The king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do what Esther has asked." So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
As they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your petition? It will be granted to you. And what is your request? Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be done."
Esther answered, "My petition and my request is this:

If I have found favor in the eyes of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and to do what I request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."
Haman went out that day joyful and in good spirits. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, and Mordecai neither stood up nor trembled before him, Haman was filled with rage against Mordecai.
Nevertheless Haman restrained himself and went home. He sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh and brought them in.
Haman told them of the glory of his wealth, the number of his sons, and all the ways the king had honored him and promoted him above the officials and the king's servants.
Haman said, "What is more, Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the banquet she prepared. And tomorrow too I am invited by her, together with the king.
Yet all this is worth nothing to me, as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting in the king's gate."

Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Have a pole made, fifty cubits high, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go with the king to the banquet in good spirits." The idea pleased Haman, and he had the pole made.
That night the king could not sleep. So he ordered the book of records, the chronicles, to be brought, and they were read before the king.
It was found written there how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the threshold, who had plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The king said, "What honor or distinction has been given to Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."
The king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just come into the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the pole that he had prepared for him.
The king's young men said to him, "Haman is standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."
So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done for the man whom the king delights to honor?" Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"
So Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor,
let them bring a royal robe that the king has worn, and a horse that the king has ridden, one with a royal crown on its head.

Let the robe and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and lead him on horseback through the city square, proclaiming before him, 'This is what is done for the man whom the king delights to honor!'"

Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry, take the robe and the horse, as you have said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits in the king's gate. Do not leave out anything of all that you have said."
So Haman took the robe and the horse. He dressed Mordecai and led him on horseback through the city square, proclaiming before him, "This is what is done for the man whom the king delights to honor!"
Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried home, mourning and with his head covered.

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him. You will surely fall before him."
While they were still speaking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman off to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
So the king and Haman went in to drink with Queen Esther.

On the second day too, as they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your petition, Queen Esther? It will be granted to you. And what is your request? Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be done."
Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be given to me as my petition, and my people as my request.

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, killed and annihilated. If we had only been sold as male and female slaves, I would have kept silent, for that trouble would not be worth troubling the king."
Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?"
Esther said, "An adversary and an enemy: this wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.

The king got up in his rage from the drinking of wine and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that the king had determined to do him harm.

When the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they had been drinking wine, Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. The king said, "Will he even assault the queen while I am in the house?" As soon as the words left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face.

Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, "Look, the pole that Haman made for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." The king said, "Hang him on it!"
So they hanged Haman on the pole that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the king's rage died down.
On that day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told him what Mordecai was to her.
The king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther put Mordecai in charge of the house of Haman.
Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept, and pleaded with him to avert the evil of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews.
The king held out the gold scepter to Esther, and Esther got up and stood before the king.

She said, "If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor with him, and if the thing seems right to the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the king's provinces.
For how can I bear to see the disaster that is coming on my people? And how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Look, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the pole because he reached out his hand against the Jews.

Now you write as you see fit concerning the Jews, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's signet ring. For a document that is written in the king's name and sealed with the king's signet ring cannot be revoked."

So the king's scribes were summoned at that time, on the twenty-third day of the third month, which is the month of Sivan. An order was written, just as Mordecai commanded, to the Jews, and to the satraps, the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Cush, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and their own language.

Mordecai wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring, and he sent letters by couriers on horseback, riding swift horses from the royal service, bred from the royal stud.

By these letters the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, kill and annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, with their children and women, and to plunder their goods,
on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
A copy of the document was to be issued as law in every province and made known to all the peoples, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to take revenge on their enemies.
The couriers, riding the swift horses from the royal service, went out in haste, urged on by the king's command. And the law was issued in the citadel of Susa.
Mordecai went out from the king's presence in royal robes of violet and white, with a great gold crown and a cloak of fine linen and purple. And the city of Susa shouted for joy and rejoiced.
For the Jews there was light and gladness, joy and honor.

In every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his law reached, there was gladness and joy for the Jews, a banquet and a holiday. And many of the peoples of the land became Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.

In the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month, when the king's command and his law were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews had hoped to gain power over them, it was turned the other way: the Jews gained power over those who hated them.

The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought to harm them. No one could stand against them, for fear of them had fallen on all the peoples.
All the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors and those who carried out the king's business supported the Jews, for fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.
For Mordecai was great in the king's palace, and his fame was spreading through all the provinces, as the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.
The Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and they did as they pleased to those who hated them.
In the citadel of Susa the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
They also killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they did not lay their hands on the plunder.
That same day the number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, "In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman. What have they done in the rest of the king's provinces? Now what is your petition? It will be granted to you. And what further request do you have? It will be done."
Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to act according to today's law, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the pole."
So the king commanded that this be done. A law was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
The Jews who were in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar, and they killed three hundred men in Susa. But they did not lay their hands on the plunder.

The rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives, and they gained rest from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they did not lay their hands on the plunder.
This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.
But the Jews who were in Susa gathered on the thirteenth day and on the fourteenth day, and on the fifteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.

That is why the Jews of the countryside, who live in the unwalled towns, keep the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting, a holiday, and a day for sending portions of food to one another.
Mordecai recorded these things, and he sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far,
to require them to keep the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and the fifteenth day every year,

as the days on which the Jews gained rest from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into joy and from mourning into a holiday. They were to make them days of feasting and joy, of sending portions of food to one another and gifts to the poor.
So the Jews accepted as a custom what they had begun to do, and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them. He had cast pur, that is, the lot, to throw them into confusion and destroy them.

But when it came before the king, he commanded by letter that the evil plot that Haman had devised against the Jews should come back on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the pole.
That is why these days are called Purim, after the word pur. So, because of everything written in this letter, and because of what they had seen concerning this and what had happened to them,

the Jews established it and took it on themselves, and on their descendants and on all who would join them, that without fail they would keep these two days every year, as it was written and at the appointed time,

and that these days would be remembered and kept in every generation, in every family, every province and every city, and that these days of Purim would never cease among the Jews, nor would the memory of them come to an end among their descendants.
Then Queen Esther daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Letters were sent to all the Jews, to the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, with words of peace and truth,

to establish these days of Purim at their appointed times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established for them, and as they had established for themselves and for their descendants, concerning their fasts and their lamenting.
Esther's command confirmed these regulations about Purim, and it was recorded in writing.
King Ahasuerus imposed forced labor on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.
All his powerful and mighty acts, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, whom the king made great, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?

For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Ahasuerus. He was great among the Jews and well liked by his many kindred, for he sought the good of his people and spoke for the welfare of all his descendants.
There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright; he feared God and turned away from evil.
Seven sons and three daughters were born to him.

His livestock numbered seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred female donkeys, and he had a great many servants. That man was the greatest of all the people of the East.
His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one in turn, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

When the days of feasting had run their course, Job would send for them and purify them. He would get up early in the morning and offer burnt offerings for each one of them, for Job thought, "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." This is what Job always did.
One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the Accuser also came among them.
The LORD said to the Accuser, "Where have you come from?" The Accuser answered the LORD, "From roaming the earth and walking about on it."
The LORD said to the Accuser, "Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth, a blameless and upright man who fears God and turns away from evil."
The Accuser answered the LORD, "Is it for nothing that Job fears God?
Have you not put a hedge around him and his household and everything he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his livestock have spread out over the land.
But stretch out your hand now and touch everything he has, and he will surely curse you to your face."
The LORD said to the Accuser, "Very well, everything he has is in your power. Only do not stretch out your hand against him." Then the Accuser went out from the presence of the LORD.
One day, when Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother,
a messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing beside them,
and the Sabeans swooped down and took them. They struck down the servants with the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The fire of God fell from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you."

While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three raiding parties and made a raid on the camels and took them. They struck down the servants with the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another came and said, "Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother,
and suddenly a great wind came from across the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It fell on the young people, and they died, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
Then Job got up, tore his robe and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped.
He said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. May the name of the LORD be blessed."
In all this Job did not sin, and he did not accuse God of wrongdoing.
One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the Accuser also came among them to present himself before the LORD.
The LORD said to the Accuser, "Where have you come from?" The Accuser answered the LORD, "From roaming the earth and walking about on it."

The LORD said to the Accuser, "Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth, a blameless and upright man who fears God and turns away from evil. He still holds firmly to his integrity, though you incited me against him to ruin him for no reason."
The Accuser answered the LORD, "Skin for skin! A man will give everything he has for his life.
But stretch out your hand now and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will surely curse you to your face."
The LORD said to the Accuser, "Very well, he is in your power. Only spare his life."
So the Accuser went out from the presence of the LORD, and he struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.
Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself with as he sat among the ashes.
His wife said to him, "Are you still holding firmly to your integrity? Curse God and die!"
But he said to her, "You are talking like a foolish woman. Shall we accept the good from God, and not accept the bad?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

When Job's three friends heard about all this trouble that had come on him, they came, each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite. They arranged to meet and come to show him sympathy and comfort him.
When they looked up from a distance, they did not recognize him. They wept aloud, and each one tore his robe, and they threw dust into the air over their heads.
Then they sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, for they saw that his pain was very great.
After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day he was born.
"Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, 'A boy has been conceived!'
That day, let it be darkness! Let God above not seek it out, and let no light shine on it.
Let darkness and deep darkness claim it; let a cloud settle over it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.
That night, let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the count of the months.
Yes, let that night be barren; let no shout of joy come into it.
Let those who curse days curse it, those who are ready to rouse Leviathan.
Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it wait for light that does not come, and let it not see the eyelids of the morning,
because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb and hide trouble from my eyes.
Why did I not die at birth, come out of the womb and breathe my last?
Why were there knees to receive me, or breasts for me to nurse?
For now I would be lying down in quiet; I would be asleep, and then I would be at rest
with kings and counselors of the earth, who rebuilt ruins for themselves,
or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.
Or why was I not hidden away like a stillborn child, like infants who never see the light?
There the wicked stop their raging, and there the weary find rest.
Prisoners are at ease together; they no longer hear the voice of the slave driver.
The small and the great are there alike, and the slave is free from his master.
Why does he give light to the one who suffers, and life to the bitter in soul,
who long for death, but it does not come, who dig for it more than for hidden treasure,
who would rejoice and shout for joy, who would be glad to find the grave?
Why give light to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
For sighing comes to me in place of my food, and my groans pour out like water.
For what I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has happened to me.
I have no ease, I have no quiet, I have no rest, and turmoil has come."
"If someone ventures a word to you, will you lose patience? But who can hold back from speaking?
Look, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened weak hands.
Your words have kept the stumbling on their feet, and you have made firm the knees that gave way.
But now it has come to you, and you lose patience; it touches you, and you are dismayed.
Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?
Think now: who that was innocent ever perished? Where were the upright ever wiped out?
As I have seen, those who plow wickedness and sow trouble reap it.
At the breath of God they perish; at the blast of his anger they come to an end.
The lion may roar, the fierce lion may growl, but the teeth of the young lions are broken.
The lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.
Now a word came to me in secret; my ear caught a whisper of it,
amid troubled thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on people.
Dread came upon me, and trembling, and it made all my bones shake.
A spirit passed before my face; the hair of my body stood on end.
It stood still, but I could not make out its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, and I heard a voice:
'Can a mortal be righteous before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?
If he puts no trust in his servants, and charges his angels with error,
how much more those who live in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed as easily as a moth!
Between morning and evening they are shattered; they perish forever, and no one notices.
Is not their tent cord pulled up within them? They die, and not in wisdom.'
"Call out now! Is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For resentment kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple.
I myself have seen a fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his home.
His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, with no one to rescue them.
The hungry eat his harvest and take it even from among the thorns, and the thirsty pant after their wealth.
For trouble does not come out of the dust, and misery does not sprout from the ground.
Rather, human beings are born to misery, as surely as sparks fly upward.
But as for me, I would appeal to God, and to God I would commit my cause.
He does great things beyond searching out, wonders beyond counting.
He gives rain on the earth and sends water on the fields.
He sets the lowly on high, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.
He frustrates the plans of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success.
He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the devious are swept away.
By day they run into darkness, and at noon they grope as if it were night.
But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty.
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.
How happy is the one whom God corrects! So do not reject the discipline of the Almighty.
For he wounds, but he binds up; he strikes, but his hands heal.
He will rescue you from six troubles, and in seven no harm will touch you.
In famine he will ransom you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.
You will be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and you will not fear destruction when it comes.
You will laugh at destruction and famine, and you will not fear the wild animals of the earth.
For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the wild animals of the field will be at peace with you.
You will know that your tent is secure; you will inspect your home and find nothing missing.
You will know that your descendants will be many, and your offspring like the grass of the earth.
You will come to the grave in ripe old age, as sheaves of grain are brought up in their season.
Look, we have searched this out; it is true. Hear it, and know it for yourself."
"If only my anguish could be weighed, and my calamity laid on the scales with it!
For then it would be heavier than the sand of the seas. That is why my words have been wild.
For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison. The terrors of God are lined up against me.
Does a wild donkey bray when it has grass, or an ox bellow over its fodder?
Can tasteless food be eaten without salt? Is there any flavor in the white of an egg?
I refuse to touch them; they are like loathsome food to me.
If only my request would be granted, and God would give me what I hope for:
that God would be willing to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!
Then I would still have this comfort, and I would leap for joy in pain that does not spare me: that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
What strength do I have, that I should wait? What end is ahead of me, that I should be patient?
Is my strength the strength of stones? Is my flesh bronze?
Is it not that I have no help in myself, and any resource has been driven from me?
One who is wasting away should have faithful love from his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
My brothers have been as treacherous as a wadi, like the channels of wadis that run away,
which are dark with ice, where the snow piles up and hides itself,
but when they are scorched they cease; when it is hot, they vanish from their place.
Caravans turn aside from their route; they go up into the wasteland and perish.
The caravans of Tema look for water; the travelers of Sheba hope for it.
They are put to shame because they trusted; they arrive there and are dismayed.
For now you have become like that; you see something terrible and are afraid.
Have I said, 'Give me something,' or 'Pay a bribe for me from your wealth,'
or 'Rescue me from the hand of the enemy,' or 'Ransom me from the hand of the ruthless'?
Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand where I have gone wrong.
How painful are honest words! But what does your arguing prove?
Do you mean to correct my words, and treat the words of a desperate man as wind?
You would even cast lots over an orphan, and bargain over your friend.
But now, please, look at me. Would I lie to your face?
Turn back, please; let there be no injustice. Turn back again; my righteousness is still at stake.
Is there injustice on my tongue? Can my palate not taste what is ruinous?
"Does not a human being have hard service on earth? Are not his days like the days of a hired worker?
Like a slave who longs for the shade, like a hired worker who waits for his wages,
so I have been given months of futility as my portion, and nights of misery have been assigned to me.
When I lie down I say, 'When will I get up?' But the night drags on, and I toss and turn until dawn.
My flesh is clothed with worms and crusts of dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks open again.
My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and they come to an end without hope.
Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good.
The eye that sees me will see me no more; your eyes will be on me, but I will be gone.
As a cloud fades away and is gone, so one who goes down to Sheol does not come up.
He will not return to his house again, and his place will not know him anymore.
So I will not restrain my mouth. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I the sea, or the sea monster, that you set a guard over me?
When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,'
then you terrify me with dreams and frighten me with visions,
so that I would choose strangling, death rather than these bones of mine.
I have had enough; I will not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.
What is a human being, that you make so much of him, that you pay attention to him,
that you examine him every morning and test him every moment?
How long will you not look away from me, or leave me alone long enough to swallow my spit?
If I have sinned, what have I done to you, you watcher of humankind? Why have you made me your target? Why have I become a burden to myself?
Why do you not pardon my offense and take away my guilt? For now I will lie down in the dust; you will search for me, but I will be gone."
"How long will you say such things? The words of your mouth are a mighty wind.
Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right?
If your children sinned against him, he handed them over to the power of their offense.
But if you will seek God earnestly and plead with the Almighty,
if you are pure and upright, then surely he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful home.
Though your beginning was small, your future will be very great.
Ask the former generation, please, and pay attention to what their ancestors searched out.
For we are only of yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are a shadow.
Will they not teach you and tell you, and bring out words from their understanding?
Can papyrus grow tall where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish without water?
While it is still green and not yet cut, it withers before any other plant.
Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless will perish.
His confidence snaps, and what he trusts in is a spider's web.
He leans on his house, but it does not stand; he holds on to it, but it does not last.
He is like a well-watered plant in the sun, whose shoots spread out over its garden.
Its roots wrap around a heap of stones; it looks for a place among the stones.
But if he is torn from his place, then it will deny him: 'I never saw you.'
See, this is the joy of his way, and out of the dust others will spring up.
See, God will not reject a blameless person, or take hold of the hand of evildoers.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouts of joy.
Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
"Truly, I know that it is so. But how can a mortal be in the right with God?
If he wanted to argue his case with him, he could not answer him once in a thousand times.
He is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has ever defied him and come out unharmed?
He moves mountains, and they do not know it, when he overturns them in his anger.
He shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble.
He speaks to the sun, and it does not rise; he seals up the stars.
He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea.
He made the Bear, Orion and the Pleiades, and the chambers of the south.
He does great things beyond searching out, wonders beyond counting.
Look, he passes by me, and I do not see him; he moves on, and I do not perceive him.
Look, he snatches away; who can stop him? Who can say to him, 'What are you doing?'
God does not hold back his anger; the helpers of Rahab bowed down beneath him.
How then could I answer him, or choose my words to argue with him?
Even if I were in the right, I could not answer him; I would have to plead for mercy with my judge.
