A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is a deceiver.
In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge.
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, for turning away from the snares of death.
In a multitude of people is a king's glory, but without people a ruler is ruined.
Whoever is slow to anger has great insight, but whoever is quick-tempered displays folly.
A calm heart gives life to the body, but envy rots the bones.
Whoever oppresses the poor insults his Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors him.
The wicked is thrown down by his own evil, but the righteous finds refuge even in his death.
Wisdom rests in the heart of the discerning, and even among fools she makes herself known.
Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people.
A king delights in a servant who acts with good sense, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise makes knowledge attractive, but the mouth of fools gushes folly.
The eyes of the LORD are everywhere, watching the evil and the good.
A soothing tongue is a tree of life, but a twisted one crushes the spirit.
A fool despises his father's discipline, but whoever heeds correction is prudent.
In the house of the righteous there is great treasure, but the income of the wicked brings trouble.
The lips of the wise spread knowledge, but the heart of fools is not so.
The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is his delight.
The way of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, but he loves the one who pursues righteousness.
Severe discipline awaits the one who leaves the path; whoever hates correction will die.
Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of humankind!
A mocker does not love the one who corrects him; he will not go to the wise.
A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by heartache the spirit is crushed.
The heart of the discerning seeks knowledge, but the mouth of fools feeds on folly.
All the days of the poor are hard, but a cheerful heart has a continual feast.
Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil.
Better a meal of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred.
A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but one who is slow to anger calms a quarrel.
The way of the lazy person is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a highway.
A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish man despises his mother.
Folly is a joy to one who lacks sense, but a person of insight walks straight ahead.
Plans fail without counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.
A person finds joy in giving an apt answer, and a word at the right time, how good it is!
The path of life leads upward for the sensible, so that he may turn away from Sheol below.
The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but he sets firm the boundary of the widow.
Evil plans are detestable to the LORD, but gracious words are pure.
Whoever is greedy for gain brings trouble on his household, but whoever hates bribes will live.
The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked gushes evil things.
The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.
Bright eyes gladden the heart; good news refreshes the bones.
The ear that listens to life-giving correction will live among the wise.
Whoever ignores discipline despises himself, but whoever listens to correction gains sense.
The fear of the LORD is the discipline of wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
The plans of the heart belong to people, but the answer of the tongue comes from the LORD.
All a person's ways seem pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirits.
Commit your works to the LORD, and your plans will be established.
The LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of disaster.
Everyone who is proud in heart is detestable to the LORD; you can be sure he will not go unpunished.
By faithful love and truth iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the LORD one turns away from evil.
When a person's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies be at peace with him.
Better a little with righteousness than great income with injustice.
A person's heart plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps.
Inspired decisions are on the lips of a king; his mouth does not betray justice.
Honest balances and scales belong to the LORD; all the weights in the bag are his work.
Doing wickedness is detestable to kings, for a throne is established by righteousness.
Righteous lips are the delight of kings, and they love one who speaks what is right.
A king's wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise person will appease it.
In the light of a king's face is life, and his favor is like a cloud that brings the spring rain.
How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is better than silver.
The highway of the upright turns away from evil; whoever watches his way preserves his life.
Pride comes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
Better to be lowly in spirit with the humble than to divide plunder with the proud.
Whoever pays attention to the word will find good, and happy is the one who trusts in the LORD.
The wise in heart are called discerning, and sweet speech increases learning.
Good sense is a fountain of life to those who have it, but folly is the discipline of fools.
The heart of the wise makes his mouth wise and adds learning to his lips.
Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones.
There is a way that seems right to a person, but in the end it leads to death.
A worker's appetite works for him, for his hunger drives him on.
A worthless man digs up evil, and on his lips it is like a scorching fire.
A perverse person spreads strife, and a gossip separates close friends.
A violent man entices his neighbor and leads him in a way that is not good.
Whoever winks his eyes is plotting perversity; whoever purses his lips has brought evil about.
Gray hair is a glorious crown; it is found in the way of righteousness.
Better to be slow to anger than a mighty warrior, and to rule one's spirit than to capture a city.
The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.
Better a dry crust with peace and quiet than a house full of feasting with strife.
A servant who acts wisely will rule over a son who acts shamefully, and will share the inheritance among the brothers.
The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the LORD tests hearts.
An evildoer listens to wicked lips; a liar pays attention to a destructive tongue.
Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker; whoever rejoices at disaster will not go unpunished.
Grandchildren are the crown of the old, and fathers are the glory of their children.
Fine speech is not fitting for a godless fool, still less are lying lips for a noble.
A bribe is a lucky stone in the eyes of its owner; wherever he turns, he succeeds.
Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but whoever repeats a matter separates close friends.
A rebuke goes deeper into a discerning person than a hundred blows into a fool.
An evil person seeks only rebellion, and a cruel messenger will be sent against him.
Better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly.
Whoever repays good with evil, evil will not leave his house.
Starting a quarrel is like letting out water; so drop the dispute before it breaks out.
Whoever acquits the wicked and whoever condemns the righteous, both are detestable to the LORD.
Why should a fool have money in his hand to buy wisdom, when he has no sense?
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for times of trouble.
One who lacks sense shakes hands on a pledge and puts up security in front of his neighbor.
Whoever loves offense loves strife; whoever makes his doorway high is looking for destruction.
Whoever has a crooked heart finds no good, and whoever has a perverse tongue falls into trouble.
Whoever fathers a fool has grief, and the father of a godless fool has no joy.
A glad heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.
The wicked accepts a bribe in secret to pervert the paths of justice.
Wisdom is right in front of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth.
A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to the mother who bore him.
It is not good to punish the righteous, or to strike nobles for their uprightness.
Whoever restrains his words has knowledge, and one who is calm in spirit is a person of insight.
Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise; whoever closes his lips is thought discerning.
Whoever isolates himself seeks his own desire; he bursts out against all sound wisdom.
A fool takes no pleasure in insight, but only in displaying his own mind.
When the wicked comes, contempt comes too, and with dishonor comes disgrace.
The words of a person's mouth are deep waters; the fountain of wisdom is a flowing stream.
It is not good to show favor to the wicked, or to deprive the righteous of justice.
A fool's lips walk into a quarrel, and his mouth invites a beating.
A fool's mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare for his life.
The words of a gossip are like tasty morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body.
Whoever is slack in his work is brother to one who destroys.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run into it and are safe.
The wealth of the rich is their strong city; in their imagination it is like a high wall.
Before destruction a person's heart is proud, but humility comes before honor.
Whoever answers before he listens, it is folly and shame to him.
A person's spirit can endure sickness, but a crushed spirit, who can bear it?
The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks knowledge.
A gift opens the way for the giver and brings him before the great.
The first to state his case seems right, until the other comes and questions him.
Casting the lot puts an end to disputes and decides between powerful opponents.
An offended brother is harder to win than a strong city, and quarrels are like the bars of a fortress.
From the fruit of a person's mouth his stomach is filled; he is satisfied with the yield of his lips.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.
He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD.
The poor speak with pleading, but the rich answer harshly.
A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
Better a poor person who walks in integrity than one with crooked lips who is a fool.
Desire without knowledge is not good, and whoever hurries with his feet sins.
A person's folly ruins his way, but his heart rages against the LORD.
Wealth adds many friends, but the poor is separated from his friend.
A false witness will not go unpunished, and one who breathes out lies will not escape.
Many seek the favor of a generous person, and everyone is a friend to one who gives gifts.
All the brothers of a poor person hate him; how much more do his friends keep far from him! He pursues them with words, but words are all he has.
Whoever gains sense loves himself; whoever keeps insight will find good.
A false witness will not go unpunished, and one who breathes out lies will perish.
Luxury is not fitting for a fool, still less for a servant to rule over princes.
A person's good sense makes him slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense.
A king's rage is like the roar of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass.
A foolish son is ruin to his father, and a wife's quarrels are a constant dripping.
House and wealth are an inheritance from fathers, but a sensible wife is from the LORD.
Laziness casts into a deep sleep, and an idle person will go hungry.
Whoever keeps the command keeps his life; whoever is careless of his ways will die.
Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.
Discipline your son while there is hope; do not set your heart on his death.
A person of great anger must pay the penalty; if you rescue him, you will have to do it again.
Listen to advice and accept discipline, so that you may be wise in the end.
Many plans are in a person's heart, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand.
What is desired in a person is faithful love, and it is better to be poor than a liar.
The fear of the LORD leads to life; whoever has it rests content, untouched by harm.
The lazy person buries his hand in the dish; he will not even bring it back to his mouth.
Strike a mocker, and the simple will learn prudence; correct a discerning person, and he will gain knowledge.
Whoever robs his father and drives out his mother is a son who brings shame and disgrace.
Stop listening to discipline, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge.
A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked swallows iniquity.
Punishments are ready for mockers, and beatings for the backs of fools.
Wine is a mocker, beer a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.
The terror of a king is like the roar of a lion; whoever provokes him forfeits his life.
It is an honor for a person to keep away from strife, but every fool bursts into quarrels.
The lazy person does not plow in autumn; at harvest he looks for a crop, and there is nothing.
The purpose in a person's heart is deep water, but a person of insight draws it out.
Many a person proclaims his own loyalty, but a faithful person, who can find?
The righteous walks in his integrity; happy are his children after him.
A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows out all evil with his eyes.
Who can say, "I have made my heart clean; I am pure from my sin"?
Two different weights and two different measures, both are detestable to the LORD.
Even a child makes himself known by his actions, whether his conduct is pure and right.
The ear that hears and the eye that sees, the LORD has made them both.
Do not love sleep, or you will become poor; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread.
"Bad, bad," says the buyer; but when he goes on his way, then he boasts.
There is gold and plenty of coral, but lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.
Take the garment of one who puts up security for a stranger; hold it in pledge for a foreign woman.
Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a person, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.
Plans are established by advice; wage war with guidance.
Whoever goes about as a gossip reveals secrets, so do not associate with one who talks too much.
Whoever curses his father or his mother, his lamp will go out in the blackest darkness.
An inheritance gained in haste at the beginning will not be blessed in the end.
Do not say, "I will pay back evil!" Wait for the LORD, and he will rescue you.
Two different weights are detestable to the LORD, and dishonest scales are not good.
A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can anyone understand his own way?
It is a trap for a person to say rashly, "It is holy!" and only afterward to think about his vows.
A wise king winnows out the wicked and drives the wheel over them.
The human spirit is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inner parts of the body.
Faithful love and truth guard a king; by faithful love his throne is upheld.
The glory of young men is their strength, and the splendor of the old is their gray hair.
Blows that wound scour away evil, and beatings, the inner parts of the body.
The king's heart is like streams of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he wishes.
All a person's ways seem right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs hearts.
Doing righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.
Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin.
The plans of the diligent lead only to profit, but everyone who is hasty comes only to need.
Getting treasures by a lying tongue is a vapor blown away, for those who seek death.
The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just.
The way of a guilty person is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.
Better to live in a corner of the roof than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.
The soul of the wicked craves evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.
When a mocker is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise person is instructed, he gains knowledge.
The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.
A gift given in secret calms anger, and a bribe in the fold of the cloak calms fierce wrath.
When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.
Whoever wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead.
Whoever loves pleasure will be poor; whoever loves wine and oil will not grow rich.
The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the treacherous takes the place of the upright.
Better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and angry wife.
Precious treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish person swallows it up.
Whoever pursues righteousness and faithful love will find life, righteousness and honor.
A wise person climbs the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold they trusted in.
Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his life from troubles.
The proud and arrogant person, "Mocker" is his name; he acts with insolent fury.
The craving of the lazy person kills him, for his hands refuse to work.
All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.
The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable; how much more when he brings it with evil intent!
A false witness will perish, but one who listens will speak forever.
A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his way.
There is no wisdom, no insight, no counsel that can stand against the LORD.
The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the LORD.
A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver and gold.
The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the maker of them all.
The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and pay for it.
The reward for humility and the fear of the LORD is riches, honor and life.
Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his life will keep far from them.
Train a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not turn away from it.
The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
Whoever sows injustice will reap trouble, and the rod of his fury will come to an end.
Whoever has a generous eye will be blessed, for he gives some of his bread to the poor.
Drive out the mocker, and strife goes out; quarreling and insults will stop.
Whoever loves purity of heart and whose speech is gracious will have the king as his friend.
The eyes of the LORD watch over knowledge, but he overturns the words of the treacherous.
The lazy person says, "There is a lion outside! I will be killed in the streets!"
The mouth of strange women is a deep pit; whoever is cursed by the LORD will fall into it.
Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline will drive it far from him.
Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, comes only to need.
Turn your ear and listen to the words of the wise, and set your heart on my knowledge,
for it is pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips.
So that your trust may be in the LORD, I have taught you today, even you.
Have I not written for you excellent sayings of advice and knowledge,
to teach you what is right and true, so that you may bring back a true report to those who sent you?
Do not rob the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted at the gate,
for the LORD will plead their case and will take the life of those who rob them.
Do not make friends with a hot-tempered person, and do not go about with a man given to anger,
or you will learn his ways and get yourself caught in a snare.
Do not be one of those who shake hands on a pledge, who put up security for debts.
If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?
Do not move the ancient boundary stone that your ancestors set up.
Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve before kings; he will not serve before obscure people.
When you sit down to eat with a ruler, consider carefully what is before you,
and put a knife to your throat if you have a big appetite.
Do not crave his delicacies, for they are deceptive food.
Do not wear yourself out to get rich; stop relying on your own understanding.
When your eyes fly to it, it is gone; for it will surely make itself wings and fly off to the sky like an eagle.
Do not eat the bread of a stingy person, and do not crave his delicacies,
for he is like one who keeps count in his mind. "Eat and drink!" he says to you, but his heart is not with you.
You will vomit up the morsel you have eaten and waste your pleasant words.
Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words.
Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless,
for their redeemer is strong; he will plead their case against you.
Apply your heart to discipline and your ears to words of knowledge.
Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die.
Strike him with the rod, and you will rescue his life from Sheol.
My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad,
and my inmost being will rejoice when your lips speak what is right.
Do not let your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all day long.
For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
Listen, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way.
Do not be among those who drink too much wine or those who gorge themselves on meat,
for the drunkard and the glutton will become poor, and drowsiness clothes them in rags.
Listen to your father, who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.
Buy truth and do not sell it, wisdom, discipline and understanding.
The father of a righteous person will greatly rejoice; whoever fathers a wise son will be glad in him.
Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice.
My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes keep to my ways.
For a prostitute is a deep pit, and a foreign woman is a narrow well.
She lies in wait like a robber and increases the number of the treacherous among men.
Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has quarrels? Who has complaints? Who has wounds for no reason? Who has bloodshot eyes?
Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed wine.
Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly.
In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper.
Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart will speak perverse things.
You will be like one who lies down in the middle of the sea, like one who lies on top of a mast.
"They hit me," you will say, "but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When will I wake up? I will look for another drink."
Do not envy evil people, and do not desire to be with them,
for their hearts plot violence, and their lips talk of trouble.
By wisdom a house is built, and by insight it is established;
by knowledge its rooms are filled with all kinds of precious and pleasant wealth.
A wise man is strong, and a person of knowledge increases his strength,
for by guidance you wage your war, and with many advisers there is victory.
Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth.
Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer.
The scheming of folly is sin, and a mocker is detestable to people.
If you lose heart in the day of trouble, your strength is small.
Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are staggering to the slaughter.
If you say, "But we did not know this," does not the one who weighs hearts understand? Does not the one who guards your life know it? He will repay each person according to what he has done.
Eat honey, my son, for it is good, and the honeycomb is sweet to your taste.
Know that wisdom is like that for your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
Do not lie in wait like a wicked man against the home of the righteous; do not destroy his resting place.
For the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of disaster.
Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart be glad when he stumbles,
or the LORD will see it and be displeased, and turn his anger away from him.
Do not fret because of evildoers or envy the wicked,
for the evil person has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out.
My son, fear the LORD and the king; do not associate with those who are given to change,
for disaster from them will rise suddenly, and who knows the ruin the two of them can bring?
These also are sayings of the wise. Showing partiality in judgment is not good.
Whoever says to the wicked, "You are righteous," peoples will curse him, nations will denounce him.
But those who rebuke the wicked will find delight, and a good blessing will come upon them.
Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips.
Put your outdoor work in order and get your fields ready; after that, build your house.
Do not be a witness against your neighbor without cause; would you deceive with your lips?
Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."
I passed by the field of a lazy man, by the vineyard of a man who lacked sense,
and look, it was all overgrown with thistles; its surface was covered with weeds, and its stone wall was broken down.
I looked and took it to heart; I saw and received discipline:
a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,
and poverty will come on you like a prowler, and need like an armed man.
These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.
It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, and the glory of kings to search out a matter.
As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the heart of kings is unsearchable.
Remove the dross from silver, and a vessel comes out for the silversmith.
Remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness.
Do not put yourself forward before the king, and do not stand in the place of the great,
for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be put lower in the presence of a noble whom your eyes have seen.
Do not go out hastily to court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame?
Argue your case with your neighbor, but do not reveal another's secret,
or the one who hears it will disgrace you, and your bad name will never go away.
Like apples of gold in settings of silver is a word spoken at the right time.
Like a gold earring or an ornament of fine gold is a wise person who corrects a listening ear.
Like the coolness of snow at harvest time is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the life of his masters.
Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.
With patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone.
If you find honey, eat only what you need, or you will have too much and vomit it up.
Seldom set foot in your neighbor's house, or he will have too much of you and hate you.
Like a club, a sword or a sharp arrow is a man who gives false testimony against his neighbor.
Like a broken tooth or a lame foot is trust in a treacherous person in a time of trouble.
Like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, like vinegar on soda, is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.
If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink,
for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.
The north wind brings forth rain, and a secret tongue, angry faces.
Better to live in a corner of the roof than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.
Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land.
Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous person who gives way before the wicked.
It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory.
Like a city broken into and left without walls is a person who has no control over his spirit.
Like snow in summer and like rain at harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool.
Like a sparrow flitting, like a swallow flying, so an undeserved curse comes home to the one who utters it.
A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the backs of fools.
Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself.
Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes.
Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence.
Like the legs of a lame person, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
Like tying a stone in a sling is giving honor to a fool.
Like a thorn that gets into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a fool or hires passersby.
Like a dog that returns to its vomit is a fool who repeats his folly.
Do you see a person wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
The lazy person says, "There is a lion in the road! A lion in the streets!"
As a door turns on its hinges, so the lazy person turns on his bed.
The lazy person buries his hand in the dish; he is too tired to bring it back to his mouth.
The lazy person is wiser in his own eyes than seven people who answer sensibly.
Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own.
Like a madman who shoots flaming arrows, arrows and death,
so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I was only joking!"
Without wood a fire goes out, and without a gossip a quarrel dies down.
As charcoal to embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.
The words of a gossip are like tasty morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body.
Like glaze coating an earthenware pot are burning lips with an evil heart.
Whoever hates disguises it with his lips, but inside he harbors deceit.
When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven detestable things are in his heart.
His hatred may be covered by deception, but his evil will be exposed in the assembly.
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on the one who rolls it.
A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth works ruin.
Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring.
Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth, an outsider, and not your own lips.
A stone is heavy and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both.
Wrath is cruel and anger is a flood, but who can stand before jealousy?
Better open correction than hidden love.
Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but the kisses of an enemy are lavish.
One who is full tramples on honey, but to one who is hungry everything bitter is sweet.
Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home.
Oil and incense make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from heartfelt advice.
Do not abandon your friend or your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house on the day of your disaster. Better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away.
Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, so that I can answer anyone who taunts me.
The prudent sees danger and hides himself; the simple go on and pay for it.
Take the garment of one who puts up security for a stranger; hold it in pledge for a foreign woman.
Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning, it will be counted to him as a curse.
A constant dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike;
whoever restrains her restrains the wind or grasps oil with his right hand.
As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another.
Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever looks after his master will be honored.
As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the person.
Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and human eyes are never satisfied.
The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, and a person is tested by the praise he receives.
Even if you pound a fool in a mortar, with a pestle among the grain, his folly will not leave him.
Know well the condition of your flocks; give careful attention to your herds,
for riches do not last forever, and does a crown last for all generations?
When the grass is gone and the new growth appears, and the plants of the hills are gathered in,
the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field,
and there will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household, and to keep your servant girls alive.
The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion.
When a land rebels, it has many rulers, but through a person who understands and knows, its stability lasts.
A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food.
Those who abandon the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law fight against them.
Evil people do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand everything.
Better a poor person who walks in integrity than one whose ways are crooked, even if he is rich.
Whoever keeps the law is a discerning son, but a companion of gluttons shames his father.
Whoever increases his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for one who is kind to the poor.
Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law, even his prayer is detestable.
Whoever leads the upright astray into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will inherit good.
A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who is discerning sees through him.
When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide.
Whoever covers his offenses will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will find mercy.
Happy is the one who is always reverent, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into trouble.
Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people.
A ruler who lacks insight is a great oppressor, but whoever hates unjust gain will live long.
A man burdened with someone's blood will be a fugitive until the Pit; let no one hold him back.
Whoever walks blamelessly will be kept safe, but whoever is crooked in his ways will fall all at once.
Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but whoever chases worthless things will have plenty of poverty.
A faithful person will have many blessings, but whoever hurries to get rich will not go unpunished.
Showing partiality is not good, yet for a piece of bread a man will do wrong.
A stingy man hurries after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him.
Whoever corrects someone will in the end find more favor than one who flatters with his tongue.
Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "It is no offense," is a companion of a destroyer.
The greedy person stirs up strife, but whoever trusts in the LORD will prosper.
Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool, but whoever walks in wisdom will be kept safe.
Whoever gives to the poor will not lack, but whoever shuts his eyes will receive many curses.
When the wicked rise, people hide, but when they perish, the righteous increase.
Whoever is often corrected yet stays stiff-necked will suddenly be broken, and there will be no healing.
When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
A man who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.
By justice a king gives a land stability, but a man who exacts contributions tears it down.
A man who flatters his neighbor is spreading a net for his feet.
An evil man is snared by his own offense, but the righteous sings and rejoices.
The righteous knows the rights of the poor; the wicked has no such understanding.
Mockers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away anger.
If a wise man goes to court with a fool, the fool rages and laughs, and there is no peace.
Bloodthirsty men hate the blameless, and as for the upright, they seek his life.
A fool gives full vent to his anger, but a wise person quietly holds it back.
If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials become wicked.
The poor and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both.
If a king judges the poor with faithfulness, his throne will be established forever.
The rod and correction give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother.
When the wicked increase, offense increases, but the righteous will see their downfall.
Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul.
Where there is no vision, the people run wild, but whoever keeps the law is happy.
A servant cannot be disciplined by words alone; though he understands, he will not respond.
Do you see someone who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
If someone pampers his servant from youth, in the end it will bring grief.
An angry man stirs up strife, and a hot-tempered man commits many offenses.
A person's pride will bring him low, but the lowly in spirit will gain honor.
Whoever is a partner with a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse but does not testify.
Fear of people sets a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe.
Many seek the favor of a ruler, but justice for a person comes from the LORD.
An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked.
The words of Agur son of Jakeh, the oracle. The man declares to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:
Surely I am too stupid to be a man; I do not have human understanding.
I have not learned wisdom, nor do I have knowledge of the Holy One.

Who has gone up to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a cloak? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!
Every word of God is refined; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him.
Do not add to his words, or he will rebuke you, and you will be found a liar.
Two things I ask of you; do not refuse me before I die:
keep falsehood and lies far from me; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread I need,
or I may become full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or I may become poor and steal, and profane the name of my God.
Do not slander a servant to his master, or he will curse you, and you will be held guilty.
There are those who curse their father and do not bless their mother.
There are those who are pure in their own eyes, yet are not washed of their filth.
There are those whose eyes are so haughty, whose eyelids are lifted high.
There are those whose teeth are swords, whose jaws are knives, to devour the poor from the earth and the needy from among humankind.
The leech has two daughters: "Give! Give!" There are three things that are never satisfied, four that never say, "Enough!":
Sheol, the barren womb, land that is never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, "Enough!"
The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother will be pecked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by the young vultures.
There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I do not understand:
the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a snake on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a young woman.
This is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have done nothing wrong."
Under three things the earth trembles, under four it cannot bear up:
a servant when he becomes king, a godless fool when he is filled with food,
an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a servant girl when she takes the place of her mistress.
Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise:
the ants are a people without strength, yet they store up their food in summer;
the rock badgers are a people without power, yet they make their homes in the rocks;
the locusts have no king, yet they all go out in ranks;
the lizard can be caught in the hand, yet it lives in kings' palaces.
There are three things that are stately in their stride, four that are stately in their walk:
the lion, mightiest among beasts, which does not turn back before anything;
the strutting rooster, or the male goat, and a king with his army around him.
If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been scheming, put your hand over your mouth.
For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife.
The words of King Lemuel, an oracle that his mother taught him.
What, my son? What, son of my womb? What, son of my vows?
Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings.
It is not for kings, Lemuel, not for kings to drink wine, nor for rulers to ask, "Where is beer?"
or they will drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted.
Give beer to one who is perishing, and wine to those who are bitter in soul.
Let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their trouble no more.
Open your mouth for those who cannot speak, for the rights of all who are destitute.
Open your mouth, judge rightly, and defend the rights of the poor and needy.
A capable wife, who can find? She is worth far more than coral.
Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he will not lack gain.
She does him good and not harm all the days of her life.
She seeks out wool and flax and works with willing hands.
She is like the merchant ships; she brings her food from far away.
She gets up while it is still night and provides food for her household and portions for her servant girls.
She considers a field and buys it; from her earnings she plants a vineyard.
She wraps herself in strength and makes her arms strong.
She sees that her trading is profitable; her lamp does not go out at night.
She puts her hands to the distaff, and her palms grasp the spindle.
She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
She is not afraid of the snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet.
She makes coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.
Her husband is known at the city gates, when he sits among the elders of the land.
She makes linen garments and sells them, and supplies sashes to the merchants.
Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come.
She opens her mouth with wisdom, and loving instruction is on her tongue.
She watches over the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.
Her children rise up and call her happy; her husband too, and he praises her:
"Many women have done capably, but you surpass them all."
Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
The words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
"Vapor of vapors," says the Teacher, "vapor of vapors! Everything is vapor."
What gain do people have from all their toil, all their toiling under the sun?
A generation goes and a generation comes, but the earth stands forever.
The sun rises and the sun goes down, and it hurries, panting, back to its place, and there it rises again.
It goes to the south and turns to the north; round and round goes the wind, and on its rounds the wind returns.
All the streams flow to the sea, yet the sea is never full. To the place where the streams flow, there they keep on flowing.
All things are weary, more than anyone can say. The eye is never satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done. There is nothing new under the sun.
There is a thing of which people say, "Look, this is new!" It was here already, in the ages before us.
There is no remembrance of those who came before, and of those who are yet to come there will be no remembrance either, among those who come after them.
I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I set my heart to seek and to explore by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy task that God has given human beings to keep them busy.
I have seen all the deeds that are done under the sun, and look, everything is vapor and chasing the wind.
What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is missing cannot be counted.
I said to myself, "Look, I have grown great and gained more wisdom than all who ruled Jerusalem before me, and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge."
So I set my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly. I learned that this too is chasing the wind.
For with much wisdom comes much grief, and whoever increases knowledge increases pain.
I said to myself, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good." But look, this too was vapor.
Of laughter I said, "It is madness," and of pleasure, "What does it accomplish?"

I explored with my heart how to cheer my body with wine, while my heart still guided me with wisdom, and how to take hold of folly, until I could see what is good for human beings to do under heaven during the few days of their life.
I did great things. I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards for myself.
I made myself gardens and parks, and I planted every kind of fruit tree in them.
I made myself pools of water, to water from them a forest of growing trees.
I bought male and female slaves, and I had slaves born in my house. I also had great herds and flocks, more than all who were in Jerusalem before me.
I also gathered for myself silver and gold, and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got myself male and female singers, and the delights of human beings: many concubines.
So I became great, greater than all who were in Jerusalem before me. My wisdom also stayed with me.
Whatever my eyes asked for, I did not keep from them. I did not hold back my heart from any pleasure, for my heart took pleasure in all my toil, and this was my portion from all my toil.
Then I turned to look at all the works my hands had done, and at the toil I had toiled to do, and look, everything was vapor and chasing the wind. There was no gain under the sun.
Then I turned to consider wisdom, and madness and folly. For what can the one do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.
I saw that wisdom has an advantage over folly, as light has an advantage over darkness.
The wise have eyes in their heads, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also knew that one fate befalls them all.
So I said to myself, "What befalls the fool will befall me too. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said to myself that this too was vapor.
For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, any more than of the fool, since in the days to come everything will already be forgotten. How the wise die, just like the fool!
So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me; for everything is vapor and chasing the wind.
I hated all my toil at which I toil under the sun, because I must leave it to the one who will come after me.
And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all my toil, all I toiled at and was wise in under the sun. This too is vapor.
So I turned and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil at which I had toiled under the sun.
For there is a person whose toil is done with wisdom, knowledge and skill, and he must give it as a portion to someone who did not toil for it. This too is vapor, and a great evil.
For what does a person get from all his toil and the striving of his heart at which he toils under the sun?
For all his days are pain, and his task is grief; even at night his heart does not rest. This too is vapor.
There is nothing better for a person than to eat and drink and let himself enjoy his toil. This too, I saw, is from the hand of God.
For who can eat, and who can find enjoyment, apart from me?

For to the person who pleases him God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he gives the task of gathering and collecting, only to give it to the one who pleases God. This too is vapor and chasing the wind.
For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:
a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot what is planted;
a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build up;
a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance;
a time to throw stones away and a time to gather stones, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek and a time to lose, a time to keep and a time to throw away;
a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to be silent and a time to speak;
a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace.
What gain does the worker have from his toil?
I have seen the task that God has given human beings to keep them busy.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that no one can find out the work that God has done from beginning to end.
I know that there is nothing better for them than to be glad and to do good while they live.
And also, when anyone eats and drinks and enjoys all his toil, that is the gift of God.
I know that whatever God does will last forever. Nothing can be added to it, and nothing taken from it. God has done it so that people will fear him.
What has been is already here, and what is to be has already been, and God seeks out what has passed by.
And I saw something else under the sun: in the place of justice, there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, there was wickedness.
I said to myself, "God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every deed there."
I said to myself about human beings, "God is testing them, to show them that they are animals, nothing more."

For the fate of human beings and the fate of animals is one and the same: as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and humans have no advantage over animals, for everything is vapor.
All go to one place. All came from the dust, and all return to the dust.
Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes upward, and whether the spirit of animals goes down into the earth?
So I saw that there is nothing better than for people to rejoice in their works, for that is their portion. For who can bring them to see what will happen after them?

Again I saw all the oppression that is done under the sun. Look, the tears of the oppressed, and they have no one to comfort them! Power is on the side of their oppressors, and they have no one to comfort them.
So I praised the dead, who have already died, more than the living, who are still alive.
But better than both is the one who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.
I saw that all toil and all skill in work comes from one person's envy of another. This too is vapor and chasing the wind.
The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.
Better one handful with rest than two fistfuls with toil and chasing the wind.
Again I saw vapor under the sun:

There is someone who is alone, without a second; he has neither son nor brother. Yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eye is never satisfied with riches. "For whom am I toiling, and depriving myself of good things?" This too is vapor and an unhappy task.
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.
For if they fall, one will lift up his companion. But pity the one who falls alone, with no second to lift him up!
Again, if two lie down together, they keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?
And if someone overpowers one who is alone, two can stand against him. A three-stranded cord is not quickly broken.
Better a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take advice.
For he came out of prison to become king, though he was born poor in his kingdom.
I saw all the living who walk under the sun following the youth, the second one, who would stand in his place.
There was no end to all the people, to all whom he led, yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. This too is vapor and chasing the wind.
Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than for fools to offer a sacrifice, for they do not know that they are doing evil.
Do not be quick with your mouth, and do not let your heart hurry to bring out a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words be few.
For a dream comes with much busyness, and the voice of a fool with many words.
When you make a vow to God, do not delay to fulfill it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Fulfill what you vow.
It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill it.
Do not let your mouth make your flesh sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?
For when dreams are many, so are vapors and words. But fear God.

If you see the poor oppressed, and justice and righteousness robbed in the province, do not be amazed at the matter, for one high official is watched by a higher one, and there are higher ones over them.
But the gain of a land in every way is this: a king for the cultivated field.
Whoever loves money will never be satisfied with money, and whoever loves wealth will never be satisfied with income. This too is vapor.
When good things increase, those who eat them increase. And what advantage is there to their owner, except to see them with his eyes?
Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich will not let him sleep.
There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: riches kept by their owner to his harm.
Those riches are lost in some bad venture, and he has fathered a son, but there is nothing in his hand.
As he came from his mother's womb, so he will go again, naked as he came. He will take nothing for his toil that he can carry in his hand.
This too is a grievous evil: exactly as he came, so he will go. And what gain does he have, who toils for the wind?
All his days, too, he eats in darkness, with much grief, sickness and anger.

Look, this is what I have seen to be good and fitting: to eat and drink and enjoy all the toil at which one toils under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him, for this is his portion.
Also, whenever God gives anyone riches and possessions, and enables him to eat from them, to accept his portion and to rejoice in his toil, this is the gift of God.
For he will not dwell much on the days of his life, because God keeps him busy with the joy of his heart.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on human beings:

a man to whom God gives riches, possessions and honor, so that he lacks nothing he desires, yet God does not give him the power to eat from them, but a stranger eats them. This is vapor and a grievous sickness.

If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, however many the days of his years may be, if he is not satisfied with good things, and he has no burial either, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.
For it comes in vapor and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered.
It has not even seen the sun or known anything, yet it has more rest than he.
Even if he lived a thousand years twice over, but did not enjoy good things, do not all go to one place?
All the toil of human beings is for their mouth, yet the appetite is never filled.
For what advantage does the wise have over the fool? What does the poor person gain by knowing how to conduct himself before the living?
Better is what the eyes see than the wandering of desire. This too is vapor and chasing the wind.
Whatever exists has already been named, and it is known what a human being is: he cannot contend with one who is stronger than he.
The more words, the more vapor; and what advantage is that to anyone?
For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the few days of his life of vapor, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell anyone what will happen after him under the sun?
A good name is better than good oil, and the day of death than the day of one's birth.
It is better to go to a house of mourning than to go to a house of feasting, for that is the end of every person, and the living will take it to heart.
Grief is better than laughter, for when the face is sad the heart may be glad.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure.
It is better to listen to the rebuke of the wise than to listen to the song of fools.
For like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This too is vapor.
Surely oppression makes the wise foolish, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
Better is the end of a thing than its beginning; better a patient spirit than a proud spirit.
Do not be quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the lap of fools.
Do not say, "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not from wisdom that you ask about this.
Wisdom is good with an inheritance, and an advantage to those who see the sun.
For to be in the shade of wisdom is to be in the shade of money, and the advantage of knowledge is this: wisdom gives life to those who have it.
Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked?
In the day of prosperity, be glad, and in the day of adversity, consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that no one can find out anything that will come after him.
In my days of vapor I have seen everything: there is a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked person who lives long in his wickedness.
Do not be too righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why destroy yourself?
Do not be too wicked, and do not be a fool. Why die before your time?
It is good that you should take hold of the one and not let go of the other, for whoever fears God will come through with both.
Wisdom makes the wise stronger than ten rulers in a city.
Surely there is no one on earth so righteous that he does good and never sins.
Also, do not take to heart all the things that people say, or you may hear your servant cursing you.
For your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others.
All this I tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me.
What exists is far off, and deep, very deep. Who can find it out?
I turned, I and my heart, to know and to explore and to seek wisdom and the sum of things, and to know that wickedness is folly and that foolishness is madness.
And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net and whose hands are chains. The one who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is caught by her.
"See, this is what I have found," says the Teacher, "adding one thing to another to find the sum,
which my soul still seeks but I have not found: one man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found.
Only see, this I have found: that God made human beings upright, but they have sought out many schemes."
Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A person's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
I say: Keep the king's command, because of the oath before God.
Do not be in a hurry to leave his presence. Do not persist in an evil matter, for he does whatever he pleases.
For the king's word is power, and who can say to him, "What are you doing?"
Whoever keeps a command will know no harm, and a wise heart knows the time and the way.
For there is a time and a way for every matter, though a person's trouble lies heavy on him.
For he does not know what will happen, and who can tell him how it will happen?
No one has power over the wind to hold back the wind, and no one has power over the day of death. There is no discharge in war, and wickedness will not save those who practice it.
All this I have seen, as I set my heart on every deed that is done under the sun, at a time when one person has power over another to his harm.
And then I saw the wicked buried. They used to come and go from the holy place, and they were forgotten in the city where they had done such things. This too is vapor.
Because the sentence against an evil deed is not carried out quickly, the hearts of human beings are fully set on doing evil.
Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and lives long, yet I also know that it will be well with those who fear God, who fear before him.
But it will not be well with the wicked, and he will not lengthen his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.

There is a vapor that occurs on earth: there are righteous people who are treated as the deeds of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked people who are treated as the deeds of the righteous deserve. I said that this too is vapor.

So I commended joy, because there is nothing better for a person under the sun than to eat and drink and be glad. That will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.
When I set my heart to know wisdom and to see the task that is done on earth (for neither by day nor by night do one's eyes see sleep),

then I saw all the work of God: that no one can find out the work that is done under the sun. However much a person toils to seek it, he will not find it; and even if a wise person claims to know it, he cannot find it out.

All this I took to heart, and I sought to make all this clear: that the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, no one knows; everything lies before them.

Everything is the same for everyone: one fate comes to the righteous and the wicked, to the good, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who offers sacrifices and the one who does not. As it is with the good, so it is with the sinner; as it is with the one who swears an oath, so it is with the one who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: that one fate comes to all. The hearts of human beings are full of evil, too, and there is madness in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
But whoever is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing at all. They have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten.
Their love and their hatred and their envy have already perished, and they will never again have a portion in anything that is done under the sun.
Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a glad heart, for God has already approved what you do.
Let your clothes always be white, and let your head never lack oil.

Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your life of vapor that he has given you under the sun, all your days of vapor. For that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your strength, for there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, where you are going.

Again I saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to the skilled, for time and chance happen to them all.
For no one knows his time. Like fish caught in a cruel net, and like birds caught in a snare, so human beings are trapped at an evil time, when it falls on them suddenly.
This too I saw as wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me.
There was a small city with few people in it, and a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built great siegeworks against it.
Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he saved the city by his wisdom. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
So I said, "Wisdom is better than strength, but the poor man's wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard."
The words of the wise, heard in quiet, are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
Dead flies make the perfumer's oil stink and ferment; a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
The heart of the wise is at his right hand, but the heart of the fool at his left.
Even when a fool walks along the road, he lacks sense, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.
If the ruler's anger rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, like a mistake that comes from the ruler:
folly is set in many high places, while the rich sit in low places.
I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking on foot like servants.
Whoever digs a pit may fall into it, and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
Whoever quarries stones may be hurt by them, and whoever splits logs may be endangered by them.
If the iron is blunt and one does not sharpen its edge, he must use more strength; but wisdom has the advantage of bringing success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no gain for the charmer.
The words of a wise person's mouth win favor, but the lips of a fool swallow him up.
The words of his mouth begin in folly, and his talk ends in evil madness.
The fool multiplies words, though no one knows what will happen; and what will come after him, who can tell him?
The toil of fools wears them out, for they do not even know the way to the city.
Woe to you, O land, whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning!
Happy are you, O land, whose king is the son of nobles, and whose princes eat at the proper time, for strength and not for drunkenness!
Through laziness the roof sinks in, and through idle hands the house leaks.
For laughter they make a feast, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
Even in your thoughts do not curse the king, and in your bedroom do not curse the rich, for a bird of the air may carry your voice, and a winged creature may tell the matter.
Send your bread out on the surface of the waters, for after many days you will find it.
Give a portion to seven, and even to eight, for you do not know what disaster may come upon the earth.
If the clouds are full, they pour out rain on the earth; and whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will lie.
Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever looks at the clouds will not reap.
Just as you do not know the way of the wind, or how the bones are formed in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the work of God, who makes everything.
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.
Light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
For if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. All that comes is vapor.

Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
Remove grief from your heart, and put away trouble from your body, for youth and the prime of life are vapor.
Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of trouble come and the years draw near when you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";
before the sun and the light, the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;
in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the women who grind stop because they are few, and those who look through the windows grow dim;
when the doors to the street are shut, as the sound of the mill grows low, and one rises at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low;

when people are afraid of what is high, and terrors are on the road; when the almond tree blossoms, and the grasshopper drags itself along, and the caper berry fails; for a person is going to his eternal home, and the mourners go about in the street;
before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is broken, and the jar is shattered at the spring, and the wheel is broken at the cistern;
and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
"Vapor of vapors," says the Teacher, "everything is vapor."
Besides being wise, the Teacher also taught the people knowledge. He weighed, searched out and arranged many proverbs.
The Teacher sought to find pleasing words, and to write words of truth correctly.
The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one shepherd.
Beyond these, my son, be warned. Of making many books there is no end, and much study wearies the body.
The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commands, for this is the whole of a human being.
For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether good or evil.
The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine.
Your oils have a pleasing fragrance; your name is oil poured out. That is why the young women love you.
Draw me after you; let us run! The king has brought me into his rooms. We will rejoice and be glad in you; we will praise your love more than wine. How rightly they love you!
I am dark, and lovely, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.
Do not stare at me because I am dark, because the sun has gazed on me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keep the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept.
Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where do you pasture your flock? Where do you make it lie down at noon? For why should I be like a woman who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions?
If you do not know, most beautiful of women, follow the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.
To a mare among Pharaoh's chariots I compare you, my darling.
Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of beads.
We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.
While the king was at his couch, my nard gave out its fragrance.
My beloved is to me a pouch of myrrh that lies between my breasts.
My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi.
How beautiful you are, my darling! How beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves.
How handsome you are, my beloved, how delightful! Our bed is green with leaves.
The beams of our house are cedars, our rafters are junipers.
I am a crocus of Sharon, a lily of the valleys.
Like a lily among thorns, so is my darling among the young women.
Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men. In his shade I delighted to sit, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.
He brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me was love.
Sustain me with raisin cakes, refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or by the does of the field: do not stir up or awaken love until it is ready.
Listen! My beloved! Look, here he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.
My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Look, there he stands behind our wall, gazing in through the windows, peering through the lattice.
My beloved spoke and said to me, "Arise, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away.
For look, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.
The blossoms have appeared in the land; the time of pruning has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.
The fig tree ripens its early figs, and the vines in blossom give out their fragrance. Arise, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away."
My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding places of the cliff, let me see your form, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your form is lovely.
Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom.
My beloved is mine and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.
Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the cleft mountains.
On my bed, night after night, I sought the one my soul loves; I sought him, but did not find him.
I will get up now and go around the city, through the streets and through the squares; I will seek the one my soul loves. I sought him, but did not find him.
The watchmen found me as they went around the city. "Have you seen the one my soul loves?"
Scarcely had I passed them when I found the one my soul loves. I held him and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, into the room of the one who conceived me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or by the does of the field: do not stir up or awaken love until it is ready.
Who is this coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of the merchant?
Look, it is Solomon's couch! Sixty warriors surround it, from the warriors of Israel.
All of them hold swords and are trained in battle, each with his sword at his side, against the terrors of the night.
King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon.
He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its inside was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.
Go out and look, daughters of Zion, at King Solomon, at the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of his heart's joy.
How beautiful you are, my darling! How beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Mount Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young.
Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your temples are like a slice of pomegranate behind your veil.
Your neck is like the tower of David, built in courses, on which hang a thousand shields, all the shields of warriors.
Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.
Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.
You are altogether beautiful, my darling; there is no flaw in you.
Come with me from Lebanon, my bride, come with me from Lebanon. Look down from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.
You have stolen my heart, my sister, my bride; you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklace.
How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than any spice!
Your lips drip honey from the comb, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon.
A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a pool locked, a fountain sealed.
Your shoots are a park of pomegranates with choice fruits, henna with nard,
nard and saffron, cane and cinnamon, with every kind of incense tree, myrrh and aloes, with all the finest spices.
You are a fountain in the gardens, a well of living water, streams flowing down from Lebanon.
Awake, north wind, and come, south wind! Blow on my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come into his garden and eat its choice fruits.

I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice, I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!
I was asleep, but my heart was awake. Listen! My beloved is knocking. "Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is wet with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."
I have taken off my robe; how could I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how could I soil them?
My beloved put his hand in through the opening, and my heart trembled for him.
I rose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with flowing myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.
I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul went out when he spoke. I sought him, but did not find him; I called him, but he did not answer me.
The watchmen found me as they went around the city. They struck me, they wounded me; they took my shawl from me, those watchmen of the walls.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am sick with love.
What is your beloved more than any other beloved, most beautiful of women? What is your beloved more than any other beloved, that you make us swear like this?
My beloved is radiant and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand.
His head is the finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven.
His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting by brimming pools.
His cheeks are like beds of spices, towers of perfume. His lips are lilies, dripping with flowing myrrh.
His arms are rods of gold set with jewels of Tarshish. His body is polished ivory, covered with sapphires.
His legs are pillars of alabaster, set on bases of fine gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
His mouth is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.
Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful of women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.
You are beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awe-inspiring as armies with banners.
Turn your eyes away from me, for they overwhelm me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young.
Your temples are like a slice of pomegranate behind your veil.
There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young women without number.

But my dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, the favorite of the one who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines saw her and praised her:
Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awe-inspiring as armies with banners?
